articles.title: Michael Wynne, Fired as SECAF Alongside CSAF Moseley, Dead at 82
articles.body:
Michael Wynne, the 21st Secretary of the Air Force died Oct. 17. He was 82 years old.
Wynne was Secretary from 2005 to 2008, a stretch of time when the U.S. military was struggling to quell insurgencies in Iraq and Afghanistan and the Army was struggling to simultaneously man occupation forces in two theaters. Roadside bombs and insurgent attacks were killing U.S. troops, and the Air Force was under intense pressure to support its sister service with increased intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance coverage and manpower and force cuts to ease the Army’s burden.
The Air Force was also fighting to protect its modernization efforts at the time, especially the F-22 Raptor program, which was less than halfway to its objective of 750 planes, new tankers (which would ultimately become the KC-46), and a future bomber (which would eventually yield the B-21).
In 2006, an Air Force B-52 took off from Minot Air Force Base, N.D., and flew to Barksdale Air Force Base, La., its crew unknowingly carrying nuclear weapons on board, a so-called “bent spear” incident. The discovery kicked off an investigation, recriminations, self-examination, and subsequent organizational, procedural, and cultural changes across the nuclear community.
The incident added to the tension between the Air Force and then-Secretary of Defense Robert Gates, who saw the service and particularly then-Chief of Staff Gen. T. Michael “Buzz” Moseley as recalcitrant in their pushback over budget, manning, and modernization. Seeing Wynne and Moseley as a close knit tandem, Gates fired both in June 2008, beheading the service—the first-ever simultaneous removal of a service chief and secretary.
Military Roots
Wynne hailed from a military family and followed his father’s footsteps to attend the U.S. Military Academy at West Point, graduating at the height of the Vietnam War. Among his 578 classmates, 30 died in Vietnam and about 100 others were wounded in fighting in Southeast Asia.
Instead of joining the Army, however, Wynne followed his older brother into the Air Force, reporting for Active Duty in August 1966.
“The day I reported for Active Duty, the report of my brother being shot down was announced,” Wynn recalled in a 2005 interview with the Washington Post. Maj. Patrick Wynne, a 1963 graduate of the U.S. Air Force Academy, had trained as a pilot, and was assigned to the 555th Tactical Fighter Squadron in Thailand. After only four months in country, his F-4C Phantom was shot down over Vietnam on Aug. 8, 1966. He was declared missing in action, and remained so until 1977, when his remains were identified and later returned to the United States. He is buried at the Air Force Academy.
The younger Wynne served seven years in the Air Force, his final tour as an assistant professor of astronautics at the Air Force Academy.
Wynne then went to work for General Dynamics. For the next 26 years, he worked as an executive there, save for a three-year stint with Lockheed Martin after Lockheed acquired GD’s Space Systems Division. His work during in those years spanned General Dynamics’ F-16 and M1A2 tank divisions as well as space systems, including work on the Atlas, Titan, and Centaur launch vehicles.
In 2001, Wynne joined Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld’s Pentagon leadership team. Following the election of President George W. Bush, Wynne was confirmed as Principal Deputy Undersecretary of Defense for Acquisition, Technology, and Logistics, the start of a seven-year run in public service. In 2003, he was made Acting Undersecretary and he remained in that role until June 2005. Among his tasks at the time were leading the Pentagon’s preparations for the 2005 Base Realignment and Closure plan, which sought to “rationalize” the Defense Department’s far-flung bases and increase cross-service cooperation.
The 2005 BRAC results proved disappointing. Projected to save the Pentagon more than $25 billion annually by 2011, the plans failed to deliver due to higher-than anticipated construction costs, inflation, and incorrect assumptions. Instead of savings, the changes yielded a net cost increase, even when spread out over 20 years.
As Air Force Secretary, Wynne opposed efforts to consolidate and adopt joint basing, having come to embrace the Air Force’s explanation that many of its units operate and fight from their home bases rather than deploy to forward theaters.
“The Air Force has a very different concept of operations,” he would tell Air Force Magazine in 2008, weeks after his departure. Putting Air Force bases under the control of other services would undermine combat effectiveness, he said, adding, “I’d probably get fired again over my objection to the way the joint basing is happening.”
More than that, Wynne was a visionary, said Richard Andres, a professor at the National War College worked with Wynne in government. Wynne’s ideas presaged numerous future defense initiatives, Andres said: “His vision of linking sensors and weapons across military domains anticipated today’s Joint All-Domain Command and Control. He was first to champion cyberspace as a warfighting domain and brought data transparency and decision dashboards into Air Force management. He understood early that America’s military advantage would depend as much on connecting information and people as on building superior weapons.”
Wynne also butted heads with Gates over the F-22. While Gates suggested the Air Force could give up the “exquisite” F-22 because the then-fledgling F-35 was scheduled to join the fleet in 2014, Wynne disagreed.
“The notion of the F-22 [is] … similar to the F-35—we need to get rid of that,” Wynne said in his 2008 debrief with Air Force Magazine. The F-35, rather, “complements the F-22, but the F-22 is clearly an air superiority and air dominance weapon. The F-35 is a multinational, multirole, [air-to-ground] versatile airplane.”
When Gates dismissed concerns about future conflict as “next-war-itis,” Wynne didn’t give in. “He was willing to put his position on the line. He understood that the demands of the wars we were fighting could not excuse neglecting the wars we might have to fight next.”
In the months leading up to his dismissal, Wynne and Andres spoke weekly, including about the possibility that Gates would fire him, Andres recalled. “He understood the risk,” Andres said. “He cared more about what the nation needed than about keeping his job.”
Gates took over as Secretary about a year after Wynne had been moved to the Air Force. At the time, USAF was bearing a heavy burden for the Army. In a 2006 C-SPAN interview, Wynne tried to justify a planned cut of 40,000 Airman, suggesting that technological advancement made it possible to do “trimming in advance of new systems coming on and planning for the future right now.” But he acknowledged that having 5,000 Airmen doing Army jobs in Iraq was not sustainable.
“At some point in the future, it doesn’t work in the math—the Army has to pick up combat service support,” he said.
The Air Force’s pursuit of a new tanker aircraft, a protracted and contentious effort that preceded him and would continue to drag on for years, was another challenge during Wynne’s tenure. As Secretary, he pressed for a single tanker aircraft rather than splitting the order between Boeing and Airbus platforms, as some urged. But after departing the Pentagon, he reconsidered, seeing value in it. He also came to regret not requiring that tankers become network nodes, an extra role for which they might have been well-suited.
And while many in the Pentagon failed to appreciate the Air Force’s contributions to the war in Iraq, Wynne became a strong advocate, noting that the 2007 “surge” of forces in Iraq was not merely an Army ground operation. “We surged 400 percent in the number of sorties and 1,000 percent in the pounds of ordnance dropped,” he said in a press conference on his final day in office. “What happened? I would tell you that what happened was the realization that we could get connectivity between the ground commanders and the air component—that there was true situational awareness available.”
Still, on June 5, 2008, Gates decided he wasn’t getting what he wanted out of Air Force leadership. Wynne and Moseley were en route to a Corona meeting of Air Force leaders at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio, when Gates dropped the bombshell, dismissing both.
The stated reason was the failures of Air Force leadership to safely steward the security of nuclear weapons, but it was no secret Gates and the Air Force were at odds on a range of issues, and few believed the public explanation. From the number of “orbits” flown by surveillance drones over Iraq and Afghanistan to support troops operating on the ground to Gates objections to “next-war-itis” and the Air Force’s focus on high-end stealth fighters and the threats of a rising China in the Pacific, the two sides were out of sync.
Moseley, in an interview, recalled his close working relationship with Wynne as “a privilege and a gift.” The two tried to meet daily and they shared a perspective both in terms of their duty and vision for the service. They also became friends.
“Mike Wynne and I had the best relationship of any that I’ve seen with 13-plus secretaries I worked with,” Moseley said. Wynne was well versed in the workings of the Pentagon hierarchy, the needs of each of the services, and how to get things done, the former chief said. “But he also understood the theater logistics, the technology to address the new world, and he understood the acquisition process better than anybody.”
Together, they worked to lay out and explain their priorities, the need for increased resources—estimated then to be $20 billion annually to modernize, in order:
- Tankers
- Search and rescue
- Satellites that could be protected from cyber and maneuver attack
- F-35s to replace the F-16
- A new bomber
They laid out that plan shortly before the firing in a Pentagon meeting with Gates and other officials. Mosely recalled that afterward Wynne declared the presentation a success.
“I think that meeting went well,” Wynne told him, draping an arm around Moseley’s shoulder as they walked the Pentagon hallway. “But I think we’re both dead.”
Wynne may have been the only one who saw it coming.
When the decision came down to fire them, both were at Scott Air Force Base, en route to Dayton for a planned Corona meeting of Air Force leadership at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio. Moseley was ordered back to Washington, where Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Adm. Mike Mullen delivered the news. In Dayton, Wynne was told to stand by for an unscheduled visit from Deputy Secretary of Defense Gordon England, who was flying in. No reason was given. Was England coming to discuss Moseley’s successor, someone wondered. “No,” Wynne said. “He’s coming for me.”
As the Corona meeting unfolded, Moseley called Wynne from Washington to say he was being relieved. Reporters began to call before England even arrived, adding to Wynne’s convictions. CNN might have been first to report the firings. Defense News Editor Vago Muradian, a rare press gallery guest at the Corona gathering, got his story out online on Defense News and Air Force Times. At the Pentagon, frustrated reporters gathered outside the press secretary’s office looking for answers; inside, staff was still trying to piece together what happened.
Two weeks later, Wynne departed the Pentagon at an official ceremony presided over by Gates, with Moseley at his side. What had been a very public firing was glossed over for public consumption as Gates pinned a medal on Wynne’s chest. Having Gates preside was Wynne’s idea, said retired Maj. Gen. Daryl Burke, Wynne’s military aide at the time. It was a challenge: Gates would either have to refuse or honor Wynne for his public service.
At the ceremony, Wynne expressed love for the service. “But it is the people of the Air Force that make the Air Force,” he added, “so in loving the Air Force, we love the people.”
Burke recalled how Wynne advised him to stand away as they awaited England’s arrival. Burke insisted he would stand with Wynne regardless, but Wynne was trying to ensure that Burke wouldn’t be damaged by association in the future by being seen as too closely associated with a politically unpopular boss. Wynne subsequently worked behind the scenes to find Burke a next assignment that would keep his career on track. In doing so, Wynne demonstrated both caring for his Airman and a savvy hand on the tiller for navigating Pentagon politics.
Lt. Gen. David Deptula, now dean of AFA’s Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, was on the Air Staff at the time, recalling that Wynne kept working on the issues he believed in up to the very end—in particular, his opposition to joint basing.
“Secretary Wynne was a leader of uncommon integrity, genuine kindness, and extraordinary loyalty,” Deptula said. “He never confused holding a position of authority with the responsibility to do what was right. I witnessed his character firsthand when, even after learning he would be removed as Secretary of the Air Force, he continued working tirelessly to strengthen the service he loved. He put principle above position, loyalty above personal ambition, and the nation’s security above all else. In a famous action, when SECDEF Gates told Secretary Wynne to fire Chief of Staff, Buzz Moseley… Wynne refused. So, Gates fired both. The Air Force and our nation are better for his service, and I am better for having known him. He will be greatly missed.”
Robbin Laird, a military analyst and prolific writer who worked for Wynne during his Pentagon tenure, wrote admiringly of the former secretary in a remembrance, citing what he called the Wynne Doctrine: “If you are ever involved in a fair fight, it is the result of poor planning.”
“It is easy to hear it as swagger. It was the opposite,” Laird wrote. “A fair fight is one whose outcome is in doubt. When the outcome is in doubt, young Americans pay for that doubt with their lives. Mike believed a leader’s first duty was to make sure it never happens. That meant technology, organization, the unglamorous work of logistics and sustainment, and the discipline to think years ahead of the adversary.”
Michael Walter Wynne was born in Clearwater, Fla. He is survived by his wife Barbara and four married daughters.

articles.title: Exclusive: Leaked trove reveals extent of far-right AfD’s efforts to court Trump and Maga allies
articles.body:
A data leak from Germany’s far-right German Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has revealed the extent of efforts by the party to court Donald Trump and other leading figures in the Maga movement, stretching back more than a decade.
The trove reveals the pains the AfD took in wooing the president, whom they saw from the beginning as a potential ally, with senior party officials agonising over the wording of an obsequious congratulatory telegram when he was elected in 2016, which included the wish that his “hopes as a person be fulfilled”.
The AfD became a home for anti-immigration voters after 1.2 million refugees arrived in Germany in 2015 and 2016. It entered the Bundestag, Germany’s parliament, in 2017 with 12.6% of the vote, came second in the February 2025 federal election with 20.8%, and now leads national polls at about 30%. In September it won 43.8% of the vote in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, and it is now trying to form Germany’s first far-right state government since the second world war.
Trump hailed the win in Saxony-Anhalt in a post on his Truth Social, concluding his message with a German version of his Make America Great Again acronym, “MGGA!!!”
Germany’s domestic intelligence agency monitors the party as a suspected rightwing extremist organisation, and state agencies classify five of its regional branches as confirmed extremist.
Its leader in the central Thuringia region, Björn Höcke, was convicted in 2024 of knowingly using a slogan of the SA, the Nazi party’s paramilitary wing. AfD politicians also attended a meeting with extremists at which a mass-deportation “masterplan” was discussed. Its 2025 election programme calls for lifting sanctions on Russia and repairing the Nord Stream gas pipelines programme. Nearly all of Germany’s other parties have kept a “firewall”, refusing to govern with it.
Media outlets including the Guardian have reported on the apparently friendly contacts between the party and the US state department during Trump’s second term.
The leaked documents show AfD officials quickly moving to requests for support from the White House on policy issues when he first won the 2016 election.
Others show a burgeoning political courtship between senior figures including the AfD’s now leader Alice Weidel and key Trump ideologue Steve Bannon.
The data, provided to reporters by the transparency organisation Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets), covers more than 420,000 emails, along with documents and personnel records, from the party’s foundation in 2013 to the present, with most coming before 2019.
The AfD said in a statement on Monday that a hosting provider used by the party had been attacked at the end of September and that “only a few mailboxes” had been copied. It told the news agency dpa that most of those mailboxes had not been used for years, and party sources were quoted as saying the published material appeared to be authentic.
The cable
AfD figures praised Trump ahead of his first election in 2016, with then leader Frauke Petry calling him a “refreshingly alternative proposition” in the spring of 2016. On the day after Trump won the presidency, Petry said the victory was “encouraging for Germany and for Europe”.
The hacked documents reveal that in the wake of his election, the party scrambled to send an ingratiating telegram to the new president.
Mainstream German politicians greeted Trump’s election with skepticism. On 9 November 2016, then chancellor Angela Merkel offered Trump “close cooperation” only “on the basis of … values” including respect for human dignity “regardless of origin, skin colour, religion, gender, sexual orientation or political views”. The then defence minister Ursula von der Leyen called the result a “huge shock”. The next day the vice-chancellor, Sigmar Gabriel, reportedly called Trump the “forerunner of a new authoritarian and chauvinist international”, and he counted the AfD among its forces.
On 10 November, Petry emailed the party’s federal board proposing “an official and brief congratulatory telegram to the future US president”. German politics, she wrote, was “once again outdoing itself in politically unacceptable behaviour”; the AfD was “already perceived as the ones who don’t join in the majority howl of the political establishment” and, “as the only German party welcoming a new beginning in the US”, should say so officially.
Eleven of the board’s 13 members replied, all in favour. Current leader Weidel wrote “Yes:-)”. Beatrix von Storch, now deputy leader of the party’s Bundestag group, wrote: “Couldn’t be more of a yes.”
Board member Dirk Driesang added that Trump should also receive, “by post (?)”, the party’s manifesto in English.
The telegram went out on 11 November under Petry’s name, “on behalf of the federal board”, and was released to the press. It told the president-elect: “We are confident that you will readjust the transatlantic relationship and end the wars in Syria and Ukraine by mutual agreement with Russia.”
A second message, for the inauguration, was planned more carefully, and included a concrete request for a political favor. On 11 January 2017, Driesang asked for it to be put on the agenda of the board’s next conference call, “this time faster and better prepared”, and proposed adding a request: “Please support us in our efforts to remove the enemy-state clause from the UN charter.”
The “enemy state” clauses were written into the UN charter in 1945, and exempted action against “any state which during the second world war has been an enemy of any signatory” from the charter’s normal rules, so that the wartime allies could move against any “renewal of aggressive policy” by Germany, Japan or their allies. The general assembly declared them obsolete in 1995 and resolved to repeal them, but the text has never been amended, because changing the charter needs ratification by two-thirds of member states and all five permanent members of the security council.
No German party currently defends the clauses, but the Bundestag’s own research service wrote in 2017 that international lawyers unanimously regard the clauses as having no practical relevance. On the German right, however, the clauses are totemic, and viewed as a limitation on German sovereignty. The AfD’s Bundestag group demanded its deletion in a 2020 motion that called it a “relic of the past” which “indirectly designates Germany an ‘enemy state’”, and every other party voted it down.
AfD’s federal board adopted the enemy state request on its call of 16 January, according to the federal office’s record of the decision contained in the leaked documents.
When the office circulated an English draft on 19 January, Georg Pazderski, then the party’s Berlin leader and a member of its federal board, objected to the tone and to the request for support: “You don’t address the president as Mr Trump, he is Mr President. Otherwise a bit wordy and flowery. I stand by it: the enemy-state clause doesn’t belong in this letter at all. You don’t do that in a letter of congratulation. It looks like a begging letter.”
Driesang replied at 6.16 the next morning: “Personally I of course find the style appropriate, otherwise I wouldn’t have written it that way.”
The office also wanted to know how the telegram should reach Trump: “directly to Trump’s campaign team … or through official diplomatic channels (e.g. the US embassy in Berlin)?”
André Poggenburg, then the party’s leader in Saxony-Anhalt, answered: “all available channels.”
The text released on the afternoon of 20 January, signed by Petry and her then co-leader Jörg Meuthen, kept the request. It told Trump that the clause stood in Germany’s way “as a strange anachronism”, and asked him to see the AfD “as natural allies at your side, because we are the only German party in clear opposition to the wrong policies of Chancellor Merkel”. The Guardian reported the telegram’s wording the next day.
Frauke Petry subsequently left the party in 2017 in the wake of a bitter internal power struggle.Meuthen, Pazderski and Driesgan have also left the party.
Frohnmaier and the embassy
Markus Frohnmaier entered the Bundestag in 2017 and is now a deputy leader of the AfD’s parliamentary group and a member of the foreign affairs committee. Before that he led the party’s youth wing, the Junge Alternative. At a rally in Erfurt in October 2015 he told the crowd: “I say to these leftwing thought-terrorists, this party cartel, quite clearly: when we come, there will be a clear-out, there will be a mucking-out!”
Germany’s domestic intelligence agency classed the Junge Alternative as “confirmed extremist” in 2023. The Junge Alternative dissolved in March 2025, and a successor organisation, Generation Deutschland, was founded in November 2025.
In April 2019 the BBC and several European partner outlets reported on documents emailed in 2017 by Petr Premyak, a Duma staffer and former naval counterintelligence officer, to a senior official in Vladimir Putin’s administration in 2017 proposing support for Frohnmaier’s candidacy, with the assessment: “We will have our own absolutely controlled MP in the Bundestag.”
Frohnmaier’s lawyers said he “was never under the control of any third party”, and he told the BBC the documents were fake.
Five weeks after those reports, on 13 May 2019, his parliamentary assistant wrote to a Gmail address in the name of Daniel Pipes, the founder of the Middle East Forum (MEF).
The US civil rights organization the Southern Poverty Law Center writes of Pipes that he has “spent the better part of three decades actively promoting anti-Muslim rhetoric”, and has reported his argument that western leaders should consider “working with” far-right parties such as Austria’s Freedom party, “not marginalizing it”. Pipes had met Frohnmaier in Berlin two months earlier, on a tour of what he calls Europe’s “civilizationist” parties; the far-right site PI-NEWS published a photograph of the two.
The email thanked “Dr Pipes” for sending his interview with the rightwing weekly Junge Freiheit, then came to the point: “On behalf of Mr Frohnmaier I should also contact you with the request to arrange a contact in the US Embassy. Mr Frohnmaier would like to meet the Ambassador in person or the Head of the Department of Economic Cooperation and Development Policy.”
The ambassador was Richard Grenell, who had told the rightwing news outlet Breitbart within weeks of taking up the post in 2018: “I absolutely want to empower other conservatives throughout Europe, other leaders.” Grenell, whose praise in the same interview for Austria’s rightwing politician Sebastian Kurz as a “rock star” prompted calls from German politicians for his expulsion. Grenell went on to serve as Trump’s acting director of national intelligence in 2020 despite having no background in intelligence, to front the evidence-free claims of “illegal votes” in Nevada two days after the 2020 election, and, in Trump’s second term, to run the Kennedy Center through its renaming as the Trump Kennedy Center, until he stepped down in March.
The archive holds no reply from the Pipes address and no record of a meeting.
Responding to a request for comment, Pipes wrote in an email: “I received that request. I did not pass the request to anyone at the US Embassy in Berlin. If Markus Frohnmaier had a meeting there, it took place without my involvement. I do not recall Mr Frohnmaier among the many politicians I met on that trip. I show no subsequent contact with him after 13 May 2019.”
Pipes added: “The Southern Poverty Law Center distorts my views, which can be summed up by my well-known adage: ‘Radical Islam is the problem, moderate Islam is the solution.’ I oppose Islamism and Islamists, not Islam and Muslims … Representing my views and work otherwise is a calumny.”
Pipes concluded: “In 2019 in Berlin, I constantly argued with AfD members and leaders, encouraging them to adopt an anti-Islamist rather than an anti-Islamic outlook, without success. Indeed, I made that point in the Junge Freiheit interview you referenced.”
Two months earlier the same office had approached Breitbart itself. On 12 March 2019 the assistant asked the Bundestag group’s press spokesman whether he happened to have “a contact at Breitbart”, then wrote to the Breitbart reporter Chris Tomlinson, describing his boss as a “young star” of the party and an expert on the UN’s “2030 Agenda” and Global Compact for Migration: “Are you maybe interested in doing an interview with Mr Frohnmaier for Breitbart about these topics and the situation in Germany?” No reply is in the archive.
There is no evidence that this pitch was successful, and no mentions of Frohnmaier on Breitbart outside quotes in a story the previous year about anti-immigrant riots in the German city of Chemnitz.
In an email replying to a request for comment, Frohnmaier wrote: “Regarding the correspondence you refer to, it must first be noted that we have so far had no opportunity to independently verify its authenticity and completeness. This applies all the more given that, according to the information available to us, the documents were obtained unlawfully.”
He added: “The contacts you refer to are to be seen in the context of the usual cultivation of international political contacts. Exchanges with international interlocutors are part of everyday political work and are, in themselves, nothing out of the ordinary. As a matter of principle, we do not comment further publicly on internal matters.”
‘We came to listen’
A year earlier the AfD’s Bundestag group had announced its first contacts with the Trump administration. A press release on 13 June 2018 said the group’s foreign affairs spokesman, Armin-Paulus Hampel, and Jens Kestner, a member of the defence committee, had travelled to the US “to inform themselves about the state of German-American relations”.
“We came to listen,” Hampel was quoted as saying in the release. “In talks at the state department, on Capitol Hill and at the Pentagon,” the release went on, “the two AfD politicians also set out the foreign-policy positions of the AfD Bundestag group.”
It named two of their interlocutors: Justin Stebbins, “security policy adviser to the influential senator Ron Johnson”, who it said “showed understanding” for the AfD’s position on Nato; and Ken Toko, “head of the ‘German desk’ in the state department”, who pressed Germany on defence spending. The Frankfurter Rundschau reported at the time that it was the group’s first official US trip and that the talks were at mid-level working level.
The AfD’s founding manifesto, adopted in 2016, says Nato membership serves Germany’s interests “insofar as Nato confines itself to its task as a defensive alliance” and calls for the withdrawal of all allied troops stationed in Germany, “and in particular their nuclear weapons”. Its 2025 manifesto keeps Nato membership only “until an independent and capable European military alliance has been built”, and rejects Nato’s eastward expansion. The 2025 manifesto also says that the party envisions Ukraine as a neutral state, aligned neither to Russia nor the west.
Steve Bannon
The most direct line into Trump’s circle was through Harris Media, a Texas digital firm that had worked for Republican senator Rand Paul, Marine Le Pen and Benjamin Netanyahu, and ran the AfD’s online campaign for the 2017 federal election, as Der Spiegel reported at the time.
On 28 February 2018 the firm’s founder, Vincent Harris, emailed Alice Weidel, by then the AfD’s co-leader in the Bundestag, to say he would be in Berlin in March and would “love to connect” about “the database for the party, and maximizing donations, and lead generation efforts”. Weidel replied the next day: “Sure! My office will get in touch with you. Btw. Do you have Steve Bannons cell phone number? I need to see him.”
Bannon, the former White House chief strategist, had left the post seven months earlier and had been forced out of Breitbart in January. On 3 March Harris wrote to both of them: “Alice, Per your email, wanted to introduce you to Steve Bannon. I believe you two will get along incredibly well, and share common vision and ideals.” He was, he added, “looking forward to seeing what you will cook up together”.
Bannon answered two minutes later from his BlackBerry, “Thanks vince”, and “Alice let me know when u can chat”. Weidel replied: “Steve, any time. I am in Berlin tomorrow, in Zurich Monday and Tuesday. Let me know.” Bannon: “I’m in zurich tuesday, wednesday”, and “Would love to meet”. Weidel: “Tuesday afternoon Zurich. When and where?” Bannon: “Perfect.”
The meeting was reported by the news agency dpa the same day, citing Weidel’s office, which said Bannon’s experience of political communication and alternative media had been of particular interest to her. What the emails add is who arranged it, and why. On 12 March Harris wrote to Weidel: “I am glad to see the other meeting went well!”
Three days later Thor Kunkel, the party’s campaign creative director, had a suggestion for Weidel. “Why not hire Bannon? For AfD-TV,” referring to the party’s in-house media organization. “Why not? The man is desperately looking for a job. I know this by chance from Dietrich Mateschitz,” name-checking the co-founder of Red Bull. Weidel forwarded it to her Bundestag office; the archive does not show that anything came of it.
By that summer the party was keeping its distance from the former White House aide in public. On 11 August 2018 Alexander Gauland, a former Christian Democrat who co-founded the AfD and was then one of its deputy leaders, told German newspapers that Weidel “had met once with Bannon” but that she saw no possibility of cooperating with him. The emails show what that looked like from inside: when CNN wrote to the AfD’s press office on 7 August asking about Bannon’s Movement foundation, and noting that “some other news outlets have been reporting that Ms Weidel met Mr Bannon in Switzerland in March”, Meuthen replied: “I will not give CNN an interview on that.” A week later the Bundestag group’s press office told every AfD MP that, “after consultation with the two parliamentary group leaders, we ask you politely to leave these requests unanswered”.
On 26 March 2019 Bannon told a press conference in Rome, at which he called Italy “the centre of the universe” because of Matteo Salvini, that he had met representatives of several parties there, including the AfD. When a Stuttgarter Zeitung correspondent asked the party who had met with Bannon, the federal office told the board it knew nothing about it. Pazderski, the party’s Berlin leader, complained of a “wild growth” in the party in foreign relations, and said that the board had to “put a stop to these will-o’-the-wisp self-promoters, because their completely uncoordinated ‘private diplomacy’ reflects negatively on the entire party”.
The second administration
The leaked mail thins out after 2019, but the party’s ongoing contacts with the second Trump administration appear through the public record and its politicians’ own newsletters.
On the eve of the January 2025 inauguration Von Storch, the party’s deputy leader and her husband Sven were at Trump’s “Make America Great Again Victory Rally” in Washington. She told her newsletter subscribers the next day, “together with many celebrities and Trump supporters”, and “met Steve Bannon and Donald Trump Jr there, among others”.
On 14 February the vice-president, JD Vance, met Weidel on the sidelines of the Munich security conference. On 23 February the AfD doubled its vote and became the largest opposition party in the Bundestag.
In September 2025, the New York Times reported that in April, Von Storch and the AfD politician Joachim Paul had met the state department official Samuel Samson in Washington. “They took a lot of notes,” Paul said.
On 1 October Darren Beattie, then the acting under-secretary of state for public diplomacy, posted that he had met Frohnmaier and a second AfD MP, Jan Wenzel Schmidt, “to discuss U.S.-Germany relations, as well as shared priorities on cultural exchange and migration”. Beattie was fired as a White House speechwriter in 2018 after it emerged he had spoken on a panel with the white nationalist Peter Brimelow. On 13 December his successor, Sarah B Rogers, met Frohnmaier too; Frohnmaier posted on X that the exchange had “made clear that Washington is looking for a strong German partner that is ready to take on responsibility”.
The Guardian reported in February that Rogers, asked about the 2019 Russian documents, which argued for supporting his candidacy in the 2017 German election, said she had “sought guidance within the state department and determined” that the allegation was “unsubstantiated – and in any event, not a bar to a meeting”.
In an emailed response to a request for comment on the meeting, Rogers wrote “Mr Frohnmaier is the foreign policy spokesman for the most popular political party in Germany. He delivers AfD’s foreign policy positions in the Bundestag, and is the person German media call when they want a policy statement from AfD. For this reason, we talk to him in his official capacity to understand AfD’s positions.”
Rogers added: “During the ‘cancel culture’ era, there was a manic focus on reputational contagion that probably hurt American civic life, and is a poor fit for American diplomacy.”

articles.title: Denmark to buy cheap U.S. cruise missile built in Germany
articles.body:
- Denmark will buy Covenant’s ground-launched Anthem cruise missiles, to be built in Leipzig, Germany, alongside Kongsberg Joint Strike Missiles for its F-35s.
- Germany’s defense ministry is also in talks with Covenant as the Bundeswehr evaluates low-cost cruise missiles for its own long-range strike needs.
Denmark will buy Anthem ground-launched cruise missiles from U.S. defense company Covenant Industries, giving the Danish military its first land-based option for striking targets deep inside enemy territory, the Danish Ministry of Defense announced on Oct. 22, 2026.
The ministry said the purchase is meant to strengthen Denmark’s national and collective deterrence, describing the new missiles as long-range precision weapons that NATO has asked allies to provide. They use advanced navigation to hit targets accurately over long distances and can both deter an attack and strike back deep inside an enemy’s territory if necessary, and the acquisitions follow a recommendation from Denmark’s chief of defense.
“The acquisitions are a significant step in making Denmark better able to defend itself and carry our share of the burden in NATO, and at the same time we are sending a strong signal that we have the ability to strike back,” said Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus, in remarks translated from Danish.
Officials told reporters at the announcement that the contracts have already been signed, but withheld quantities, prices and delivery dates for security reasons. They said one reason for choosing the weapon was that it can be delivered relatively quickly and at a competitive price, and the Anthem missiles for Denmark will be built in Leipzig, Germany, where Covenant is setting up its European production line.
Anthem is a jet-powered cruise missile designed from the start for low cost and mass production. Covenant says it can carry a 200 kg (440-pound) warhead for precision strikes deep in enemy territory, and the missile reportedly has a range of more than 1,000 km (620 miles), with some media reports putting it as high as 1,500 km (930 miles). The company plans to sell it for a six-figure sum, under $1 million per missile, compared with the several million dollars typically charged for comparable cruise missiles.
Anthem first flew in August 2025, and Covenant says it has since been used in more than 200 tests, including several flight tests with U.S. forces in the United States and abroad, although the missile has not yet been used in combat. Choosing it marks a departure for Denmark, which has traditionally bought proven, production-ready systems for its armed forces.
Covenant opened a 10,000-square-meter (108,000-square-foot) plant in Leipzig earlier this month to build missiles for European NATO allies. Production is set to begin in 2027, with the company planning 1,000 missiles in the first year and 5,000 in 2028, and Covenant aims to source more than 95% of the components for its European version from inside Europe, with the Leipzig facility handling assembly and warheads integrated later at customer locations.
Germany is also studying the missile, and the German defense ministry has said it is in talks with Covenant about closing its own long-range strike gap, although no German order has been publicly confirmed. Lt. Gen. Christian Freuding, the head of the German Army, has confirmed that the Bundeswehr wants to buy new low-cost cruise missiles for mass use and is evaluating two systems already on the market, though he did not name them. Anthem has been reported as one of the candidates, alongside the Flamingo cruise missile from Ukrainian company Fire Point, and Covenant has brought in Andreas Marlow, a retired lieutenant general and former deputy commander of the German Army, as an adviser.
Denmark is pairing Anthem with a second, air-launched weapon, the Joint Strike Missile, built by Norway’s Kongsberg with Raytheon. The stealthy JSM fits inside the internal weapons bays of Denmark’s F-35 fighters, weighs 416 kg (917 pounds) with a 120 kg (265-pound) warhead and has a range of more than 350 km (217 miles). It is derived from Kongsberg’s Naval Strike Missile, which Denmark already operates on its frigates and for coastal defense.
Russian Ambassador to Denmark Vladimir Barbin responded quickly to the announcement, saying Danish policy is built on confrontation and preparation for a possible conflict with Russia, and calling it a dangerous illusion to think precision strike weapons could pose a military threat to a nuclear power.
Denmark’s military planning has traditionally focused on defending its own territory, and the new missiles give it a way to strike targets in an adversary’s rear areas for the first time. With Covenant’s Leipzig line due to start production in 2027, the first Anthem missiles for Denmark are expected to come from that plant.

articles.title: Zelenskyy accuses Russia of using cluster warheads in deadly strikes
articles.body:
Zelenskyy accuses Russia of using cluster warheads in deadly strikes hours after U.S. prisoner release
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Russia of using cluster munitions overnight as it renewed strikes on Kyiv and multiple other locations.
At least four people were killed, according to Ukraine's foreign ministry. Another 34 people were injured, including five children, Zelenskyy said Thursday, hours after Russia released American Stephen Hubbard and U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff met with Russian President Vladimir Putin and called him a humanitarian.
"Last night, the Russians used, among other weapons against Kyiv, three ballistic missiles with cluster warheads," Zelenskyy wrote on X Thursday. "The distinguishing feature of these missiles is that they detonate in the air as they approach the target, striking everything within a 400-meter diameter."
More than 100 countries have banned the use of cluster bombs under the Convention on Cluster Munitions, an international treaty that was adopted in 2008. The munitions spread smaller "bomblets" over a wide area that can hit civilian locations indiscriminately.
Russia, like the United States, did not sign on to the treaty.
Russia's Defense Ministry said, meanwhile, that air defenses downed 808 Ukrainian drones overnight, and that two people were reported injured, The Associated Press reported. More than 600 drones were fired toward Moscow between late Wednesday and early Thursday, according to Mayor Sergei Sobyanin.
The developments came after Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was quoted by Russian news agencies as saying Moscow would study proposals on the Ukraine war brought to St. Petersburg by Witkoff, but that the talks would take a long time.
"Almost immediately after another round of talks, Russia launched a pointed attack," Zelenskyy said. "This means there has been no real change in its attitude toward everything that is happening."
Twelve regions came under attack from Russia overnight, according to Zelenskyy, who said one attack hit Pechersk, Kyiv's historic center, and damaged monastery buildings, homes, shops, cafés and other civilian infrastructure.
Since Oct. 11, there have been 170 strikes on energy infrastructure sites across Ukraine, the Ukrainian president said.
Zelenskyy said earlier this week that if President Trump "cannot rein Putin in," he should provide long-requested interceptor missiles so Ukraine can defend itself. Secretary of State Marco Rubio later said that Mr. Trump has been "frustrated" by what he described as false accusations that "he is doing things to deliberately harm Ukraine." He insisted that nothing had been "deliberately denied to Ukraine," but added: "It's simply, it's a balance between our obligations to other partners and frankly our own ... requirements for our own facilities as well."

articles.title: US-Iran war, then and now: How the landscape has changed since February
articles.body:
US-Iran war, then and now: How the landscape has changed since February
The positions of Washington and Tehran have changed dramatically since US-Israeli strikes began the war, analysts say.
Iran says seven oil tankers have caught fire or sustained damage in and around the Strait of Hormuz as its Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) warns that renewed US attacks could trigger a wider response and the world braces for the possibility of renewed hostilities.
Although analysts consider a US attack before the November 3 midterm elections unlikely, sabre-rattling on both sides has raised fears that escalating rhetoric could give way to renewed attacks with control of the Strait of Hormuz and Iranian nuclear facilities at the heart of the conflict.
But the critical Gulf waterway, through which one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies were shipped before the war, was not even an issue before the United States and Israel first launched strikes on Iran on February 28. Furthermore, talks over Iran’s nuclear programme were under way at the time.
As the US wrestles with depleted defensive weapons stocks and a global energy crisis mounts, how does the land lie now before potential renewed strikes and how does it differ from February before any of this began?
Here is what we know:
How has the geography of the war changed?
Unlike in February before the war began, the US and Iran would be fighting it out on several different fronts if attacks resume.
Iran’s regional allies and Lebanon
While the objective of US-Israeli strikes on Iran was initially to topple its leadership, another aim was to weaken Iran’s regional allies, including Hamas and Hezbollah. Announcing the offensive, Trump pledged to prevent Tehran-backed groups from attacking US forces and destabilising the region.
While the offensive failed to force a change in Iran’s government, Hamas has been severely weakened as Israel continues to attack Gaza – with more than 1,400 Palestinians killed since a US-backed “ceasefire” was announced in October last year.
Hezbollah’s retaliation against targets in northern Israel after the killing of Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei in the first US-Israeli air strikes brought Lebanon into the war in early March.
Israel launched a bombing campaign against sites in southern Lebanon and the suburbs of Beirut it considers Hezbollah strongholds and, at one point, occupied about one-fifth of the country, displacing more than one million people. It still occupies significant land on Lebanon’s southern border.
Waterways, energy facilities now battlegrounds
The biggest geographical change, however, has been the emergence of the Gulf’s waterways and energy infrastructure as key targets. Iranian attacks on US military assets and civilian infrastructure have exposed Gulf countries to the consequences of a war they had hoped to avoid.
Urban Coningham, a research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, told Al Jazeera: “US-Iran negotiations had previously centred on Iran’s regional allies and nuclear programme. The Strait of Hormuz and attacks on the Gulf have now become central points of contention.”
While the Gulf has experienced attacks before, Coningham said the scale and “velocity” of recent Iranian strikes, including on oil and gas infrastructure, have marked a significant shift.
The Strait of Hormuz between Iran and Oman, which had been freely open to international shipping before the war, now gives Tehran a means of imposing costs far beyond its borders. Iran continues to threaten and attack shipping there while the US maintains its own blockade of Iranian ports. Traffic has been severely disrupted and supplies of oil and gas have been sharply reduced.
In March, CNN reported that the Pentagon and US National Security Council had significantly underestimated Iran’s willingness to restrict passage through the strait and the consequences of that. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth rejected the reporting, insisting the military had planned for that possibility.
Renewed fighting in Yemen
Renewed fighting between the forces of the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government of Yemen and the Iran-backed Houthis has added another front to the regional crisis. Yemen’s war has expanded to Saudi Arabia as Houthi missile and drone attacks target Saudi airports and oil infrastructure.
This front has brought another trade chokepoint into sharper focus – Bab al-Mandeb, the strait that links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. Houthi threats against Saudi-linked shipping there could compound transportation disruptions in Hormuz, undermine efforts to move Gulf exports through alternative routes and place additional pressure on the US.
How have the political stakes changed?
The two countries’ leaders face different constraints. Iran’s rulers remain concerned about unrest and their own survival but do not face the same electoral reckoning as Trump’s Republican Party, which faces midterm elections in less than two weeks.
In Iran
Before the February strikes, Iran’s government faced deep public anger after its deadly crackdown in January on nationwide protests against high inflation and the plummeting value of Iran’s currency. US-Israeli attacks subsequently killed Khamenei, who had ruled since 1989, and security chief Ali Larijani. But they did not topple the Islamic Republic.
Khamenei’s son Mojtaba succeeded him. His elevation and the influence of the IRGC has reinforced the position of hardliners within the government.
Coningham cautioned that the absence of demonstrations during a war should not be interpreted as support for the government.
“While the conflict had produced a rallying effect around resistance to foreign attacks, that did not mean Iran had emerged stronger,” he said.
In the US
Meanwhile, Trump faces much tougher political pressure before any renewed strikes. His approval rating has fallen from 40 percent in a Reuters/Ipsos poll reported days before the war began to just 31 percent in a survey released on Monday – the lowest recorded by the pollster across either of Trump’s presidential terms – amid frustration over high petrol prices and the deep unpopularity of the war on Iran among Americans.
How has the economic balance changed?
In Iran
Iran’s economy was already struggling before the war, weighed down by sanctions and assets frozen abroad. The conflict has deepened those pressures as the US combines military force, more sanctions and a naval blockade to squeeze the country further.
In April, Iran’s government estimated the direct and indirect damage from US-Israeli attacks at $270bn. The pressure intensified in late August when Washington launched Operation Economic Outcast, seeking to isolate Iran from international trade by imposing penalties on those doing business with it.
Official figures showed Iran’s gross domestic product contracted by 10.1 percent year-on-year from March 21 to June 20. Energy exports have been severely curtailed by the US blockade while the rial has plunged in value.
In the US
The US has also incurred substantial costs. In September, the Congressional Budget Office estimated that the conflict had cost the Department of Defense $38bn as of August 1. It said continued operations were expected to cost about $2bn to $3bn a month, depending on the intensity of fighting.
As a result of the additional costs of the war, US government debt surpassed a record $40 trillion in August – two years before it had been expected to reach that level.
How has the military balance changed?
For the US
While the US has demonstrated its ability to strike deep inside Iran, that destructive capacity has not brought down Iran’s political system nor has it finished off Tehran’s ability to retaliate with strikes on US assets and energy infrastructure in neighbouring countries.
Coningham said the difficulty for Washington is “translating military superiority into strategic results”. He also described recent troop redeployments as possible military posturing, but he added that the deployments do represent a shift from earlier efforts to reduce the US military footprint in parts of the region.
US media reports suggested there is now a severe shortage of weapons in the US arsenal in the Middle East as expensive defensive missiles have been depleted against a bombardment of cheap Iranian drones.
Fox News reported that the USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit were expected to reach the Middle East by the end of November, bringing about 10,000 military personnel. The deployment would expand Trump’s military options as he weighs further action.
For Iran
Coningham said, for Iran, the conflict fits a longstanding narrative of resistance against what its leadership portrayed as US and Israeli colonialism and imperialism.
Since February 28, the IRGC has demonstrated its skill at “asymmetric warfare” as it has held off expensive US military might with cheap, mass-produced drones.
Furthermore, its use of “decentralised structures” has allowed it to continue operating despite disrupted communications and the loss of senior decision-makers, Coningham said.
US strikes have severely damaged Iran’s navy and increased its reliance on smaller vessels, including speedboats used in recent attacks in the Strait of Hormuz. On that front, geography is on Iran’s side as it can fire at ships in the Strait of Hormuz from ground positions along its coast. It can also place sea mines in the strait using rockets to drop them.
These are tactics the US had not necessarily expected to contend with when it initiated the strikes on Iran but will certainly face now.
How has global trade changed?
A mounting global energy crisis was not on the cards in February, but it is certainly looming now.
Disruptions to Gulf energy supplies caused by the war and fears of further escalation have pushed oil prices sharply higher. Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil prices, settled at $72.48 a barrel on February 27, the day before the war began.
It hit $126.41 on April 30, its highest level in four years. By early trading on Friday, it stood at $114.47.
But the crisis extends beyond crude oil. Damage and disruptions to fuel production in the Middle East alongside sanctions on Russian supplies have tightened diesel markets while the global supply of liquefied natural gas has also been heavily affected. The International Energy Agency warned in October that supply constraints could persist well into 2027.
Diesel, which has doubled in price in the US, is a big problem for Trump because farmers and businesses in the US, key voting blocs for him, rely on it for production and transport.
Alternative ports, pipelines and ship-to-ship transfers have helped Gulf producers restore exports but at higher logistical costs and with continuing exposure to attacks.
Re-establishing shipping through vital waterways in the Middle East, therefore, has now become a primary objective in the war.

articles.title: The Economist: Trump's peace plan is dangerous for Ukraine, Europe and US
articles.body:
The Economist: Trump's peace plan is dangerous for Ukraine, Europe and US
The 28-point peace plan that US President Donald Trump is actively promoting as a basis for ending the war in Ukraine is dangerous not only for Ukraine but also for Europe and even the United States, The Economist writes.
Source: The Economist
Details: The Economist says the plan is "so poorly put together, so vague, unbalanced and impractical that, in a more normal world, it would never have seen the light of day".
"But these are not ordinary times. It remains entirely possible, perhaps probable, that President Donald Trump will insist on Ukraine accepting the plan or something very like it by Thanksgiving. If President Volodymyr Zelensky refuses, Mr Trump may cut off Ukraine's access to American intelligence and advanced weapons systems – as he did with devastating effect briefly earlier this year," the article says.
According to The Economist, among other things, the plan prohibits Ukraine from launching missiles against Moscow or St Petersburg while imposing no restrictions on Russian strikes. It requires Ukraine to limit the size of its armed forces to 600,000 personnel, while placing no restrictions on Russia.
It also prohibits NATO troops from being stationed on Ukrainian territory, effectively ending European plans – which had until now been thought to have US backing – to deploy a "reassurance force" there.
"Russia is rewarded for halting its invasion, by keeping all the territory it has seized and more that it has not; by being welcomed back into the international community, including the G8; and by being given relief from sanctions and generous opportunities to make money," the outlet writes.
The Economist says such a generous reward would give Russian ruler Vladimir Putin "an incentive to strike Ukraine again", while also providing him with the money and time to rebuild the armed forces needed to pursue his long-term goal of threatening and putting pressure on countries bordering Russia, from the Arctic to the Black Sea.
"Mr Putin is a serial breaker of international agreements. He will know that, under Mr Trump at least, America holds its European allies in contempt; they were not consulted in the drawing up of the plan. That is not good for America. Japan and South Korea will take note. Eyeing Taiwan, so will China," the article says.
Trump's supporters argue that such a pessimistic interpretation overlooks the security guarantees the US is offering Ukraine, pointing out that point 10 of the plan states that, in the event of another Russian invasion, the US would initiate a co-ordinated military response.
However, the outlet notes that since the presidencies of Barack Obama and Joe Biden, America has consistently made clear that it would not enter into a direct war with Russia over Ukraine.
"Under Mr Trump it is not clear that America would go to war with Russia even over NATO. The plan for Ukraine makes its 'guarantee' entirely dependent on the whim of Mr Trump, and the pledge is not even going to be backed by America's Congress," The Economist writes.
The outlet stresses that throughout the war, "America and Europe have supplied Ukraine with too little, too late".
"These days America is being paid for supplying it with weapons. Just last month Europe failed to agree on a plan to seize Russian assets in order to supply Ukraine with €140bn (US$160bn). (Under Mr Trump's plan that money would now fall under American control and be used to generate profits for America.) European leaders, meeting today in panic mode, are paying a bitter price for their failure to seize the initiative. That is an indictment of their short-sightedness," the Economist writes.
The Economist says Ukraine should do everything possible to avoid a confrontation with Trump and seek to improve the terms of the plan through negotiations. European leaders, meanwhile, should immediately reach out to sympathetic Republicans in Congress to warn Trump against striking a deal in its current form or, if negotiations fail, to prevent him from lashing out at Ukraine.
The Economist also says that "despite Europe's grave fiscal problems, its leaders need to find the money to keep Ukraine in the fight, which may well now mean fighting on without America".
"The struggle would be desperate and the bill would be high, but far lower than the cost of defending NATO against the aggravated threat from Russia should Ukraine crumble. The current American plan is dangerous not just for Ukraine but for Europe; so its leaders must now move from indignation to action. They have already wasted far too much time on wishful thinking," the article says.

articles.title: Ukraine receives 50,000 rounds of ammunition for F-16s from Denmark

Ukrainian military stands next to the first General Dynamics F-16 Fighting Falcon received by Ukraine, on the Day of Ukrainian Air Force in Ukraine on Aug. 4, 2024. (Vitalii Nosach/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images)
Denmark has delivered 50,000 rounds of 20 mm ammunition for the autocannons on Ukraine's F-16 fighter jets, Ukraine's Defense Ministry said on Oct. 23.
First delivered to Ukraine in 2024, the U.S.-made jets have become a key part of the country's defenses against Russian attacks on its rear areas, particularly jet-powered drones.
"Ukrainian pilots are already using them to intercept jet-powered attack drones," the ministry said on social media.
"We are grateful to Denmark for its quick and efficient response to our request for additional ammunition."
In addition to mounting points for various air-to-air and air-to-ground missiles,F-16 fighter jets are equipped with 20 mm M61 Vulcan rotary cannons designed for close-range engagements.
While missiles are often used to shoot down Russian cruise missiles during mass attacks, the cheaper autocannon ammunition is frequently used against Russian jet-powered drones, which are too fast for most Ukrainian interceptor drones to intercept.
On Sept. 30, Bloomberg reported that Kyiv was seeking to procure additional 20 mm rounds for its F-16s, with sources saying an average of 150 rounds was required per interception.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 5 that Ukraine was "scouring munitions for F-16s virtually all over the world." Zelensky also praised the jets as one of the most effective means of countering jet-powered drones.
Denmark, the Netherlands, Belgium, and Norway have collectively supplied Ukraine with around 50 F-16 fighter jets.
Intensive use in defending Ukrainian airspace means the jets require frequent maintenance, which can currently be carried out only by Kyiv's partners.
Francis Farrell is a senior reporter at the Kyiv Independent. He is the co-author of War Notes, the Kyiv Independent's weekly newsletter about the war. For the second year in a row, the Kyiv Independent received a grant from the Charles Douglas-Home Memorial Trust to support his front-line reporting for the year 2025-2026. Francis won the Prix Bayeux Calvados-Normandy for war correspondents in the young reporter category in 2023, and was nominated for the European Press Prize in 2024.
Francis speaks Ukrainian and Hungarian and is an alumnus of Leiden University in The Hague and University College London. He has previously worked as a managing editor at the online media project Lossi 36, as a freelance journalist and documentary photographer, and at the OSCE and Council of Europe field missions in Albania and Ukraine.
