articles.title: The view from Russia: The Ukraine conflict is entering its final phase
articles.body:
The view from Russia: The Ukraine conflict is entering its final phase
Andrey Sushentsov, dean of the Faculty of International Relations at MGIMO and a member of the Scientific-Expert Council under the Security Council of the Russian Federation, discusses why Western Europe is so afraid of a direct confrontation with Russia, how the US is shifting the burden of the Ukraine crisis onto the EU, why the “pyramid of trust” surrounding Kiev is crumbling, and when the Ukraine conflict might come to an end.
His interview, first published in Russian by TASS, was translated and edited by the RT team.
America sails away, Europe gets the bill
Evgeny Kuznetsov: You have noted that the US is seeking to extricate itself from the Ukraine crisis by shifting the burden onto Western Europe. If Washington does indeed distance itself, are these Europeans prepared, politically and economically, to assume the role of Ukraine’s principal “security guarantor”?
Andrey Sushentsov: The US strategy in the Ukrainian crisis initially reflected its archetype as a maritime power employing a “continental sword” in its confrontation with a major continental power. This involves a neighboring country with military resources, which the maritime power supports in order to weaken its rival.
Ukraine was well suited to this role, as a large state with substantial armed forces, motivated to confront Russia. But the limitation of such a strategy is that you can’t fully control the behavior of the “sword.” Nor is it entirely resource-efficient, there’s a limit to the resources that can be allocated to it, and if no turning point is reached in the confrontation, further support yields no additional gains in effectiveness.
The Americans realized early on that many of their interests in this crisis had been achieved and prepared to withdraw. They did what a maritime power usually does when it decides to turn its attention elsewhere as they sailed back to their own region. The main difference between a maritime power and a continental power lies in the freedom to choose where to deploy military forces. A maritime power can choose where to deploy them and launch strikes across various parts of the world’s oceans. This is usually carried out in the form of raids, as large-scale expeditionary campaigns rarely prove successful. The US decided it was time to leave.
But they didn’t want the withdrawal to be accompanied by the collapse of the Ukrainian regime. The US incorporated its withdrawal and the reorientation of its priorities towards East Asia into its policy towards its NATO allies. It handed over responsibility for supporting Ukraine to them and assumed the role of “moderator” as a negotiator who, rather than being the instigator of the crisis, is steering it towards a resolution. US strategic documents state an interest in bringing the Ukraine crisis to an end.
Yet the US behaved treacherously toward both Ukraine and its European allies, saddling them with this burden without warning. The Western Europeans lack military resources, technological capabilities, strategic thinking, and awareness of their own interests comparable to those of the Americans, qualities that enable them to weigh up causes and consequences, to discern what is achievable and what is not by military means, and to identify where their bloc’s interests lie in this crisis.
These Europeans currently have a financial instrument of considerable weight at their disposal, in essence, the only one they can draw upon. They are using it wastefully, given the domestic debt of most major European states is approaching or exceeding 100% of GDP. They can’t obtain external compensation for their military expenditure, and there’s no hope of a Ukrainian victory.
If there were any hope, they would be counting on recouping their losses through Russian resources, through new deals with Russia on new terms. None of these hopes is being realized.
Moreover, due to a lack of strategic experience, lost as a result of American patronage and the nuclear umbrella, these Europeans are beginning to deny their own geography. To deny that Russia is on the continent alongside them.
Geography is a constant, an immutable part of the foreign policy system. Governments and historical circumstances may change, but geography remains unchanged.
The course towards a long-term confrontation with their largest neighbor, a source of many benefits for the Western European economy, which they have now lost, demonstrates the narrowness of their vision. Domestic political processes in the EU suggest that, following the Americans’ example, it is time for these Europeans to reflect on what their interests are, which of these are achievable in the course of the Ukraine crisis, which are not, and what the possible trajectory might be. So far, the Western Europeans haven’t made any good moves.
When there are no good moves, it is better to pass a turn and stop making mistakes. So far, as our President [Vladimir Putin] put it, it looks like a series of mistakes, one after another.
Big spending, little strategic power
Evgeny Kuznetsov: Won’t they get tired of playing this game?
Andrey Sushentsov: Western Europeans states don’t possess the full strategic autonomy enjoyed by Russia and the US, and are not entirely capable of acting collectively from a unified position. Every major decision requires the consensus of nearly 30 countries.
The European Commission doesn’t have a very substantial budget of its own but relies on the budgets of the nation states. Despite the single currency, debt is measured separately for each country.
There is no unified army. It’s a far cry from even the most loosely organized confederation. They would carry strategic weight if they were capable of acting in unison, but there’s no sign of this. Western Europeans are terrified of being directly drawn into a military crisis with Russia. Speculation about sending troops into Ukraine always ends with the caveat that this will only happen once a lasting peace and a ceasefire have been achieved.
In part, their enthusiasm is fueled by what they perceive to be the relatively low cost of supporting Ukraine and this proxy conflict. They have no qualms about Ukraine. They are indifferent to what will become of it, its borders or its population. They express rhetorical outrage, flock to summits, pose for “family photographs,” and make categorical statements. But in essence, this is a gathering of onlookers who are not directly involved in the military crisis.
The tool at their disposal is debt financing at Ukraine’s expense, amounting to nearly $500 billion. An astronomical sum which has failed to deliver the strategically necessary results, whilst worsening their own position. All that money has gone up in smoke.
Russia as the glue holding Europe together
Evgeny Kuznetsov: The EU is not abandoning its plans to impose ever more restrictions on Russia. Incidentally, Brussels has also added you to its sanctions list. At the same time, some European leaders are calling for dialogue with Russia. Is that possible at present?
Andrey Sushentsov: Western Europeans are using the Ukraine crisis as a platform for unity, to become a more cohesive entity. Their strategic lack of autonomy, the prominent role of the Americans, and their internal fragmentation mean that the only platform for solidarity is an anti-Russian one.
The relevance varies from country to country. For Southern Europe, it’s not so obvious. For Spain, despite its anti-Russian government, Palestine and the Middle East are more important. The Baltic states and Northern Europe have an alarmist and militaristic outlook. Some share a border with us. The people in charge are a peculiar lot; one can expect all sorts of things. But no one wants to involve their armed forces in the Ukraine crisis, as North Korea has done on our side.
They are using Ukraine to strengthen their own agency and take steps towards coordinated action. These steps are not particularly effective. However, joint plans are being drawn up and substantial funding is being allocated.
One unresolved issue is the restructuring of the Western European defense industry; it’s fragmented and produces around 15 different types of main battle tank with guns of varying calibers. Standardization is a major and difficult challenge. A catalyst is needed. In other words, they are, to some extent, tackling an internal challenge.
Peace alongside Russia – or a strategic dead end
Evgeny Kuznetsov: Do the NATO Europeans want to sit at the negotiating table with Russia, representing a “united Europe,” in order to compensate for their strategic lack of autonomy?
Andrey Sushentsov: Their tactics for establishing agency include providing financial aid to Ukraine, the theft of Russia’s gold and foreign exchange reserves, the withholding and disposal of revenues, and an attempt to share the blame for this crime amongst everyone. If it’s a crime, then it’s a collective one, so that no single country is held solely responsible. And they are resolving many technical issues.
The US doesn’t resolve such issues, nor does Russia. We can afford to take strategic, autonomous, purposeful and consistent action. These Europeans take a step back, a step forward, two steps back; they look over their shoulders and seek consensus.
It’s in Russia’s interests to invite them to the negotiating table only if it is clear that these Europeans prioritize a stable world on the continent, based on the principle of “peace alongside Russia,” rather than against Russia. The “peace against Russia” approach is inherently unstable and a dead end for Western Europe. It dooms them to fall behind, to strategic defeat, and to never becoming a true player on the world stage. The more internal contradictions there are within the bloc regarding priorities, the more fragile it becomes, and the Russian question is gradually becoming precisely such an issue.
Ukraine’s ‘pyramid of trust’ is crumbling
Evgeny Kuznetsov: You said that the “pyramid of trust” surrounding Ukraine will soon crumble. When will this finally happen?
Andrey Sushentsov: From the Russian perspective, the logic behind this crisis is that we are waging a war to wear down our opponents and deplete their resources. We are targeting their rear lines and breaking their “continental sword.”
We are demonstrating that their strategy is irrelevant; its objectives are unattainable. And the resources they are expending will, over time, be needed in ever-greater quantities. The existing ones are becoming obsolete, as are the systems for utilizing them on Ukrainian territory. They need to be replenished and rebuilt.
Building infrastructure is extremely costly; in wartime conditions, it is simply impossible. In time, Western countries themselves will realize the unviability of this strategy. The opposition within those countries is already openly voicing its outrage and stating that this is a dead end.
[Friedrich] Merz’s visit to Kiev was heavily criticized by the entire opposition, at a time when Germany’s national debt is rising, the chancellor travels to Kiev and once again promises money and resources, essentially at the expense of the German people. The scale of the resources being invested is becoming so significant that the question arises as to what justifies it. What are Berlin’s objectives, what is it achieving, and what is it failing to achieve?
There are increasingly insistent calls for the Ukrainian leadership to take a realistic view of the situation and understand what is achievable and what is not. The “pyramid of trust” is crumbling. One after another, the parties involved are adopting an increasingly detached stance on this issue.
Their primary and secondary hopes have not been realized. Now they are almost left high and dry. We must admit, it was a mistake.
No one wants to take responsibility for it. It has not only a political but also a financial dimension. Who should be held to account for the hundreds of billions of euros spent on a strategically futile venture that has antagonized Russia and undermined security on the continent?
That is why we are talking about a short-term historical perspective. It may come to an end in the coming months, or perhaps in the coming years. But we are not talking about a decade-long war. The point is that this will still remain a crisis with its own distinct phases, and we are currently in the final phase of its resolution.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Zelensky says fresh Russian strikes show ‘no change’ in Kremlin position
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Zelensky says fresh Russian strikes show ‘no change’ in Kremlin position
- Russia launched fresh missile and drone strikes across Ukraine just after US envoy Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin, showing, Zelensky said, “no real change” in Moscow’s war stance.
- Kyiv said two people were killed and more than 30 wounded in the capital, while an attack on a crowded market in Lozova killed two women and wounded dozens.
- Talks on peace remain weak. Trump said negotiators were “maybe now the closest we’ve been”, but Ukraine, Europe and NATO still fear Russia will keep pressing its demands.
AI generated
KYIV – Ukraine on Oct 22 accused Russia of failing to change its position on the war, by firing a wave of ballistic missiles just after US envoy Steve Witkoff met President Vladimir Putin to discuss the resumption of peace talks.
Air raid sirens sounded throughout the night and into the day in Kyiv, where two people were killed and more than 30 others wounded, the city authorities said.
Two women aged 50 and 60 were killed and dozens more people were injured in an attack on a crowded market in the eastern city of Lozova. Two were wounded in the Moscow region after Ukraine launched its own large-scale drone attack.
The strikes came after the Kremlin said it was willing to restart trilateral talks with Kyiv and Washington in November, but dismissed new ideas brought by Witkoff that were developed with European countries and Ukraine.
In all, a dozen Ukrainian regions were hit overnight, including houses, energy sites, shops, cafes and a monastery damaged in Kyiv, where strikes have intensified before winter sets in.
All families and children were told to evacuate the front-line towns of Kramatorsk and neighbouring Sloviansk in the east after a spate of attacks killed dozens of civilians.
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky said the onslaught began “almost immediately” after Witkoff and Putin held hours-long talks in St Petersburg, scoffing at the US envoy’s description of the Russian leader as a “humanitarian”.
“This means there has been no real change in its attitude towards everything that is happening,” he added.
Moscow emboldened by sanctions easing
Ukraine has repeatedly called on its allies, including the United States, to supply it with advanced US-made Patriot interceptors to shoot down missiles and fast-moving attack drones.
Zelensky warned of more strikes to come and suggested that Moscow – emboldened by an easing of sanctions pressure – was “clearly taking advantage of the slowdown in air defence supplies from our partners”, in a clear nod to Washington.
In Brussels, NATO said it was allowing Ukraine to buy weapons through the alliance’s central procurement agency on a “case-by-case basis”.
US President Donald Trump sought an optimistic tone as his envoy returned from Russia and on Oct 21 said negotiators were “maybe now the closest we’ve been” to ending the war. But in Kyiv and European capitals, hopes for a breakthrough were slim, with many worried the White House was siding with Moscow.
Zelensky accused Russia of deliberately targeting civilians in Kyiv, including with cluster munitions, which disperse in the air, showering dozens of smaller explosive devices or bomblets indiscriminately over a large area.
Human Rights Watch in August reported an apparent increase in the use of the weapons, which are fired in rockets and missiles or dropped from aircraft. Doing so could be a war crime, it added.
Moscow invaded Ukraine in February 2022 in what it hoped would be a swift attack to topple Zelensky and seize land.
Instead, it has become bogged down in Europe’s biggest conflict since World War II. Hundreds of thousands have been killed, millions forced from their homes and much of eastern and southern Ukraine destroyed.
Zelensky backs resuming trilateral talks
Zelensky met Witkoff in Norway on Oct 20 as relations between Kyiv and Washington plunged to their worst state since Trump publicly berated Zelensky in the Oval Office in February 2025.
In recent days, Trump has blocked new sanctions on Russia, struck a deal to buy Russian diesel, and called for the Ukrainian leader to be replaced.
Zelensky has backed resuming trilateral talks – several rounds of which over the last 18 months have failed to move the sides closer to a deal.
Russia is demanding Ukraine pull out of territory in the eastern Donetsk region that it still controls, and wants sweeping political and military restrictions on the size of its army and Western alliances. Ukraine rejects the demands as tantamount to a capitulation that would leave it exposed to a fresh attack.
Moscow said that a summit between Trump, Putin and China’s President Xi Jinping was being prepared in China for November, with Europeans and Ukraine worrying a deal could be struck over their heads.
Witkoff called his talks with Putin “constructive” but said “there is still important work left to do” and technical-level talks would continue between all three sides.
Putin has consistently rejected face-to-face talks with Zelensky and insisted Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine – either through a deal or on the battlefield. AFP

articles.title: Denmark to purchase long-range air and ground precision missiles
articles.body:
Denmark has announced that it will be purchasing its first long-range precision missiles as Russia continues to carry out hostile actions against Europe.
The missiles are air-launched Joint Strike Missiles (JSM) made by Norway’s Kongsberg for the Nordic country’s F-35 stealth fighter jets and the ground-launched Anthem missile made by Covenant.
“The purpose of the acquisitions is to strengthen national and collective deterrence. These are weapons that are in demand by NATO and that contribute to Denmark's security,” Denmark’s Defense Ministry said in a statement on Thursday, adding that “they can both deter attacks from outside and strike back deep inside enemy territory if necessary.”
The JSM is a fifth-generation air-to-surface missile that fits in the internal weapons bays of the F-35A, allowing the aircraft to retain its stealth profile. The high-subsonic missile has a range of 350 kilometers and autonomous target recognition capabilities. It is in use by 15 other countries, including the United States, Germany, Norway, Romania, and Poland.
Covenant, which has operations in the US, Germany, and Israel, emerged from stealth last month. Covenant’s flagship system, Anthem, is built to deliver heavy payloads at extended ranges while remaining affordable enough to produce in large quantities. The company has disclosed relatively little about Anthem’s specific performance characteristics, including its precise range, payload, and unit cost.
According to the company, most of Anthem’s components are commercial‑off‑the‑shelf (COTS) parts, supported by long‑term agreements for critical parts. Covenant says this approach allows the missile to be produced quickly and reliably, even during wartime, by drawing on supply chains across allied nations.
“Covenant Industries is proud to partner with Denmark as it moves with urgency to strengthen European defense and NATO’s collective security. As a global defense company with a growing European industrial footprint, Covenant is committed to delivering affordable, long-range precision strike capabilities at scale. This agreement, signed through our German company, represents an important step in our commitment to producing Anthem in Europe, for Europe, supported by a sovereign European supply chain,” Abby Denburg, its president and CGO told Defense & Tech by The Jerusalem Post.
Denmark’s Minister Defense Jeppe Bruus said that “the acquisitions are a significant step toward making Denmark better able to defend itself, strengthening NATO, and increasing our ability to strike back.”
Last year, Denmark said that it would be spending 58 billion Danish crowns ($9.20 billion) on European-made air defense systems, its largest arms purchase ever. A week later, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen made the announcement that it would be purchasing long-range precision missiles because the country “must be able to credibly deter attacks on Denmark and NATO, and it is not enough to just have strong air defenses.”
Reuters reported that the Russian embassy in Copenhagen said that Denmark's missile policy aims at confrontation with Moscow and warned of "inevitable disastrous consequences.”
"Copenhagen is enthralled by the dangerous illusions that purchasing offensive high-precision long-range weapons to pose a military threat to a nuclear power will help strengthen Denmark's security and defense," the embassy said.

articles.title: Regional powers, European heavyweights meet in Istanbul for 1st joint talks
articles.body:
The R4 meeting was attended by Pakistani Foreign Minister Muhammad Ishaq Dar (2nd L), Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty (L), and Saudi Arabian Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan (R). (AA Photo)
Istanbul hosted high-level diplomatic talks on Oct. 23, bringing together foreign ministers from regional and European powers to discuss the Iran conflict, maritime security, the Palestinian issue and the Russia-Ukraine war. 
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan chaired the inaugural joint meeting of the R4 and E3 diplomatic groups, bringing together Türkiye, Egypt, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia under the R4 framework, alongside Britain, France and Germany, which constitute the E3.
The Oct. 23 meeting marked the first joint gathering of the two mechanisms, reflecting efforts to expand cooperation between European powers and key regional actors amid mounting geopolitical tensions.
Italian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani was also expected to attend the talks, bringing the number of participating countries to eight.
Fidan held separate meetings in Istanbul with British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and Pakistani Foreign Minister Mohammad Ishaq Dar.
The discussions were scheduled to begin in the R4 format before being expanded to include top diplomats from the E3 group and Italy.
According to Turkish diplomatic sources, Fidan was expected to emphasize that regional security requires countries in the region to assume primary responsibility for addressing their own challenges.
Within this framework, he was expected to highlight Türkiye's commitment to strengthening cooperation mechanisms founded on regional ownership.
Fidan was also expected to stress that existing disputes must not exacerbate one another, conflicts must not spread to new fronts, and regional tensions must not escalate into wider instability.
The Turkish foreign minister was expected to identify Israel's policies toward the Palestinian territories, which he considers an obstacle to peace efforts, and its expanding military actions across the region as major drivers of instability in the Middle East.
Fidan was also expected to underline that tensions between the United States and Iran could be resolved only through diplomacy and dialogue, warning that military approaches fail to deliver lasting solutions and instead deepen regional vulnerabilities.
Ensuring freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on a lasting basis was another key priority on the agenda, given the waterways' significance for regional and global stability.
The discussions were also expected to cover Houthi attacks targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia. Fidan was expected to reaffirm Türkiye's support for Saudi Arabia's security and highlight the principle of collective security and solidarity underpinning the Mecca Defense Agreement.
Ahead of the talks, Miliband's office said the discussions would focus particularly on the Strait of Hormuz and the security situation in Saudi Arabia.
He was also set to warn that Iranian tactics were being replicated elsewhere in the region, with attacks on Saudi Arabia further destabilizing the Middle East and placing additional pressure on strategic maritime routes, including Bab el-Mandeb and the Suez Canal.
The meeting was also expected to address the security implications of the Russia-Ukraine war, particularly the risk of the conflict spreading into the Black Sea.
Fidan was expected to reiterate that Türkiye, as a Black Sea littoral state, would continue presenting proposals to the parties to prevent further escalation and contain the conflict's impact on regional security.
Attacks on commercial vessels, frequently involving drones, have increased in recent months as the conflict has extended its reach across the Black Sea, placing Turkish shipping at growing risk.
Türkiye submitted a proposal to Russia and Ukraine last month aimed at halting attacks on maritime targets. However, strikes have continued in recent weeks, particularly in waters near Romania and Bulgaria.
NATO announced on Oct. 20 that it was deploying additional aircraft, drones and radar systems to the Black Sea to improve regional surveillance and situational awareness through enhanced sensor coverage and greater information-sharing.
The R4 mechanism, established this year by Türkiye, Egypt, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, is intended to promote lasting regional stability and strengthen dialogue on shared challenges through an approach based on regional ownership.
The four countries have held six foreign ministers' meetings, beginning in Riyadh on March 18, with the most recent taking place in New York on Sept. 21 on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly's high-level week.
The E3, comprising Britain, France and Germany, emerged from diplomatic coordination on Iran's nuclear program launched in 2003. Initially focused on the nuclear issue, the grouping has gradually developed into a platform for joint diplomatic initiatives on a broader range of regional and international matters.

articles.title: Russia hit Kyiv with missiles carrying cluster warheads, Zelensky says
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump called Elon Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starlink, the Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday, citing US officials.
The Starlink system was working more normally on Thursday, shortly after the Trump-Musk conversation, according to US and Ukrainian officials cited by the WSJ.
Some Ukrainian officials told the newspaper the system was not restored to full functionality but was working at higher speeds than under the cap.
President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said earlier on Thursday that Starlink speed had not been restored for Ukraine, adding that he hoped for talks with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in the coming days.
Trump told Musk he was frustrated the system's speeds remained capped at around 100 mph (160 kph), the Journal said, citing officials.
Rubio said on Wednesday that decisions regarding Ukraine's access to Starlink were up to its parent company SpaceX and its CEO Musk, not the White House.
Starlink restrictions hamper Ukraine's drone operations
Ukraine uses Starlink for battlefield communications and drone operations. Restricting the satellite service hampered the country's attack and air defense drone missions against Russia.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Thursday that Russia hit Kyiv overnight with three ballistic missiles carrying cluster munition warheads.
Zelensky said the missiles were designed to detonate in the air as they approached their targets, spreading damage across an area 400 meters wide. He added that one of them struck Kyiv's historic district, hitting the area near the monastic buildings of Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra.
Ukraine's Foreign Ministry reported at least four deaths in the strikes, while President Volodymyr Zelensky said 34 others were wounded, including five children, according to CBS News.
The attacks came just hours after Russia freed American citizen Stephen Hubbard and US special envoy Steve Witkoff met with Russian President Vladimir Putin, whom he described as a humanitarian.
Ukraine's energy facilities hit over 170 times since October 11
He also said that Russia had kept targeting Ukrainian energy infrastructure with more than 170 strikes on critical energy facilities since October 11.
Cluster munitions are prohibited in more than 100 countries under the 2008 Convention on Cluster Munitions. The weapons release multiple smaller explosives across large areas, putting civilians at risk both during attacks and afterward, when unexploded bomblets can remain dangerous. Neither Russia nor the US is a party to the treaty.

articles.title: Pentagon Bets Big on Drone-Killing APKWS Laser-Guided Rockets
articles.body:
The Pentagon has concluded a new agreement to buy laser-guidance kits that turn rockets into drone-killing weapons.
BAE Systems and the Defense Department announced a framework deal of up to seven years for 25,000 Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System guidance kits annually for the U.S. military.
Another 10,000 kits could be produced each year for international customers, who are increasingly interested in the system.
APKWS is a laser-guidance kit that converts 2.75-inch unguided rockets into precision munitions. It is currently fielded by the U.S. Air Force, Army, Marine Corps, and Navy, as well as U.S. allies.
APKWS has become the preferred method for U.S. warplanes to down drones fired by Iran and Iranian-backed militias in the Middle East over the past few years. But it is not just an air-to-air weapon. APKWS munitions can also be fitted to various platforms for air-to-surface, surface-to-surface, and surface-to-air use.
APKWS is an attractive capability for the Pentagon because of its low cost—roughly $35,000, according to officials. That gives the Air Force a way to shoot down drones without expending costly air-to-air missiles.
For compraison, Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missiles cost roughly $1 million each, and AIM-9s cost hundreds of thousands of dollars depending on the variant. The most capable model is the AIM-9X, which costs around $500,000. APKWS was first tested in an air-to-air role in 2019. The Air Force did not pursue the idea heavily until a few years later, before fielding it in combat in 2024.
“We were on the wrong side of the cost curve in our munitions employment,” former Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. David Allvin said in an interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine.
“The great thing about it is that there wasn’t a formal requirement set out for this. This was sort of organic. People started figuring it out without it being a big program of record,” Allvin added. “Good thing they did.”
Now, just a few years later, the Pentagon is betting big on APKWS’ future.
APKWS scored its first combat air-to-air kill in the fall of 2024 in the Middle East by F-16 from the 510th Fighter Squadron at Aviano Air Base, Italy, current and former officials told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
When the 480th Fighter Squadron from Spangdahlem Air Base, Germany, deployed to the Middle East soon after, they scored dozens more aerial kills—108 in total using all weapons during their deployment.
By the spring of 2025, the Air Force began flight testing APKWS on F-15E Strike Eagles, and fielded the capability in the Middle East within roughly a week. Around the same time, U.S. Air Forces in Europe also fielded APKWS for its air-to-air training. The system has also been on A-10s to shoot down drones.
The APKWS has its origins in the decades-old Hydra rocket system and was first used as precision air-to-ground weapon during the Global War on Terror, deploying in 2012.
It was adapted to serve in an air-to-air role when Air Forces Central, commanded by then-Lt. Gen. Alexus G. Grynkewich from 2022-2024, began looking for an alternative to using costly air-to-air missiles against drones. CENTCOM and the Air Force supported the effort.
The framework agreement is intended as a signal of what the Pentagon plans to buy, subject to specific contracts and the congressional funding needs for those deals.
BAE says the new agreement will help expand production at its facilities in Hudson, N.H., and Austin, Texas.
“This agreement highlights the importance of sustained investment in critical munitions to strengthen readiness and equip forces for evolving operational needs,” BAE Systems president and CEO Tom Arseneault said in a statement.
“By securing multiyear demand, this agreement keeps production lines running at capacity, provides our forces with interceptor inventory, and flips the cost calculus in the taxpayer’s favor,” Michael Duffey, undersecretary of defense for acquisition and sustainment, added.
APKWS can also be used in a ground-to-air role, as the modifications needed to hit aerial targets are largery limited to software and the use of a proximity fuse. It can be fitted to anti-air systems such as Sierra Nevada Corporation’s BRAWLR, which is deployed overseas by the U.S. military, and L3Harris’ VAMPIRE, which is used by Ukraine and is being supplied to the U.S. It has been fitted to other nations’ fighter platforms and has been tested on the MQ-9 Reaper as well.
“This drone problem is not going away,” retired Lt. Gen. Derek C. France, who led Air Forces Central from April 2024-August 2026, said in a recent interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine. “It’s accelerating in tactics, speed, advancements, and the numbers. That’s the direction that we’re going.”

articles.title: Russia bombs Ukrainian cities despite Putin's openness to peace talks
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Thursday that future talks on a settlement of the war in Ukraine should focus on security guarantees for both countries and an overall framework for security throughout Europe.
Putin, interviewed on Russian television a day after meeting US presidential envoy Steve Witkoff, confirmed that Russia was ready to resume US-mediated talks with Ukraine next month.
He restated longstanding Kremlin policy that Russia never wanted to launch a war, but had run into hostile reactions from Ukraine on key issues of concern to Moscow.
Talks on a variety of matters could lead to a positive outcome, he said, but Russia remained intent on a solution ending the conflict rather than a short-lived ceasefire.
"The goal of these talks will be to ensure the security of Ukraine and Russia after reaching peace agreements, in their final form, not as a result of a temporary ceasefire for some short period of time. We are ready to resume these contacts to achieve this goal," Putin said.
Witkoff says Ukraine supports 'any proposals for a ceasefire'
The Russian president said Witkoff also stressed that discussions had to extend to "the architecture of European security as a whole. And I agree with that too. Well, let's see how things develop in the coming days."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who met Witkoff in Norway on Tuesday, said Ukraine was ready for talks likely to take place by early next month. Ukraine, he said, supported "any proposals for a ceasefire, an end to the war, an energy ceasefire as well as humanitarian initiatives."
Efforts headed by the United States to pursue talks stalled in February with the outbreak of the US-Israeli conflict with Iran.
Many of the Ukraine war issues focus on territory, with Russia demanding Ukraine cede all of eastern Ukraine's Donbas region. Kyiv rejects any notion of giving up land it currently holds.
In his comments, Putin said any discussion on territory in eastern Ukraine had to consider what he said was the fact that the area was "historically Russian land."
And residents there, he said, had voted to be a part of Russia in referendums staged seven months after Moscow launched its invasion.
"Firstly, my attitude on this matter is that this is not their territory. It’s the territory of historical Russia," he said.
Russia strikes Ukraine despite openness to peace talks
Russia pounded Kyiv with ballistic missiles, and Ukraine sent hundreds of drones towards Moscow on Thursday, as the warring sides kept up a barrage of attacks despite the latest US push to end the conflict.
US President Donald Trump said SpaceX SPCX.O CEO Elon Musk had restored Ukraine's Starlink access, one of the issues linked to a rift between Washington and Kyiv that has cast doubt on US support for Ukraine.
Ukraine said Russia fired at least 21 ballistic missiles in three waves. President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said three carried cluster munitions — "bomblets" that disperse over a wide area and are banned by many countries because of the danger to civilians. Russia's defense ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Russia said Ukraine launched 630 drones towards Moscow during the night.
The two sides held an exchange of war dead, with Moscow handing over 252 bodies and Ukraine handing over 25, according to the Belta state news agency in neighboring Belarus. Such exchanges have accompanied moves towards talks in the past.

articles.title: Turkish army gets more Tayfun ballistic missiles
articles.body:
- Türkiye delivered a new batch of Roketsan Tayfun Block 2 ballistic missiles to its Land Forces Command, following earlier deliveries in May and June 2026.
- The Tayfun Block 2 has a range of more than 500 km and a reported accuracy of under 10 meters.
Türkiye’s Ministry of National Defence has delivered a new batch of Roketsan Tayfun Block 2 ballistic missiles to the Turkish Land Forces Command, adding to a missile force that began entering service only five months ago.
The delivery was reported on Oct. 22, 2026, and in line with previous handovers, the ministry kept the number of missiles classified. The new batch is at least the third known delivery this year: the ministry announced on May 20, 2026, that Tayfun Block 2 missiles had been accepted into the Land Forces inventory for the first time, and a second batch followed on June 25.
Tayfun, Turkish for “typhoon,” is the longest-range ballistic missile Türkiye has developed on its own. Roketsan, the state-owned missile maker, describes the Block 2 as having a range of more than 500 km (310 miles) and designed to strike high-value targets deep behind enemy lines, including air defense systems, command and control centers, aircraft hangars and other critical military facilities.
The missile is about 6.5 meters (21.3 feet) long and 610 mm (24 inches) in diameter, with a launch weight of 2,300 kg (5,070 pounds). It is fired from a wheeled transporter-erector-launcher, a truck that carries, raises and launches the missile and holds two rounds, which allows crews to move quickly between firing positions.
Roketsan says the Tayfun Block 2 lands within 10 meters (33 feet) of its target, measured as circular error probable, the radius within which half of the missiles fired are expected to land. It uses coordinate-based guidance, meaning it flies to a fixed point programmed before launch, and the company says it is highly resistant to GPS jamming and can operate day or night in poor weather. The missile carries a pre-formed fragmentation warhead, which breaks into a pattern of fragments on detonation.
Türkiye first test-fired Tayfun in October 2022 from Rize-Artvin Airport on the Black Sea coast, when the missile flew 561 km (349 miles) in 456 seconds before striking a target area off Sinop. That distance was roughly twice the 280 km (174-mile) range of Roketsan’s earlier Bora missile, previously the longest-range ballistic missile in Turkish service. Further test firings followed in May 2023 and in later years as the program moved toward serial production.
Roketsan has continued to expand the family alongside the Block 2 deliveries. In July 2025, the company unveiled the much larger Tayfun Block 4 at the IDEF defense fair in Istanbul, a missile about 10 meters (33 feet) long and weighing roughly 7,200 kg (15,900 pounds), which Roketsan presents as a hypersonic ballistic missile system. In July 2026, Roketsan released footage of a Tayfun Block 3 striking an unmanned boat at sea, which the company said was the first time a Tayfun had been used against a naval target and the first use of a seeker on the missile.
With three batches delivered since May, the Tayfun Block 2 is now steadily building up inside the Turkish Land Forces, while the Block 3 and Block 4 versions continue through development and testing at Roketsan.

articles.title: The Price of Faustian Bargains with Trump
articles.body:
For the past week, President Donald Trump and his aides have traded accusations with Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX, over who restricted Ukraine’s access to a military-grade version of Starlink, SpaceX’s satellite network product that Ukrainian forces depend on to intercept incoming Russian projectiles and target Russian launchers.
Musk blamed Trump and the U.S. military for the decision, writing on X, “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.” Trump insisted that his administration did not disrupt Ukraine’s access to the network. Secretary of State Marco Rubio argued that decisions about Ukraine’s access to the network were in the hands of SpaceX and Musk and not the White House. The Wall Street Journal and CBS News reported that the decision had been Musk’s.
On Mar. 9, 2025, Musk had promised that, whatever his disagreements with U.S. policy toward Ukraine, “Starlink will never turn off its terminals. We would never do such a thing or use it as a bargaining chip.” Critics have raced to blame Musk alone, casting him as the puppeteer behind the throne, the first business titan to achieve what William Randolph Hearst, Marcus Alonzo Hanna, and J.P. Morgan only aspired to: a latter-day Cornelius Vanderbilt, who is reputed to have scoffed, “Law? What do I care about the law? Hain’t I got the power?”
That gets the story backward. Musk’s businesses are uniquely dependent on the blessings of Washington: a fifth of SpaceX’s revenue comes directly from federal agencies, its satellites require federal authorization to launch and operate, and the possible merger of Tesla and SpaceX will live or die by the decisions of federal regulators.
Confronted with a White House that appeared determined to squeeze Ukraine, whatever its public denials, Musk faced a familiar choice for anyone dependent on political patronage: capitulate, resist, or retreat into ambiguity. He chose ambiguity, revealing the limits of his power. The wealthiest man in the world still answers to someone else.
The finger-pointing creates a haze of ambiguity, giving both men plausible deniability. The apparent aim is to force Ukraine into a settlement by depriving it of the means to resist: a way to secure a quick, short-term peace and lower oil prices at the expense of Ukrainian sovereignty and international law.
But that calculation mistakes capitulation for stability. Rewarding President Vladimir Putin of Russia could encourage him to test NATO’s resolve in the Baltic states, Poland, Finland, or Sweden, raising the risk of a direct confrontation with the alliance. It would also signal to other U.S. adversaries that sufficient pressure can fold Washington’s commitments.
For now, Trump could claim to have brokered peace between Russia and Ukraine, even if the peace he delivers is the silence of a defeated country. Musk can evade responsibility by presenting himself as merely one supplier among many across the defense industry whose failures have weakened Ukraine’s defenses. He could point to weapons manufacturer RTX, whose Patriot interceptors are so scarce that Ukraine reportedly ran out of them this month, or to delays in delivering F-16s manufactured by Lockheed Martin that were promised two years earlier.
Faustian bargains
Beneath the public quarrel lies a familiar pattern: surrender political independence and retain the freedom to accumulate extraordinary wealth. The historians who have studied Putin’s Russia most closely would recognize the pattern instantly. Timothy Snyder has written that Russia’s oligarchs “were tamed, but not by a neutral state.” Rather, “Putin himself became the head oligarch, the boss of bosses.” Anne Applebaum echoed the insight and described Putin as making himself “godfather to all of the other oligarchs.”
Putin laid out the terms of that bargain on Jul. 28, 2000, when he met with 21 of Russia's richest men in the Kremlin, less than three months after his inauguration. The message was simple. The fortunes they had amassed in the chaos of the 1990s were theirs to keep, as long as they stayed out of politics entirely. Keep your distance from power, and the state would leave you alone.
Those who refused the deal faced immediate reprisals. Boris Berezovsky and Vladimir Gusinsky, whose television networks refused to bend the knee, were driven into exile within the year. Gusinsky’s NTV was seized by state-controlled Gazprom. Mikhail Khodorkovsky, then Russia’s richest man, funded opposition parties and lectured the Kremlin on corruption. In Oct. 2003 he was pulled off his plane at a Siberian airport and arrested. He spent a decade in prison and watched his oil company, Yukos, dismantled and its assets transferred to state-controlled companies.
Those who accepted the deal are the ones who got rich, and they have never been richer. Forbes counted a record 155 Russian billionaires this year, the fourth straight year that number has grown, with a combined fortune of $696.5 billion—up 11% from the previous year, even as Putin’s war against Ukraine entered its fifth year. Their collective wealth reportedly now exceeds the bank term deposits of the rest of Russia’s population: 155 oligarchs with fortunes greater than the savings of roughly 146 million ordinary Russians.
“Oligarchies are unstable,” Snyder has observed. “Members disappear.” For those who might have forgotten the terms of Putin’s bargain, an instructive reminder came in 2023, when Yevgeny Prigozhin, the head of the Wagner Group, did the one thing the bargain forbade: he challenged the Kremlin’s authority. Prigozhin seized a military headquarters in Rostov-on-Don and sent his forces toward Moscow. His column advanced to within 125 miles of the capital before he agreed to stand down under a deal brokered by Aleksandr Lukashenko, the Belarusian dictator.
Putin publicly called the mutiny treason, then appeared to forgive him. Two months later, on Aug. 23, 2023, Prigozhin’s private jet crashed north of Moscow, killing everyone aboard. The Kremlin denied involvement, the U.S. intelligence concluded that the plane had been blown up, and The Wall Street Journal later reported that the operation had been ordered by Putin’s Security Council chief. Putin’s eulogy, delivered the next day, described Prigozhin as a man who had “made serious mistakes in life.” No oligarch in Russia needed the rest of the sentence spelled out.
Prigozhin’s fate is only the most spectacular entry on a longer, murkier list. Since the invasion of Ukraine began in 2022, at least 85 Russian businessmen and officials have reportedly died in unexplained or violent circumstances, many of them figures in the energy industry. Among the dead are three Lukoil executives: board member Alexander Subbotin, who died in May 2022 after a visit to a “shaman” outside Moscow; chairman Ravil Maganov, who fell from a sixth-floor window that September; and vice president Vitaly Robertus, who was found dead in his office in March 2024.
In April 2022, two former energy and banking executives were found dead alongside their families. Vladislav Avayev, a former Gazprombank vice president, was found shot dead in his Moscow apartment with his wife and 13-year-old daughter. Sergei Protosenya, a former Novatek executive, was found hanged at a rented villa in Lloret de Mar, Spain, with his wife and daughter stabbed to death inside. Catalan police concluded that Protosenya had killed his family, then himself. His son rejected that finding, insisting that his father had been in good spirits and had no reasons to kill them and himself.
Transneft vice president Andrei Badalov fell from a 17th-floor window in July 2025. The Moscow Times has counted 18 such fatal falls from windows since 2002. Three days later, Russia’s transport minister, Roman Starovoit, was found shot dead in his car hours after Putin fired him. Another transport official died of supposedly acute heart failure the same day.
A shadow over America
Putin’s Russia offers an extreme and grotesque example of the bargain. Yet some critics see an emerging American version, in a far less violent form. Snyder and Applebaum have warned that Western billionaires risk repeating the mistakes of Russia’s oligarchs under Boris Yeltsin, believing they can manage a strongman for profit, only to discover that he is managing them.
Musk spent more than $277 million to help elect Donald Trump, took a desk in the West Wing, and ran the Department of Government Efficiency like a man who believed he was co-president. When that arrangement flamed out in May 2025, he tried to exercise independent political power by turning against Trump, calling his signature legislation, the Big Beautiful Bill, a “disgusting abomination.” Musk threatened to form a third political party and then briefly launched one. He even taunted Trump about Jeffrey Epstein, posting that the president “is in the Epstein files.”
After Trump publicly mused about terminating his contracts, Musk quickly retreated. He deleted the posts, and conceded that they “went too far.” He returned to the fold, shook Trump’s hand at Charlie Kirk’s memorial, accepted the National Medal of Science from him this month, and became the biggest known donor of the 2026 midterms, giving at least $366 million to Republican groups. He has grown vastly richer in the process: SpaceX’s June IPO made him the world’s first trillionaire, while the company remains the U.S. government’s dominant launch provider, with competitors such as Blue Origin winning only a fraction of the contracts.
Musk’s retreat illustrates the bargain: surrender the freedom to oppose the president and preserve the ability to enrich yourself. By that measure, Musk’s political defeat has come with an extraordinary financial windfall. He won by losing. The throttling of Starlink in Ukraine appears to fit this pattern. Last week, after Trump demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian refineries and Kyiv did not comply, its access to a military-grade version of Starlink was restricted and responsibility disappeared into a haze of accusation and denial.
The costs of such Faustian bargains fall on everyone excluded from them. In Russia, soldiers die at the front by the hundreds of thousands while politically compliant billionaires accumulate obscene fortunes. In Ukraine, drone operators lost contact with their interceptors in mid-flight last week while Russian missiles were in the air; the consequences of a disrupted connection are immediate and potentially fatal. Other customers face the question: can a contract with Starlink be relied upon?
In America, democratic government rests on the principle that neither political office nor private places anyone above the law. Businesses must be free to challenge a president without fearing retaliation, and their owners must remain accountable for their conduct. Those protections help distinguish America from an authoritarian dictatorship like Putin’s Russia.
The Starlink saga does not suggest that America has become Russia. But it raises a troubling question: is political obedience becoming the price of commercial success in America? Putin’s oligarchs struck that bargain in 2000 and have been collecting on it ever since. Whether Americans accept a version of it will depend on how forcefully our institutions and business leaders defend our freedom to say no.

All 14 Indian nationals on a yacht involved in an incident off Yemen's coast are reported safe, the Indian embassy in Yemen said on Friday.
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Thursday they were rescuing a boat carrying 14 Indians that was attacked off Jabal Zuqar island near the Bab al-Mandeb strait, and blamed Saudi Arabia for the attack.

The United Arab Emirates reported an oil spill from a tanker off its coast on Friday, as numerous vessels in Gulf waters come under attack during the US-Israeli war on Iran.
The authorities "detected a tanker oil spill affecting Umm Al Quwain's beaches," the Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said in a statement, referring to an emirate north of Dubai.

The Future Investment Initiative had been due to take place from 26 to 29 October.
The authority said it postponed the UN data forum and the Saudi statistical forum to ensure broad international participation by speakers, experts and partners, and the delivery of an event that meets the expectations of the global data and statistics community.

articles.title: Denmark sends ammo to Ukraine for F-16 guns to down drones
articles.body:
- Denmark delivered more than 50,000 rounds of 20 mm ammunition to Ukraine on an expedited basis for the cannons on its F-16 fighters.
- Ukrainian pilots are already using the rounds to shoot down Russia’s jet-powered Shahed-type attack drones, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said.
Denmark has rushed more than 50,000 rounds of 20 mm ammunition to Ukraine for the cannons on its F-16 fighter jets, and Ukrainian pilots are already firing them at Russia’s jet-powered Shahed-type attack drones, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said on Oct. 23, 2026.
The ministry announced the delivery on X, saying Denmark sent the rounds on an expedited basis in response to a Ukrainian request. It described aviation, and the F-16 in particular, as one of the most effective tools against jet-powered Shaheds, and said destroying them requires sufficient stocks of ammunition.
“We are grateful to Denmark for its quick and effective response to our request for additional ammunition. This speed matters directly for strengthening Ukraine’s air defence and protecting people from Russian air attacks,” said Minister of Defence Evgeniy Khmara.
Every F-16 carries an internal M61A1 Vulcan, a six-barrel rotary cannon that fires about 6,000 rounds per minute. Using the gun against drones lets pilots save their far more expensive guided missiles for cruise missiles and other high-priority targets, and 20 mm rounds are held in much larger quantities around the world than Patriot interceptors or Western air-to-air missiles.
The guns burn through ammunition quickly, with Bloomberg reporting that destroying a single jet-powered drone can take about 150 rounds and that, at the current intensity of Russian attacks, Ukraine could need around 10,000 rounds a day. At that rate, the Danish shipment would cover roughly 330 engagements.
Russia began using jet-powered versions of its Geran drones, the Russian-built derivatives of the Iranian Shahed-136, in significant numbers in early 2026. The newer jet models can carry up to 90 kg (198 pounds) of explosives, fly up to 1,000 km (620 miles) and reach speeds of up to 600 km/h (373 mph), making them much harder to catch than the earlier propeller-driven drones. Ukrainian Air Force spokesman Yurii Ihnat has said Ukraine shoots down about 60% of the jet-powered drones, compared with roughly 90% to 95% for other types.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said combat aviation, primarily the F-16, accounts for 55% to 60% of all intercepts of jet-powered Shaheds, and that Ukraine has expanded contracts to keep its F-16 squadrons supplied with 20 mm rounds. Germany has delivered its first batch of F-16 ammunition for countering the drones, and Belgium and Spain have also sent urgent shipments.
Denmark has been one of Ukraine’s main F-16 partners, pledging 19 of the jets and hosting early training for Ukrainian pilots. Ukraine is also testing several domestically built interceptor drones designed to catch jet-powered Shaheds, while its F-16 pilots continue to use their cannons against the drones with the new Danish rounds.

articles.title: US lawmakers urge Trump to ask Musk to let Ukraine use Starlink to strike Russian ballistic missile launchers
articles.body:
US lawmakers urge Trump to ask Musk to let Ukraine use Starlink to strike Russian ballistic missile launchers
A bipartisan group of nearly two dozen members of the US House of Representatives has urged President Donald Trump to ask Elon Musk to give Ukraine access to Starlink systems to target missile launchers on Russian territory.
Source: a letter sent on Wednesday and obtained by The Hill, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The signatories are seven Republican members of the House of Representatives and 16 Democrats.
"We are writing to urge you to ask Elon Musk to let Ukraine use the Starlink satellite internet system to hunt for missile launchers inside Russia. With one phone call, you could both save lives and give Vladimir Putin greater incentives to negotiate," the lawmakers wrote.
"If Ukraine cannot reliably intercept Russian 'arrows', it must be able to shoot the 'archer'. The Starlink system run by Mr Musk's company SpaceX could help with that," they added.
The Republican signatories are staunch supporters of Ukraine: Joe Wilson, Brian Fitzpatrick and Don Bacon, as well as Carlos Gimenez, Jeff Hurd, Andy Harris and Max Miller, who represents a district with a sizeable Ukrainian population.
"Mr President, we all share the goal of bringing an end to the war in Ukraine and the devastating loss of life it has caused. Unfortunately, Putin presently has no intention of stopping the bloodshed," the lawmakers wrote.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has also called for greater US assistance in striking missile launchers on Russian territory.
The bipartisan letter comes as growing numbers of Republicans are expressing their outrage over disruptions to Starlink and its military version, Starshield, in Ukraine.
Background:
- The Wall Street Journal reported that Elon Musk had ordered Starlink services to be slowed down. It is unclear to what extent Trump was involved in discussions about the slowdown.

articles.title: Ukraine troops report ongoing problems with Starlink satellite network
articles.body:
Ukrainian forces continue to report widespread disruptions to the Starlink satellite network, despite Donald Trump’s claim that Elon Musk had lifted restrictions on the service.
The slowdown, which has affected the key communications system used by Ukrainian troops, began last week after Trump and Starlink founder Musk publicly criticised Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, over continued strikes on Russian oil refineries.
The restrictions have raised questions and confusion about who ordered the slowdown and why, with both Trump and Musk denying responsibility.
“I don’t comment one way or the other,” Trump said on Thursday when asked about reports that he had personally called Musk to demand the restrictions be lifted.
“The bottom line: he put it back.”
But Ukrainian officials said on Friday morning that speeds remained capped at about 100mph, with no indication that the restrictions had been lifted.
“At present, we have not observed any lifting of the restrictions on Starlink,” said Serhii Beskrestnov, a military expert who advises Zelenskyy.
“There have been isolated cases in which Starlink has operated at speeds slightly above the imposed limits, but this is likely due to SpaceX’s algorithms or specific conditions of use, rather than any lifting of the restrictions,” Beskrestnov added.
The speed restrictions have prevented Ukrainian military equipment, including drones, from maintaining a connection to the satellite network when travelling at high speeds, hampering both offensive drone operations and efforts to intercept incoming Russian attacks.
The slowing down of Starlink, coupled with Zelenskyy’s complaints that Washington had temporarily suspended intelligence-sharing with Kyiv, have plunged relations between Ukraine and the US to a new low in recent days.
Tensions first flared after Washington’s surprise decision to lift sanctions on Russia and begin importing Russian diesel, as Trump sought to bring down US energy prices before the midterm elections. Maritime tracking data showed that the first tanker carrying Russian diesel was en route to New York on Thursday.
Meanwhile, Russia launched another overnight barrage against Ukraine, even as Moscow said a fresh round of US-brokered talks aimed at ending the war could take place next month.
The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said on Friday that trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US were expected to resume in Abu Dhabi in November. Previous rounds of negotiations have failed to produce a breakthrough, with Moscow and Kyiv far away over the terms of any peace settlement.
Among Russia’s maximalist demands are that Ukraine withdraw its forces from territory it still controls in the east of the country, drastically reduce the size of its military and adopt a neutral status that would rule out Nato membership.
Speaking to a Russian state television reporter late on Thursday, Putin once again questioned Ukraine’s sovereignty, echoing claims he has repeatedly made throughout the war.
“The lands lost by Kyiv are not their territory, they are Russia’s historical lands,” Putin said.
The Russian president also cited unspecified genetic research to revive his longstanding claim that Russians and Ukrainians were “one people”, before insisting that Moscow would achieve all the objectives of its full-scale invasion.

articles.title: Yemeni army strikes Houthi militia weapons sites in Taiz: state media
articles.body:
The Yemeni army has launched air strikes on Houthi militia missile launchers and weapons depots in the southwestern province of Taiz, according to state television.
Yemen TV said on Thursday that the strikes hit missile launchers, radars, military communications systems and weapons depots in western, southern and eastern Taiz.
Fighting between government forces, backed by a Saudi-led coalition, and the Houthi militia has intensified in the province since July.
Separately, Yemen’s interior ministry said on Thursday that shelling by the Houthi militia had caused extensive damage to a mosque and a school in Al-Najd village in the Mashra’a Wa Hadnan district, south of Taiz.
In a statement on X, the ministry reported significant material damage but did not say whether there were any casualties.
The official Saba news agency, citing a local source, identified the buildings struck as the Omar al-Tayyar Mosque and School.
Houthi militia claims attacks on Saudi Arabia
Meanwhile, Houthi militia military spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed on Thursday that the Houthi militia had carried out four operations targeting sites in Saudi Arabia with ballistic missiles and drones over the previous 48 hours.
In a statement on X, Saree said the attacks targeted the Saudi defence ministry building in Riyadh, King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu and Abha International Airport.
He claimed the strikes had hit their targets, disrupted operations at Dammam airport and caused a fire at the Aramco facility in Yanbu.
Saree also alleged that Saudi forces had carried out more than 2,900 airstrikes and missile attacks over the past 100 days, killing or injuring more than 562 people.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthi militia seized Sanaa and several other provinces in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognised government.
The Houthi militia controls much of northern and western Yemen, while government forces and their allies hold Aden and large parts of the south and east.

articles.title: Saudi-led coalition says it intercepted 11 Houthi drones and a ballistic missile
articles.body:
Saber Ghanem Ibrahım Eıd
23 October 2026•Update: 23 October 2026
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthi group said Thursday that its air defenses intercepted and destroyed 11 drones and a ballistic missile.
The drones were intercepted over Riyadh, Medina, the Eastern Province and the southern region, while the ballistic missile was intercepted as it headed toward Najran in southwestern Saudi Arabia, coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki said in statements posted on the US social media platform X.
In its latest statement Thursday, the coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed two drones launched toward the southern region.
Earlier, it reported the interception of four drones over Riyadh and Medina, one over Riyadh and four over the Eastern Province.
The statements did not provide details on where the drones were launched from or whether the interceptions caused damage or injuries.
The announcements came a day after Saudi authorities reported that four people had been killed in attacks in the country’s Eastern Province.
Two died from falling debris after air defenses thwarted an attempted drone strike on an Aramco oil facility, while two others were killed in an attack targeting King Fahd International Airport in Dammam.
The coalition also reported intercepting seven drones Wednesday, including one heading toward the southern region and six over Medina and the Eastern Province.
The latest developments come amid an ongoing escalation between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthi group since July, alongside renewed fighting between the Houthis and Yemen’s internationally recognized government.
Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting Yemen’s government against the Houthis since March 2015.
The group has controlled the capital, Sanaa, and other parts of Yemen since September 2014.

articles.title: Ukraine Brings Home 270 in POW Exchange, Including 5 Previously Believed Dead in Olenivka Attack
articles.body:
Ukraine has brought home 270 people in a prisoner exchange with Russia, including military personnel and nine civilians, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Friday, Oct. 23.
Most of those released had been held in Russian captivity since 2022, and five were previously believed to have died in the July 2022 Russian attack on the Olenivka prison.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“270 of our people are home. A very important result,” Zelensky wrote on Telegram.
Those released include members of Ukraine’s National Guard, including fighters from the Azov unit, as well as border guards, Territorial Defense members, and personnel from the Navy, Ground Forces, Air Assault Forces, and State Special Transport Service.
According to Zelensky, most of those returning are soldiers who defended the besieged southern port city of Mariupol. Others served in the Donetsk, Luhansk, Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia, Kherson, Kyiv, Mykolaiv, and Chernihiv sectors.
Many of the released Ukrainians had been illegally convicted in Russia, Zelensky said.
Among those returning are five people who were previously believed to have died during Russia’s July 2022 attack on the Olenivka prison, where Ukrainian prisoners of war were held.
According to open-source data, more than 53 Ukrainian defenders were killed and over 130 wounded in the mass killing of Ukrainian prisoners of war at Penal Colony No. 120 in Russian-occupied Olenivka (Donetsk region) on the night of July 29, 2022. Most of the victims were members of the Azov Regiment who had defended the Azovstal steel plant in Mariupol.
Ukraine Expands Satellite Cooperation With Finland as Starlink Doubts Linger
“We remember every single person and continue the search for everyone,” Zelensky wrote, thanking those involved in securing the exchanges.
He also thanked Ukrainian troops on the front lines for capturing Russian personnel, which he said helps Ukraine bring its own people home through prisoner exchanges.
150 Russian soldiers traced by families through Ukrainian project
Meanwhile, the Ukrainian state project I Want to Find (Khochu Nayti), which provides information about Russian military personnel captured, missing, or killed in Ukraine, reported on Telegram that 270 Russian soldiers had returned to Russia in the exchange.
More than half of those released – 150 people, or 56 percent – had been located by their relatives through the project. It helped their families confirm their captivity, enabling them to secure official prisoner-of-war status for the soldiers in Russia.
According to the project, 40 percent of those exchanged had spent less than a year in captivity, while another 43 percent had been held for one to two years. Only 17 percent had been in captivity for more than two years.
“For comparison: in the August exchange, more than half of the military personnel whom Russia brought back from captivity had spent less than a year there,” the report stated.
Half of those returned were between 35 and 44 years old, while young men aged 19 to 24 accounted for the next-largest group, at 21 percent. The exchange also included 11 prisoners of war aged over 55.
Ahead of the elections, Russian authorities announced they were prepared to include residents of the Russian-occupied parts of Donetsk and Luhansk regions who had been recruited into the Russian Armed Forces on prisoner-exchange lists. Before that announcement, Russia had refused for years to facilitate the return of these prisoners of war.
“As soon as the elections were over, officials predictably tried to ‘forget’ their promises. However, the prisoners of war themselves and their families continued to push for them to be honored,” the project said.
POWs from the so-called “LDNR” (Donetsk and Luhansk People’s Republics) recorded video appeals and repeatedly asked Russia to include them in exchange lists during interviews.
Many had been in captivity since the beginning of the full-scale war. During that time, they had witnessed numerous exchanges in which Moscow brought home service members who had spent only a few months in captivity, the project noted.
Following public pressure, Russian authorities included dozens of Russian Armed Forces personnel from the so-called “LDNR” in Friday’s exchange. Among them were Dmitry Ryabtsev and Sergey Kharitonov, who had been held in captivity for more than four years.
First major POW exchange in two months
The most recent known return took place on Aug. 24, when Ukraine brought home 10 servicemen via Belarus as a special stage of an exchange previously agreed between the two sides. All 10 had fought in the Donetsk sector and had been listed as missing – two since 2024 and eight since 2025.
Earlier, on Aug. 19, Ukraine and Russia exchanged 103 prisoners each. Those released to Ukraine included members of the Armed Forces, Border Guard Service, and National Guard who had fought in Mariupol and other sectors.
In April, Kyrylo Budanov, head of Ukraine’s Presidential Office, announced preparations for another exchange shortly after Ukraine brought home 182 people in its 72nd prisoner swap.
The group included 175 military personnel and seven civilians, many of whom had been held in captivity since 2022. Among them were defenders of Mariupol and the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant.
At the time, Budanov said a larger group could not be returned immediately because of what he described as bureaucratic delays on the Russian side.

articles.title: Witkoff Meets Putin: the Upshot?
articles.body:
Following the meeting between Vladimir Putin and US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg, talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US are set to resume. However, Witkoff describing Putin as a “humanitarian” during the meeting has drawn criticism even from US Republicans. The press looks at who stands to benefit from Trump’s attempts at mediation.
Embarrassing and incompetent
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Der Standard (Austria) takes issue with the American special envoy’s fawning praise of Putin:
“No one has ever called him that before. That’s a first. How will Vladimir Putin react to Donald Trump’s envoy, Steve Witkoff, calling him a ‘humanitarian’? Witkoff is a property developer and Trump’s golfing buddy, and together with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, he keeps meeting up with Russian envoys and Putin himself in a bid to end the war in Ukraine. Two wheeler-dealers with no clue about foreign policy who have achieved absolutely nothing so far.”
Kremlin relying on attrition
The US’s haste risks rewarding Russia for its patient strategy, La Stampa (Italy) warns:
“Putin can already derive political advantages from the negotiations, without having to halt the war. Winter will put this strategy to the test. Moscow will seek to weaken Ukraine while the Ukrainians try to protect their cities and hold the front line. In the meantime, acts of sabotage, cyber-attacks and disinformation aim to undermine European unity and the consensus on aid to Ukraine. Putin is banking on wearing down Ukrainian resistance and the West’s willingness to support Ukraine.”
US Reportedly Plans to ‘Offer’ Ukraine EU Membership for Dropping NATO Bid
Russia’s victory by no means certain
Ukraine is not about to throw in the towel, says Aamulehti (Finland):
“Even if the United States were to side fully with Russia, the war in Ukraine would not end. The massacre in Bucha has shown what happens to Ukrainians at the hands of the Russians, which is why Ukraine will not give up the fight. How long would the war last, and how would it end? Recent history answers that question. France waged war in Indochina for eight years. The US fought the Vietnam War in that region for 20 years, ten of which with its own troops. The Soviet Union waged war in Afghanistan for ten years, and the US for twenty. Each of these wars ended in defeat for the major power waging the war.”
Diabolical old men
Writing on Facebook, author Carina Cockrell-Ferre (Russia) discusses the possibility of a Russian attack on Europe:
“The greatest danger facing Europe is that Putin could form a full alliance with Trump, who then assures him that he will not honour the terms of Article 5 of the Nato Treaty. ... This could indeed lead to a Russian attack on Europe. This is the common ground over which these two diabolical old men have joined forces. ... While Europe may be able to block a bad deal for Ukraine, it is powerless to push through a good one. All it can do is delay a Russian attack on Europe by supporting Ukraine and its armed forces.”
Kremlin giving no sign of being ready to negotiate
Future meetings are also unlikely to yield any tangible results, The Spectator observes (Germany):
“There has been nothing to suggest yet that the Russian president is genuinely ready to make a deal or concede on his war aims. ... Facing the prospect of brutal midterm results for the Republicans in two weeks’ time, Trump is desperate for a win with Russia. Putin can sense this and appears to be using this to play for time ahead of a winter in which he hopes to make substantial progress on subjugating Ukraine. Not for the first time, it is Zelensky who is being forced to jump through hoops and show willing in the hope that doing so will save his country from a stitch-up by an enemy and supposed ally.”
Encouraged to escalate
The US’s policies of recent weeks are having repercussions across the world, the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (Germany) points out:
“Putin and his inner circle are convinced that in the war against Ukraine and their struggle against the West as a whole, they will firstly have the greater staying power, and secondly be able to play the Americans and Europeans off against one another. Everything the American leadership has done in recent weeks confirms this belief. Consequently, the prospect of a ceasefire, not to mention peace in Ukraine, has become even more remote. Instead, the Kremlin is likely to feel emboldened to escalate the conflict even further. ‘Restoring justice of Russians’ takes place above all on the battlefield, Putin’s foreign minister has said.”
Moscow can take its time
Unlike Trump, Putin is not in a hurry, notes Corriere della Sera (Italy):
“For five years now, Vladimir Putin seems to have been applying the old Russian proverb ‘The slower you go, the further you’ll get’ to a war that he originally thought would last no more than two weeks. … So Putin is biding his time, waiting to see how events unfold and what happens with the elections in the US and Europe – and taking whatever he can get without making any concessions. He has the chance to achieve in Washington what he is unable to achieve on the front line; but he also knows that this window of opportunity could be closed again by a single social media post in the middle of the night. ... What the Russian president needs to work out now is whether the path available to Trump will be long enough.”
Trump wanted Putin to win all along
The US President’s supposedly new stance on the war in Ukraine is not really new at all, argues Dagens Nyheter (Sweden):
“Some interpret this as the US changing sides with regard to Ukraine, and it’s easy to understand why Zelensky feels betrayed. Yet this development is nothing new. The difference is that Trump is no longer making a secret of what he has wanted all along: for Russia and his friend Vladimir Putin to win the war. ... Trump’s eagerness to help Putin now is particularly good news for the Kremlin. Russia is in a bad way, both on the front line and at home, where all its oil depots are burning. So it’s good that it has an ally in the White House.”
What is going on in his mind?
Experts will continue to puzzle over the US president’s policy on Ukraine, says Ilta-Sanomat (Finland):
“A clear intention can certainly be discerned behind Trump’s confused remarks on Ukraine and Russia. He wants to take credit for bringing about peace. But does anyone still believe he could actually achieve such a thing? After all this, can anyone still trust Trump’s word when it comes, for example, to security guarantees for Ukraine, which are a key safeguard for peace? ... When the war in Ukraine eventually ends and Trump is no longer president, a lot will be written about current events. Perhaps the most important question then will be: what on earth was going through Trump’s mind? It won’t make for pleasant reading.”
