articles.title: Ukraine Still Recording Starshield Connectivity Losses at 161 Kph, Defense Ministry Source Says
articles.body:
Ukraine is still recording satellite connectivity losses at speeds of 161 kph (100 mph), with no confirmation that restrictions on Starlink and Starshield have been lifted, a source in Ukraine’s defense ministry told Kyiv Post on Friday, Oct. 23.
“Ukraine’s Defense Forces and defense ministry specialists are continuously monitoring Starlink/Starshield connections and recording the results. As of this morning, cases of connectivity loss at speeds of 161 kph are still being observed,” the source said.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“There is currently no confirmation that the restrictions have been lifted,” the person added.
Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, an adviser to the Ukrainian president, also said in a Facebook post that there was no evidence the restrictions had been removed.
“We are not currently seeing the restrictions on Starlink being lifted. There are occasional cases when Starlink can move somewhat faster than the limit, but these are likely the result of SpaceX’s algorithms or specific operating conditions, rather than the removal of the restriction,” Beskrestnov wrote.
The latest assessment comes a day after US President Donald Trump said Elon Musk had restored Ukraine’s satellite service, but did not confirm whether he had personally intervened to lift the restrictions.
“I guess the bottom line, he put it back,” Trump told reporters on Thursday, responding to a Wall Street Journal report that he had called Musk and asked him to restore the service.
Russian Diesel Tanker Heads to New York After Trump-Putin Deal
It remains unclear whether the reported restoration has significantly improved Ukraine’s satellite communications capabilities.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told CNN’s Christiane Amanpour in an interview published Thursday that restrictions were still affecting Ukraine’s military satellite communications.
“Now it’s still limited,” Zelensky said.
CNN reported that some Ukrainian military units saw higher connection speeds after the reported restoration, but improvements were uneven, and restrictions remained.
A source familiar with the situation told CNN that the available speeds were “clearly not enough to intercept jet-powered drones.”
Starlink restrictions undermine Ukraine’s interceptor drones
On Oct. 17, Zelensky said Starlink speeds in Ukraine had been capped at 161 kph, making the system unusable for some interceptor drones designed to destroy Russian jet-powered Shahed attack drones and endangering Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian attacks.
“When an Iranian drone goes with a speed of 450 or 500 kph [280 to 311 mph], and you limit [the speed] one night to 70 or even 100, you cannot intercept anything,” Zelensky told CNN. “And this is terrible.”
Zelensky said Ukraine does not use Starlink to attack Russian military or energy targets inside Russia.
“We don’t attack Russian military targets or energy targets using Starlink. Never,” he said. “That’s why it was strange they limited us in Ukraine. It means limiting our ability to defend ourselves.”
The inability to intercept Russian drones effectively has become a major threat to Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.
Ukraine’s acting chargé d’affaires in the United States, Denys Senik, previously said Kyiv was awaiting an official response from the Pentagon and SpaceX on the full restoration of Starshield services. The system’s performance remained unstable, he said.
According to The Telegraph, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk proposed that Trump restrict Starlink speeds in Ukraine.
The Wall Street Journal subsequently reported that Trump called Musk and asked him to lift the speed restrictions imposed by the SpaceX chief.
Responsibility for restrictions remains unclear
Asked who ordered the restrictions, Zelensky said he did not know whether the decision came from SpaceX or US government institutions.
“I don’t know,” he said. “Technically, I think SpaceX can do it. But whether the decision comes from them or from some institutions, I don’t know.”
Musk said Starshield, SpaceX’s military-grade satellite service, is controlled by the US government.
But US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has maintained that Starlink is a commercial product whose operating decisions are made by SpaceX, while saying Ukraine’s request for broader access to Starshield remained under discussion.
The Pentagon has denied issuing instructions to slow the system.

articles.title: Countering China’s web of spies and proxies
articles.body:
After a car struck comedian Huang Yi-hao (黃逸豪) while he rode a scooter near his home in New Taipei City on Sept. 11, prosecutors said the collision was staged and a person in China identified only as “K” paid five Taiwanese men NT$450,000 (US$13,900) to seriously injure him.
They did so to allegedly prevent him from performing on Sept. 20 after he mocked Chinese leader Xi Jinping. The case illustrates a broader danger.
Beijing’s campaign against Taiwan increasingly relies not only on military pressure but on covert networks that exploit an open society: surveillance, influence operations, recruitment, criminal facilitation and transnational repression. Taiwan should treat these sub-threshold threats with the same seriousness as a conventional military attack.
Chinese Communist Party organs and intelligence services operate through layers of intermediaries. The United Front Work Department helps cultivate political, religious, business and diaspora contacts, while the Ministry of State Security and Ministry of Public Security conduct intelligence, security and repression operations.
These agencies do not merely gather information. They seek local collaborators who can map communities, move money, monitor critics and amplify divisions.
Taiwan’s counterintelligence agencies have described a spectrum of activity. Professional intelligence officers operating under nonofficial cover, “white glove” intermediaries who conceal funding and instructions, talent spotters who identify vulnerable targets, local collaborators who provide logistics or amplify narratives, and informants who pass along unclassified but useful information. Some networks also use criminal groups for intimidation or violence.
Executive security and coercion
The Huang case fits this pattern. Prosecutors said the alleged organizer used local proxies to track Huang with a GPS device, collect personal information and stage the collision. It was transnational repression carried out through deniable local intermediaries.
Beijing also seeks leverage over Taiwan’s leadership. In October, the FBI arrested Wanying “Heather” Zhang, a California real estate agent, at Los Angeles International Airport on charges that she acted as an unregistered agent of China.
Federal prosecutors allege that Zhang and another person traveled to the Seattle area in September 2025, surveilled the home of Lai Ting-yu (賴廷與), the adult son of President Lai Ching-te (賴清德). They allegedly sent photographs, video and vehicle license-plate information to a Chinese government official.
The case remains pending, and the allegations have not been tested at trial. But if proven, they would show how Chinese intelligence can extend pressure beyond Taiwan’s borders and seek information useful for coercion.
In August, New Taipei District Court sentenced Hsu Chun-ying (徐春鶯), a Taiwan-based advocate for spouses born in China, to seven years in prison. The court found that she conspired with Chinese officials and proxies to influence Taiwanese politics and illegally transferred NT$24.5 million (US$760,000) outside regular banking channels.
The case shows how foreign-linked funding can enter domestic politics through informal financial channels. It does not prove that every recipient of such money knowingly acted as a Chinese agent, but it demonstrates why Taiwan needs stronger transparency rules for political financing, lobbying and cross-border money flows.
Money and legislative pressure
Beijing also benefits when Taiwan’s own democratic processes delay defense spending. Opposition lawmakers have repeatedly delayed or altered parts of the defense budget.
Critics argue that some changes have weakened operational readiness, while supporters describe them as legitimate legislative oversight. The more defensible point is that Beijing has an interest in exploiting political division, and Taiwan’s parties should avoid actions that create avoidable gaps in defense readiness.
Frontline agencies have also been penetrated. Chuang Tsung-hui (莊宗輝), former director of the duty command center of the Coast Guard Administration’s Kinmen-Matsu-Penghu Branch, was detained in May 2025 and indicted in August 2025 on national security and corruption charges. Authorities said he leaked duty rosters, personnel files, vessel deployment schedules and radar-related data to Chinese officials in exchange for bribes. He was convicted in March.
Such leaks can help Beijing understand patrol patterns, radar coverage and deployment routines. In a blockade or quarantine scenario, that intelligence could reduce Taiwan’s ability to detect and respond to coercive maritime activity.
Taiwan has also confronted attempted defections. Prosecutors said an Army lieutenant colonel surnamed Hsieh (謝) was recruited through a retired officer and offered NT$488 million to fly a CH-47 Chinook helicopter to a Chinese naval vessel near the median line of the Taiwan Strait.
The plot was not merely about stealing an aircraft. A successful defection could have provided China with a Western-made heavy-lift helicopter and delivered a psychological blow to Taiwan’s military and public.
Technology and academia
China also targets Taiwan’s semiconductor sector and universities. Taiwanese investigations have accused Chinese-linked entities of using shell companies and recruitment schemes to obtain semiconductor expertise and proprietary information.
The policy concern is straightforward: Taiwan’s “silicon shield” depends not only on fabrication capacity but on the protection of engineers, intellectual property and supply-chain knowledge.
Academic exchanges also create exposure. The 2017 case involving Zhou Hongxu (周泓旭), a Chinese national who studied at National Chengchi University and was later convicted of espionage, showed how student or professional cover can be used to identify and approach politically connected targets.
Taiwan should preserve academic openness while applying consistent security screening, transparency requirements and counterintelligence awareness to high-risk exchanges.
Taiwan cannot meet this challenge by treating every Chinese national, Taiwanese businessperson, temple group or China-born spouse as a spy. Such an approach would damage social cohesion and play into Beijing’s strategy of division.
Instead, Taiwan should:
- Prosecute coercion, espionage, illegal political financing and transnational repression firmly and impartially
- Require greater disclosure of foreign funding in political campaigns, lobbying, civil society organizations and media
- Harden protection for political figures, military personnel, Coast Guard and other frontline agencies
- Improve counterintelligence training for universities, technology firms and local governments without stigmatizing entire communities
- Treat cognitive warfare and influence operations as national-security threats, while protecting free speech and due process
The Huang Yi-hao case is a warning. Beijing does not need to invade Taiwan to weaken it. It can use money, intermediaries, intimidation and information operations to make Taiwan more fearful, divided and difficult to govern. The response must be firm, lawful and democratic.
Guermantes Lailari is a retired US Air Force Foreign Area officer who holds advanced degrees in international relations and strategic intelligence.

articles.title: Why Russia wants peace between Iran and the Gulf
articles.body:
Why Russia wants peace between Iran and the Gulf
On October 18, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov visited Manama, where he attended the ninth ministerial meeting of the Russia-Gulf Cooperation Council strategic dialogue and held separate talks with the foreign ministers of Saudi Arabia and Kuwait. The following day, he traveled to Tehran to meet with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and President Masoud Pezeshkian.
In Manama, discussions centered on de-escalation in the Persian Gulf, maritime security, and Russian proposals for a collective security framework, while bilateral meetings provided an opportunity to clarify individual countries’ positions. Lavrov and his Kuwaiti counterpart stressed the need to reduce tensions quickly and agreed that a political and diplomatic settlement is the only viable way forward. In Tehran, regional affairs featured alongside Russian-Iranian cooperation, with Moscow reaffirming its commitment to economic and investment agreements despite the deteriorating security environment.
Diplomacy between the Gulf’s two shores
The trip aimed to prevent a new divide between Iran and the Arab monarchies from becoming entrenched, as the consequences of the US-Israeli aggression against Iran are affecting the security of the entire region. Yet rebuilding trust also requires acknowledging that the Gulf states have their own grievances against Tehran over strikes on their territory and threats to maritime routes.
During the Manama talks, Arab representatives explicitly said they hope Moscow would use its relationship with Iran to convey their concerns. Discussions also covered Yemen, maintaining the ceasefire in Gaza, humanitarian access, and the resilience of energy and food supply chains – the various and interconnected sources of instability plaguing the Middle East.
In Tehran, Lavrov reaffirmed Moscow’s support for restoring security and shipping conditions to what they were before the US-Israeli military operation began. Iran, which sees the attack as the primary cause of the current crisis, likewise stated its commitment to resolving disputes through diplomacy. Agreement on broad principles, however, does not yet amount to agreement on the specific obligations that the parties must accept.
Russia could mediate efforts to de-escalate tensions and mitigate the deterioration in relations between Tehran and the Gulf monarchies, since it maintains close ties with Iran while developing political, economic, and energy cooperation with the Arab states. These relationships allow Moscow to relay messages, identify the scope for compromise, and facilitate direct dialogue, which can easily give way to competing ultimatums during a crisis.
However, this two-way access does not mean Moscow can dictate what its partners actually decide, and its closeness to Tehran may raise questions among Arab participants. The effectiveness of Russian mediation will ultimately depend on whether the parties themselves are willing to negotiate, acknowledge one another’s concerns, and take practical steps to address them.
Inclusive security as an alternative to permanent crisis
In Manama, Lavrov once again presented Russia’s updated concept of collective security in the Persian Gulf as a potential contribution to a lasting settlement. The proposal continues a longstanding initiative rather than a document developed solely for this visit. As early as June, he reported that updated proposals had been circulated to regional capitals and that Moscow was receiving initial responses.
The approach rests on the premise that the Arab monarchies and Iran must take part in a shared framework, because attempts to secure one group of states by isolating another reproduce the causes of confrontation. Confidence-building measures and regular contact are intended to reduce uncertainty gradually, while the Gulf countries and their immediate neighbors should have the decisive voice in shaping the regional order.
An earlier Russian concept circulated at the United Nations in 2019 already envisaged a gradual normalization of conditions, respect for sovereignty, the peaceful settlement of disputes, and the development of collective security mechanisms. The current proposals can be assumed to carry over the same spirit, even if specific provisions have changed or been updated.
Moscow has argued that the region needs an inclusive security system of its own, free from external military intervention and imposed political arrangements. This does not rule out international assistance, however, as Russian diplomacy allows for support from outside actors, including members of the UN Security Council, provided that it serves the interests of regional states.
The practical value of this model will depend on whether broad principles can be translated into agreed procedures for preventing incidents, protecting civilian infrastructure, and keeping maritime routes open. These arrangements could provide the first steps towards a more stable order, whereas an attempt to resolve every political disagreement at once could obstruct even limited measures to ease tensions.
Why expensive oil does not make war good for Russia
Western media and expert debates, including those focused on Middle Eastern politics, frequently portray Russia as a beneficiary of the war, arguing that disruptions to Gulf supplies drive up energy prices and create opportunities for Russian exporters.
A short-term price benefit is certainly possible, but to assume that war gives Russia a strategic advantage is analytically unsound, because the country’s national interests are not limited to a single source of export revenue. Additional income from commodity sales says little about the cost of damaged partnerships, postponed investment, and worsening conditions for long-term projects.
The Middle East matters to Russia as a political and economic partner, and stable relations depend on predictable institutions, transport routes, and financial transactions. A prolonged war raises shipping and insurance costs, complicates infrastructure agreements, and forces partners to divert resources from development toward immediate security needs.
This is evident in Russia’s cooperation with Iran, where its projects require a stable operating environment. In Tehran, Lavrov spoke of Russian specialists gradually returning to the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant, as well as prospects for cooperation in hydrocarbon production and transportation. A protracted war creates additional risks for these activities, and higher oil prices cannot remove them.
Moreover, a sustained energy shock can weaken the global economy, while the resulting decline in demand limits exporters’ initial gains. Even if some consequences of a Middle East war can benefit Russian suppliers in the short term, claims that Moscow wants endless war in the region are superficial at best. Russia’s strategic interest lies in the region’s long-term stability, which would allow it to preserve partnerships, markets, and opportunities for economic engagement.
Regional autonomy in a changing world order
The transformation of the world order and the erosion of Western hegemony give Middle Eastern states greater scope to pursue independent policies, but a redistribution of international influence does not in itself resolve regional disputes. If dependence on external guarantees is merely supplemented by new competing patrons, while mechanisms for direct dialogue remain weak, the Middle East will continue to serve as an arena where local conflicts intersect with rivalry among major powers.
Regional autonomy requires that neighboring states agree on rules for coexistence, even when their foreign policy priorities and perceptions of threats differ substantially. A durable system will require mutual respect for sovereignty, a rejection of imposed military solutions, and recognition that lasting security cannot be built on another state’s permanent vulnerability.
Russia can support this process by providing diplomatic channels and helping identify a workable sequence of agreements, but only the countries of the region can build a peaceful future. External mediation delivers results when it supports an existing willingness to compromise, while even substantive initiatives can remain on paper if that willingness is absent.
Lavrov’s visits to Manama and Tehran highlighted an opportunity to connect urgent de-escalation with discussions about a more durable regional order. Seizing this opportunity will take time and difficult political decisions, because the parties will need to constrain their own use of force, rebuild damaged trust, and accept reciprocal obligations. Moscow can mediate this process, but its outcome will depend on the desire and readiness of the Gulf states and Iran to reach an agreement.

articles.title: US midterms: Where key candidates stand on Israel, Gaza and Iran
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US midterms: Where do candidates in key Senate races stand on Israel, Gaza, and Iran?
Washington, DC - The midterm elections in the United States are in full swing, with early voting starting in most states.
The results will set the tone of US foreign and domestic policy for the rest of President Donald Trump's term. Control of both chambers of Congress - the Senate and the House of Representatives - is at stake.
If the Democrats flip one of the two chambers, which are currently under the control of Trump's Republican Party, they can thwart Trump's legislative agenda.
And if they can gain control of the Senate, they can block his judicial nominees. The upper chamber is also responsible for confirming cabinet appointees, ratifying treaties and holding impeachment trials.
There are 35 seats in the 100-member chamber up for grabs in this year's election, which will conclude on 3 November.
The current makeup of the Senate is now 53-47, so the Democrats need to flip four seats without losing any to reclaim the majority in the legislative body.
In most Senate races, the results are all but known before the votes are cast due to the political makeup of the states where the contests are playing out.
Barring a miracle, Republicans will win in Alabama, and Democrats will win in Massachusetts. That leaves a handful of competitive states that will determine the fate of the Senate.
The New Arab looks at the candidates in five key close races and where they stand on the issues.
Michigan (open seat): Abdul El-Sayed (Democrat) v Mike Rogers (Republican)
The Senate contest in Michigan is one of the most closely watched races in the election. Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive public health advocate, is taking on Mike Rogers, a Trump-backed former Congress member.
In recent weeks, Rogers and his allies have tried to focus the race on El-Sayed's Muslim identity, smearing him with baseless accusations of ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, Hezbollah, Hamas, and Iran.
Trump has repeatedly mocked El-Sayed's name. "His name is actually Abduladadalalala. It's Adulbabababababa Mohammed Al-Sayed," the US president said at a rally last week.
El-Sayed has pushed to refocus the race on the issues - particularly the affordability crisis, tariffs and the rise in the price of gasoline linked to the Iran war and his support for universal healthcare.
The progressive Democrat opposes US aid to Israel and argues that Washington should focus on investing in communities at home.
He has accused Israel of carrying out a genocide in Gaza - an allegation backed by leading human rights groups and United Nations investigators.
"I oppose the illegal and unjustifiable war in Iran and demand an immediate end to the hostilities," El-Sayed says on his platform.
Rogers initially supported the war with Iran, calling the decision to launch the conflict the "right thing to do".
But the former Republican legislator curbed his enthusiasm for the conflict as it dragged on and proved unpopular with voters. "The war with Iran needs to end, and end quickly," he said in a campaign ad in September.
Rogers is a staunch supporter of Israel. "When I get to the United States Senate, I will continue to unconditionally support Israel's right to defend itself," he said earlier this year.
Texas (open seat): James Talarico (Democrat) v Ken Paxton (Republican)
In a sign that highlights the declining popularity of Republicans, Democrats are mounting a competitive Senate challenge in deep-red Texas, which has been a Republican stronghold for decades.
Public opinion polls have shown Democratic State Representative James Talarico neck-and-neck with Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton.
Talarico has focused his campaign on fighting corruption, closing tax loopholes and lowering the cost of living. Paxton has presented himself as a defender of Trump's agenda, emphasising securing the southern border against irregular migration.
On foreign policy, Talarico calls for conditioning US aid to Israel. He broadly backs Israel's right to "defend itself", while focusing his criticism of Israeli atrocities in Gaza and the West Bank on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"As a former teacher, seeing the death and the destruction in Gaza, seeing what’s happening to children in particular, makes me sick to my stomach," he said at a CNN townhall last week.
Talarico has stopped short of calling the atrocities a genocide, saying that the issue is a legal determination that should be made by international courts.
He has pledged to work to "end the forever war in Iran that’s driving up the cost of gas and groceries".
In contrast, Paxton has backed Trump's military action in Iran, but in a recently leaked audio recording he bemoaned the war's impact on gasoline and diesel prices.
"It's the war, it's gas prices, it's diesel," he said when asked about the issues dragging his campaign, according to Axios, which first reported on the leaked remarks.
Paxton is a strong supporter of Israel. As attorney general, he has defended and enforced laws to penalise companies and individuals that boycott Israel.
Maine: Susan Collins (Republican incumbent) v Troy Jackson (Democrat)
Maine generally leans Democratic in presidential elections, but Republican Susan Collins has won five consecutive elections in the northeastern state, earning her a reputation as one of the most tenacious politicians in the country.
This time, Democrats are hoping to use the mounting anger against Trump to finally topple the 73-year-old senator.
But the Democratic push was off to a terrible start after the party's nominee, Graham Platner, stepped down due to allegations of sexual misconduct.
Platner was replaced by former state Senate President Troy Jackson.
Collins, who has shown willingness to break with Trump, has promoted herself as an experienced and hardworking "common sense" leader.
Jackson has focused on his deep roots in the state as a former logger and supporter of workers' rights.
The Democrat agrees that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza. "When I'm in the US Senate, I’ll never vote in favour of US taxpayer-funded military aid to Israel," he wrote in a social media post in July.
Collins is an unflinching advocate for Israel and has backed continuing military aid to the US ally, calling herself a "strong supporter" of the assistance, which totals at least $3.8 billion annually.
On Iran, the Maine senator has been a rare Republican dissenter against the conflict, voting repeatedly with Democrats to curb Trump's war powers.
Jackson, however, has argued that Collins' presence in the Senate tilts the balance in favour of Republicans and enables Trump's agenda, including the Iran war.
"Senator Susan Collins says that she voted against [the war] nine times, but she didn’t have the votes," Jackson said during a debate earlier this month.
"Well that sounds like then we probably ought to have Democrats in charge of the US Senate so that we have the votes."
Alaska: Dan Sullivan (Republican incumbent) v Mary Peltola (Democrat)
Alaska is another traditional Republican stronghold where Democrats are making gains and hoping to stage a big surprise.
The race pits Trump-backed two-term senator Dan Sullivan against former Democratic Congresswoman Mary Peltola. The Democratic candidate's campaign slogan is "fish, family, freedom", focusing on lowering costs in Alaska.
Sullivan is running on his record of helping push large tax cuts and "historic investments" in the US military. The senator has voted consistently against Democratic efforts to restrict Trump's ability to continue the war with Iran.
Last week, he appeared to blame the Democrats' energy regulations for the rising fuel prices in an effort to defend the war with Iran.
"Ladies and gentlemen, the conflict in the Middle East is temporary. The true forever war is the national Democrats’ war against Alaska oil and gas and our jobs. That’s the forever war," he said, according to Alaska Public Media.
Peltola has been overtly critical of the war and Sullivan's votes in support of Trump's military campaign in Iran.
"This war is driving up our energy bills and hurting Alaskans with no end in sight," she said earlier this month.
Both Peltola and Sullivan are staunch Israel supporters. Sullivan has voted repeatedly on pro-Israel measures in Congress, including sponsoring a measure to deepen military cooperation with the US ally.
When she served in the House of Representatives between 2023 and 2025, Peltola was one of the most uncompromising pro-Israel Democrats.
In 2024, she joined Republicans in voting to ban then-President Joe Biden from withholding weapons from Israel. She backed a bill to impose sanctions on the International Criminal Court in response to the arrest warrant against Netanyahu.
Ohio: Jon Husted (Republican incumbent) v Sherrod Brown (Democrat)
Former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown is attempting to make a comeback in the Midwestern state that has been trending in Republicans' favour over the past decade.
He is taking on Jon Husted, who replaced Vice President JD Vance in the Senate after the Trump administration took office last year.
Beyond the single seat, the contest is of symbolic importance. It would restore the Democrats' competitive edge in the Midwestern state and serve as an early dig at Vance, who is expected to run for president in 2028.
Brown has made his opposition to the Iran war a key theme in his campaign.
"Jon Husted has voted 14 times to continue the reckless Iran war as gas and grocery prices continue to rise," he recently wrote in a social media post. "I’ll vote to end the war the first chance I get."
In March, Husted proclaimed that the war was going "much better than anyone thought it would".
But like other Republicans in competitive races, he has tempered his support for the conflict.
"The war needs to come to an end as quickly as possible so that we can lower gas prices," he told Politico earlier this month.
Husted and Brown are more closely aligned when it comes to Israel. Both are strong supporters of the US ally.
Ali Harb is a journalist based in Washington, DC. His work focuses on US foreign policy, elections, and Arab American communities

articles.title: Trump Invokes Defense Production Act to Boost Oil Production
articles.body:
President Donald Trump has invoked a Cold War-era law in an effort to boost oil production and lower energy prices.
In a presidential memorandum issued Thursday, Trump determined that petroleum production, refining, and related activities are essential to national defense under the 1950 Defense Production Act. The determination follows Trump’s declaration of a national energy emergency in January 2025.
“Ensuring resilient domestic petroleum production, refining, and logistics capacity is central to United States defense readiness,” the memo reads. “Without immediate Federal action, United States defense capabilities will remain vulnerable to disruption.”
The memo comes as the price of gas and diesel has soared across the country amid supply disruptions caused by the U.S. and Israel’s war against Iran. Brent crude futures rose 1.2% to $114.47 a barrel early Friday, extending gains after Thursday hit a five-month high. U.S. diesel pump prices averaged $6.32 a gallon, slightly higher than Thursday but below the September record, according to AAA. The high energy prices, and related inflation, have become a defining issue for voters in the coming midterm elections.
Here’s what to know.
What does the memo mean for energy production?
The memo means that energy production shortfalls are seen as a national defense risk.
The memo invokes Section 303 of the Defense Production Act, a law that allows the federal government to intervene in private industry for national defense. Section 303 allows the President to make purchases, purchase commitments, provide financial support and equipment, and expand production through other measures.
The memorandum also removes certain Section 303 requirements through an emergency waiver, including ordinary congressional notification and authorization constraints.
While the memo does not specify which projects could be funded, Vice President J.D. Vance said last week that the Administration would use the Defense Production Act to expand capacity at a Delek U.S. Holdings-owned refinery in Texas.
Without taking action, the memo said, U.S. industry would be unable to provide sufficient energy services in a “timely manner due to constrained financing, long lead times, permitting and infrastructure bottlenecks, and supply chain limitations.”
Has the Defense Production Act been invoked before?
Enacted during the Korean War, the Defense Production Act was first used to expand domestic industries in critical materials, such as aluminum and titanium, for national defense.
Section 303 of the act was also used during the pandemic to fund domestic production of medicines and vaccines. Former President Joe Biden also invoked the statute to support clean energy manufacturing and supply chains, including minerals used in electric vehicle batteries and the production of of energy-efficient heat pumps and insulation.
In April, more than a month after Iran began disrupting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz in retaliation for U.S.-Israeli Feb. 28 strikes, Trump invoked the act to declare petroleum, natural gas, coal, electricity grid, and other energy infrastructure essential to national defense. Citing April’s natural gas determination, the Department of Energy on Monday committed up to $42 million to advance the proposed Constitution Pipeline linking Pennsylvania and New York. The department also announced up to $50 million last week for transmission upgrades in Virginia and West Virginia, citing April’s grid determination.
Last year, Trump signed legislation providing $1 billion for Defense Production Act activities, including energy projects deemed critical to national security.
Trump’s use of Section 303 of the act for fossil fuel projects has drawn criticisms from environmentalists, with the Center for Biological Diversity calling the April memoranda, which waived congressional notification, “unlawful.” Nevertheless, the statute expressly includes energy production and construction in its definition of national defense.
How else has Trump tried to lower energy prices?
The Trump Administration has pursued a number of other measures aimed at lowering energy prices since the Iran War began. Earlier this month, Trump signed an executive order temporarily expanding access to tax-exempt dyed diesel, which is typically reserved for off-road farm and construction vehicles. The Group of 7 countries, including the U.S., also agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil reserves to the world over four months.
In August, the Administration extended the Jones Act waiver for another 90 days, allowing foreign-flagged ships to transport oil and certain other commodities between U.S. ports.
Trump also announced an agreement with Putin earlier this month to import diesel from Russia, alongside temporary sanctions relief. The deal has faced significant backlash from lawmakers.
For many of these measures, industry analysts and stakeholders have said the reduction in energy prices is likely to be limited and possibly short-lived. Analysts estimated that the Jones Act waiver was expected to reduce gasoline prices by only pennies per gallon. Capital Economics economist Hamad Hussain said the reserve release could lower diesel prices temporarily, but would not resolve the underlying supply crunch. And analysts warned that the dyed diesel measure would have a limited effect on most consumers since the tax-exempt fuel isn’t widely available at ordinary commercial pumps. A Council on Foreign Relations analysis also suggested that damaged Russian refining capacity may make a near-term effect of the Russia deal on diesel markets unlikely, although Trump said the agreement would supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to U.S. and global markets immediately.
Meanwhile, oil exports from the Middle East topped prewar levels last week, marking a rebound in regional oil shipments despite continuing security risks. Ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz, however, still face attacks from Iran, while the Bab el-Mandeb Strait near Yemen has been threatened by the Houthi rebels. Analysts previously told TIME in June that the risk of further attacks and damage to facilities could delay a full-scale recovery.
Thursday’s memorandum could support investment in fuel capacity, but it’s uncertain how quick or measurable an effect it will have on energy prices. Gas prices still depend heavily on globally traded crude, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, although they can be influenced by domestic refining and distribution conditions. The U.S. was the largest crude producer globally last year, averaging 13.6 million barrels of crude a day.
Analysts warned, after the April memorandum, that federal support would not necessarily translate into immediate price relief.
“Until the pipes are in the ground and the fuel is flowing or transported, it may not be able to be called a true structural shift,” Cyrus Brooks, director of marketing at energy research firm RBAC, wrote in April.
Still, Brooks said of the April action that federal recognition of energy as important to national security could support important infrastructure investment, potentially relieving a bottleneck in domestic fuel production, refining or transportation.
“Energy security seems to be the brightest neon sign flashing,” he wrote. “Not because it’s everything, but because nothing works without it.”

articles.title: Trump turns to Cold War-era law to tackle fuel crisis
articles.body:
Trump turns to Cold War-era law to tackle fuel crisis
US President Donald Trump has invoked a Cold War-era national security law to boost domestic oil production and refining, as rising fuel prices threaten the Republicans’ chances in November’s midterm elections.
Speaking on Thursday at a Republican campaign rally in Iowa – an agricultural state where farmers have been hit hard by the oil crisis – Trump announced that his administration would use the Defense Production Act (DPA) to provide up to $150 million to expand American refining capacity and produce diesel and gasoline “at record levels.”
He also predicted that the Iran and Ukraine conflicts would end soon, sending gasoline and oil prices “tumbling down.”
Enacted in 1950, the DPA allows Washington to financially support industries deemed essential to national defense. In a presidential memorandum, Trump designated domestic petroleum production, refineries, pipelines, and storage facilities as critical to national security, arguing that private companies could not expand capacity quickly enough without federal intervention.
Energy Secretary Chris Wright promised the funds would be deployed in cooperation with private companies, while the Department of Energy separately projected the initiative would increase refining output by millions of gallons of gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, and other products per day.
Vice President J.D. Vance had earlier announced plans to invoke the law to expand a Delek-operated refinery in Tyler, Texas, although such projects typically take months, if not years, to complete.
Trump’s announcement comes as his approval rating has plunged to a record low of 31% – compared with 47% when he began his second term – ahead of the midterm elections on November 3, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll published Monday. The survey also found that 68% of Americans disapproved of his handling of the economy.
Fuel prices in America sharply rose after the US and Israel launched their war against Iran in late February, disrupting global energy supplies. According to the US Energy Information Administration, average gasoline prices have climbed from $2.94 per gallon immediately before the conflict to $4.28 in the week ending October 19, while diesel has jumped from $3.81 to $6.28 over the same period.
The Trump administration has sought to tackle the fuel crisis through several emergency measures, including releasing 172 million barrels from strategic oil reserves, relaxing gasoline-blending requirements, temporarily easing diesel regulations, and announcing additional subsidies for struggling farmers.
In early October, Trump also announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to release more than 300,000 tons of Russian diesel onto global markets, with additional supplies expected later. He has also repeatedly pressed Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, which he blamed for rising fuel prices.
The president’s pressure sparked pushback from Zelensky, who called Trump’s diesel deal with Moscow “a weak decision” and “not fair and not honest” while refusing to comply with the refineries ultimatum. In response, Trump suggested that Ukraine should “get a new president” instead of Zelensky, whose term expired more than two years ago, while calling continued Ukrainian strikes a “disgrace.”

articles.title: Pentagon and Lockheed announce deal for 850 F-35 jets over 10 years
articles.body:
The Pentagon and Lockheed Martin have announced a 10-year agreement for the production of 850 F-35 warplanes, underscoring Washington's long-term commitment to the high-tech stealth aircraft.
The two sides announced the deal on Thursday but did not specify a value for the agreement, which comes as the Pentagon seeks to strike multi-year deals to expand American weapons production and boost the US defence industrial base.
The announcement "cements (the plane's) role as the free world's key frontline fighter for years ahead," Lockheed Chairman, President and CEO Jim Taiclet said on a call with investors.
F-35s — which Washington's forces have used in combat during the US-Israeli war on Iran — come in three versions that can cost more than $100 million per plane.
The "framework agreement," which the Pentagon said would "modernise and expand" the F-35 programme, still requires congressional approval and funding.
"We have fundamentally changed how we stabilise the American defence industrial base to produce at speed and scale," top acquisition official Michael Duffey said in the Pentagon's announcement.
"By aligning financial incentives with actual performance, we are ensuring our warfighters are equipped with the lethal capabilities they need to fight and win," Duffey said.
The F-35, a joint project between the United States and a number of allies, is one of the world's most advanced military aircraft. There are more than 1,375 F-35s based around the world, according to Lockheed.
The deal, if approved, would give Washington a "predictable, affordable, and resilient" fighter jet programme, Lockheed said, pointing to billions of dollars in expected savings thanks to "long-term pricing and industry volume discounts."
'Greater certainty'
In exchange for the Pentagon's 10-year commitment, Lockheed Martin will fund $7 billion in projects supporting the F-35s, the Pentagon said.
"With the greater certainty that comes from the US government's transformative approach to F-35 production and sustainment, we can make the upfront investments needed to expand capacity, improve efficiency, and build a more resilient supply chain," Lockheed's Taiclet said in a statement.
"That's good for the taxpayer, good for our suppliers and, most importantly, good for the United States and its allies," he added.
In addition to the F-35s themselves, the agreement also covers "initial spares, 10 years of modification kits and sustainment, and international customer orders," Lockheed said.
The United States recently announced the approval of a $24.3 billion sale of 48 of the stealth planes to Saudi Arabia last month.
Lockheed said the F-35 programme will support more than 315,000 jobs and generate nearly $80 billion in economic activity in the next 10 years, "strengthening the nation's industrial base and providing long-term stability for suppliers."
The company on Thursday announced better-than-expected earnings for the third quarter, once again benefiting from higher activity levels across all of its segments.
Lockheed shares surged more than seven percent in Thursday trading, closing at $590.2.

articles.title: Trump's midterm election calculations are complicating US policy on Ukraine – Reuters
articles.body:
Trump's midterm election calculations are complicating US policy on Ukraine – Reuters
The upcoming US midterm elections in November may help explain changes in US President Donald Trump's approach to Russia's war against Ukraine and his displays of support for Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
Source: Reuters
Details: Reuters said Trump has shifted his position quite openly on a major political issue over the past month. After criticising Putin, he has begun to show support for him.
Quote from Reuters: "What explains the turnabout? The November midterms may offer a clue."
Details: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, whom Reuters once described as "once Washington's most celebrated wartime ally", has found himself caught in the crossfire of US election politics. Trump is putting increasing pressure on him to reach a peace deal with Putin.
"With US voters increasingly frustrated by high energy prices and the cost of living, Trump has turned renewed attention to the war in Ukraine in recent days, arguing that a negotiated settlement there could help ease economic pressures at home, even though US consumers would be unlikely to feel the effects of any peace deal ahead of the 3 November vote," Reuters said.
Trump has said the war may be closer to ending than ever before and that he wants the death and destruction to stop.
However, Reuters suggested that he may also be calculating that settling the four-year conflict could ease pressure on the US economy, voters' wallets and his own political prospects. Russia is a major oil supplier and has not ruled out a broad economic deal with Washington.
Trump has struck a deal with Putin in the past few weeks, temporarily easing some US sanctions on Russian diesel fuel and lifting others in exchange for Moscow supplying more diesel to global markets.
He is considering meeting Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping next month without Zelenskyy's participation.
Meanwhile, Kyiv has complained that the US satellite system operated by SpaceX installed on high-speed drones stopped working, limiting Ukraine's ability to strike Russian targets and defend itself against attacks.
Quote from Reuters: "The moves are a shift from Trump's earlier criticisms of Putin and a return to more prickly relations between the US and Ukrainian leaders. Ukraine and several European allies have expressed alarm at an apparent pivot by Trump."
Details: Trump has accused Ukraine of driving up global diesel prices through its attacks on Russian oil refineries. He has also suggested that Ukraine needs a new leader.
"Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine," he said at the White House on 19 October.
Trump's envoy Steve Witkoff later called Putin a "humanitarian" for releasing a retired American teacher who had been detained in Russia since 2022.
Quote from Reuters: "The Ukrainian attacks have contributed to higher diesel prices, although market analysts attribute most of the increase to disruptions in fuel shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. That's a consequence of a different war: the US-led one with Iran."
"Trump wouldn't be the first politician to lay blame for inflation abroad. His Democratic predecessor, Joe Biden, pointed to Putin after Russia's invasion of Ukraine caused gasoline prices to surge ahead of congressional elections in 2022."
Details: Reuters noted that voters are not convinced by Trump's arguments. According to a Reuters/Ipsos poll, around 78% of Americans believe his policies are at least partly responsible for rising prices. Most Republicans and Democrats alike identified the cost of living as their main concern.
Meanwhile, Zelenskyy told visiting US lawmakers on 19 October that the latest "decisions on the American side… are hard to explain".
Background: Zelenskyy said he believed Trump could help end Russia's war against Ukraine if he changed his rhetoric towards Putin.

Targets hit
According to the ministry, the Poltava railcar depot in Poltava Region was hit. Its grounds are used by the Ukrainian armed forces to store and repair military equipment.
Russian forces also struck two temporary deployment sites for unmanned surface vessel (USV) operators, a boat mooring area and a USV storage site at the port of Vilkovo in Odessa Region, as well as port infrastructure used to store USVs and prepare them for deployment.
In addition, a cargo ship carrying supplies for the Ukrainian armed forces to the port of Odessa was struck at sea.
Russian troops used Geran drones to strike Norwegian-made mobile NASAMS surface-to-air missile systems in Zaporozhye and Dnepropetrovsk Regions, the Russian Defense Ministry reported, releasing footage of the strikes.
Russian forces also used Geran drones to strike a parked Mi-24 helicopter, a military supplies depot and a production building at one of Ukraine’s industrial enterprises.
Situation in Ukraine
A thermal power plant in Ukraine was damaged in explosions, and electricity generation was halted, Ukrainian energy holding company DTEK said on its Telegram channel.
The company did not disclose the name or location of the thermal power plant.

articles.title: The money starts as bags of cash in a Moscow market and ends up clean in China, leaked files show
articles.body:
Russia's state-backed payment firm A7 took in at least 283 tons of cash rubles, worth more than $14 billion, between November 2024 and July 2025, and turned much of it into payments to China that hide where the money came from, the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ) and Russian investigative outlet Proekt reported on 21 October, citing leaked internal records.
Cut off from Western banks over its war against Ukraine, Russia now moves money the way drug gangs launder theirs: cash goes in, and clean-looking wire transfers come out abroad. The overlap is literal.
Last year, UK investigators found that a network laundering British drug gangs' cash had bought a Kyrgyz bank that was handling payments for Promsvyazbank, Russia's state defense bank. That same bank co-owns A7, which "is also likely to facilitate cash-based money laundering," anti-money-laundering expert George Voloshin told ICIJ. On 1 October, the US Treasury named A7 a "significant transnational criminal organization." Most of the market cash pays Chinese suppliers, and China supplies about 90% of the high-priority Western-restricted items Russia imports for its weapons. Drone makers working for the Russian army are among A7's clients, Proekt found in April.
From market stalls to a defense bank vault
Much of the cash came from Moscow's giant Sadovod market, where broker teams known as "departments" collect bags of rubles from traders, the records show. Vans take the numbered bags to an A7 office, where about 50 cashiers count the money before it is trucked to Promsvyazbank. The bank vaults it and credits A7. At its peak, A7 handled at least 58 tons of cash a month.
Russia's central bank has flagged the problem itself. Money of unknown origin comes "primarily" from Moscow's wholesale and retail markets and from illegal crypto exchanges, a senior Central Bank official said in September, as quoted by ICIJ.
Clean money for Chinese factories
A7 then orders shell companies outside Russia to pay its clients' suppliers, mostly Chinese exporters. The money moves through Kyrgyzstan, largely via the state-owned Trading Company of the Kyrgyz Republic, and the wire transfers carry no trace of cash or of Russia. The records list accounts at ICBC, Bank of China, Agricultural Bank of China, and China Construction Bank. One $287,000 transfer went through Standard Chartered's Hong Kong branch with "Sadovod" recorded as the client.
Chinese banks began refusing Russia-linked payments in December 2023 under the threat of US secondary sanctions. Stripping the funds of their origin makes them easier for Chinese banks to accept, illicit-finance expert Zachary Tvarozna told ICIJ. "The only company that sees everything is A7 itself," Voloshin said.
A7, Promsvyazbank, the Chinese banks, and Kyrgyzstan's economy ministry did not answer ICIJ's questions. A7 has publicly rejected the US accusations, saying it runs "a modern, multi-tiered compliance system."
US Treasury cracks down on Russia-China-Kyrgyzstan payment network, expands sanctions
Sanctioned, but still moving
A7 launched in late 2024, co-owned by Promsvyazbank and led by Moldovan oligarch Ilan Shor, a "sanctioned and convicted criminal fraudster," according to the US Treasury. Ukraine sanctioned its network in February, and the UK followed in May. A7 claimed to have moved more than 7.5 trillion rubles, about 13% of Russia's 2025 foreign trade transactions, and its network also helped Iran sell oil and buy weapons, the Treasury said.
Sanctions did hit A7's crypto side. Daily volume of its ruble token A7A5 fell 96% from its peak by June 2026, blockchain analytics firm Elliptic found. The cash channel is harder to touch: Western banks can see where A7's money lands, but not where it starts.
