- Russia has kept the Red Cross away from Ukrainian POWs since 2024. Now about 1,500 captives it never confirmed as prisoners face prosecution
- Russia keeps hitting Ukraine’s arms plants. Now private developers can dig them space underground—and sell or rent it to them

articles.title: Streeting declines to discuss Faslane shelters
articles.body:
The Secretary of State for Defence has declined to discuss reported ballistic shelters at Faslane in open session, telling the Defence Committee there is a difference between what others report and what the department is willing to say.
Wes Streeting was giving evidence to the committee on the work of his department.
Michelle Scrogham, the Labour member for Barrow and Furness, raised air and missile defence, noting the committee had heard that covering what is needed would cost a billion pounds per city. She said: “I am interested to hear it reported that Faslane is getting ballistic shelters. Are you looking at rolling that out in other areas?”
Streeting said: “There is a danger of my being dragged into a level of operational security detail that I would not want to share in this format.”
Scrogham replied: “It is public knowledge. It is in the UK Defence Journal.”
Streeting said: “There is a difference between what others report and what we are willing to say. Given the spirit in which we engage with this Committee, first, I would always be happy to try to share with the Committee in a closed format as much as we can of that which we would not want to share in an open session. Given your constituency interest in this, I can reassure you that the security of our nuclear deterrent and the enterprise that underpins it is obviously of the highest importance to us. I would be very happy to make sure that we properly brief you as the Member of Parliament for Barrow.”
Faslane on the Clyde is the base for the Vanguard class ballistic missile submarines that carry the continuous at-sea deterrent, and for the Astute class attack submarines. Coulport, a few miles away, stores and loads the warheads. Barrow-in-Furness, which Scrogham represents, is where the submarines are built by BAE Systems.
Earlier in the same exchange Streeting addressed homeland air defence more generally, saying the government is putting £790 million into integrated air and missile defence to modernise older systems and that a layered approach is needed. He noted that Luke Pollard had described the idea of an iron dome for Britain as an iron sieve.
Ministers confirmed in Parliament this month that a future requirement for hardened aircraft shelters across Royal Air Force bases in the United Kingdom has been identified, and that hardened shelters may form part of future infrastructure considerations at RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus.
The Defence Committee reported this week that Russian submarine and sabotage forces in the High North pose direct risks to the North Atlantic and to Britain, including to the nuclear deterrent, and that failure to deter Russia from underwater threats puts subsea data cables and energy pipelines in British waters at particular risk.

articles.title: Sudan: El Fasher civilians suffer unlawful killings, detention and torture one year after city’s capture by the RSF – new testimony
articles.body:
- Surveillance and detentions rife in city
- With limited humanitarian aid, risks of child malnutrition remain high
- “A pervasive pall of fear hangs over El Fasher today” – Agnès Callamard
Civilians in El Fasher in North Darfur, Sudan, are still suffering detention, torture and limited access to humanitarian aid one year after the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) captured the city and committed brutalities against civilians, Amnesty International said today.
In new testimony, residents who recently escaped the city told Amnesty International how schools had been turned into detention centres, how their movement was strictly controlled, and that unlawful killings were rife.
According to figures gathered by humanitarian organizations working in the city, fewer than 70,000 people are present in El Fasher, compared to its pre-war population of more than one million. Humanitarian access remains limited, and humanitarian workers and other civilians in the city are constantly surveilled or monitored. Arbitrary detention risks, for both civilians and humanitarian workers, remain extremely high.
A pervasive pall of fear hangs over El Fasher today
Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General
“The RSF’s claims that El Fasher is safe for civilians to return to after the horrific massacres that took place one year ago could not be further from the truth,” said Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General.
“A pervasive pall of fear hangs over El Fasher today. Men and women live under constant RSF surveillance, and with the ongoing threat of detention, torture and killing.
“One year since El Fasher fell to the RSF, the international community has failed to take the necessary actions to address the desperate plight civilians face as the conflict rages. There has been little accountability for abuses in North Darfur. The moves towards a ceasefire have been half-hearted, and Amnesty International is not aware of any diplomatic attempts to establish an international force that would meaningfully protect civilians.
“Crucially, the United Arab Emirates has continued to support the RSF, while governments with the required influence have largely failed to name and denounce their role or hold them to account.
“Without a ceasefire, accountability, and a protection force, civilians will continue to suffer in El Fasher and across Sudan. The Sudanese Armed Forces have consistently opposed the extension of an arms embargo and a ceasefire, continuing to believe that a military ‘solution’ to the conflict remains possible, thereby also setting aside the suffering of the Sudanese people.”
In August and September 2026, Amnesty International interviewed 25 civilians, including 19 residents and six humanitarian workers, regarding the situation in El Fasher. Of the residents, 15 left El Fasher between July and August 2026 and one was still in the city; the other three had fled earlier.
On 9 October, Amnesty International wrote to the RSF regarding the findings. At the time of publication, no response had been received.
In July 2026, Amnesty International released a major report that documented how the RSF committed crimes against humanity and ethnic cleansing during its campaign to seize El Fasher, with certain ethnic groups, including the Zaghawa, singled out for abuse. Amnesty International continues to document flagrant abuses committed by both parties to the conflict in Sudan, including in El Obeid, North Kordofan, as well as in South Kordofan and Blue Nile States.
Detention, torture, and unlawful killings in prisons
Of the 19 residents interviewed, 17 were detained by the RSF. Most were arbitrarily detained during the RSF capture of the city, while several were detained when they returned to retrieve belongings from their homes or to search for missing family members. They were all held in captivity for months. Several noted that people of particular ethnic groups, notably Zaghawa and Masalit people, were more likely to be detained and abused.
Most men were held in detention centres or prisons, where they witnessed unlawful killings, suffered torture and other ill-treatment, and were given minimal food or water. All were released only after family members paid ransom, or by escaping.
If you sleep a lot, they don’t like that, they will execute you
Modathir*, a 29-year-old Zaghawa man, who was detained in Shala prison
Modathir*, a 29-year-old Zaghawa man, was detained in Shala prison. He was regularly beaten and witnessed unlawful killings. He told Amnesty International: “Torture is something which is permanent in any [RSF] detention. They executed people who tried to look at them… If you sleep a lot, they don’t like that, they will execute you. They ask, ‘You want to take a rest? We will give you permanent rest’.” In July 2026, Modathir escaped, fleeing from house to house in order to reach safety.
Mamoun*, a 33-year-old Zaghawa man, was also held in Shala prison until July 2026. He said he witnessed the RSF shooting prisoners, and the death of a man with untreated diabetes who the RSF refused to help. Mamoun was regularly beaten, and said: “They take people out [of the cell] randomly, they accuse you of being with the Joint Forces or the military… And they beat you until you faint… Sometimes I was beaten four times a day… It just depends on their mood.” Mamoun was eventually released after his family paid a ransom.
Paying ransom was not always a guarantee of freedom. Musa*, a 23-year-old Zaghawa man, said that he and his father were detained at El Fasher Children’s Hospital in October 2025. They were released more than a month later after they paid a ransom. However, instead of being allowed to leave the city, Musa said the RSF took them to an RSF-guarded house and held there until around May 2026 when they were able to escape.
Musa and his father were forced to work for the RSF including collecting corpses, and were sometimes forced to speak on camera to say that the city was inhabitable, encouraging people to return. He said: “They paraded us inside the city and told us to talk [about how] El Fasher is good and safe.”
Detention in schools
Women, children, and some older or injured men were held in schools that were de facto detention centres. They described high rates of malnutrition, including among their own children.
Amnesty International interviewed nine people who were detained by the RSF in schools. They had extremely limited access to food and medical treatment; some women said that their children became malnourished during their detention there. All of these individuals were released or managed to escape by July or August 2026.
Haram*, a 45-year-old Zaghawa woman, and her young children were detained at a school in the Daraja Oula neighbourhood. She told Amnesty International: “[The RSF] were verbally abusing people… Zaghawa people were beaten, [the RSF] would just select and randomly beat [people]. They called us falangayaat women [a slur that indicates slavery or servitude].”
Hadia*, a 30-year-old Gimir woman whose husband was shot by the RSF during their capture of El Fasher, was detained in a school with her children, along with hundreds of other women and children. The RSF provided them very limited food and water.
Hadia was too malnourished to provide her youngest child, aged 18 months, with sufficient breast milk. When she finally escaped and reached Tawila in August 2026, all three of her children were diagnosed with malnutrition; one was hospitalized. Hadia told Amnesty International: “My children were very skinny and weak.”
Aloya*, a 54-year-old Zaghawa woman, spent several months detained in a school. She was afraid that her Zaghawa identity would be discovered and so never spoke the language while there. She said: “Daily there were four to five people dying… mostly from lack of food.”
Hatim*, a 38-year-old Berti man with a serious shrapnel injury in his jaw, was detained by the RSF when he returned to El Fasher to retrieve personal belongings from his house in spring 2026. He was taken to a school where he was kept for about four months with an estimated 300 people, mostly women. He told Amnesty International: “You could not move freely, you had to stay there… [The RSF] beat me up two times I tried fleeing… including on my wounds.” On his third attempt, Hatim was able to escape.
Amnesty International analysed satellite imagery of school detention sites between October 2025 and September 2026. While several sites indicated signs of human activity in previous months, by September 2026 there was little daily activity, suggesting that these detention sites may have been closed. Shala prison and Mina al-Bari detention centre, another facility where residents were held, still showed significant signs of human activity.
‘Everybody is terrorized’: RSF surveillance and limited humanitarian access
El Fasher residents told Amnesty International that while a small number of humanitarian organizations were operating in the city again as of September 2026, the RSF closely monitored their movements and prevented residents from speaking freely to them.
One resident who had returned to El Fasher in June 2026 told Amnesty International: “The El Fasher I knew is gone, it is a completely destroyed city. The public infrastructure, the schools, government institutions, hospitals, all are destroyed… It seemed like everybody is watched very closely, they don’t give humanitarian workers any private space to talk… Everybody is terrorized.”
Another resident said: “There is no complete blockage of [humanitarian] access, but… when organizations are implementing activities [the RSF] will monitor implementation… There are no pictures, no interviews, no interactions of any kind.”
Humanitarian workers expressed concerns about malnutrition, particularly amid a poor harvest season. According to official assessments, IPC Level 5 famine, the highest threshold possible, is highly likely in North Darfur, including in El Fasher, in the months ahead.
Forced labour
Both men and women were subjected to forced labour, such as collecting dead bodies and rubble from El Fasher’s streets, or cooking and cleaning for the RSF without pay.
Misbah*, a 32-year-old Zaghawa man, was detained by the RSF in October 2025. He was brought to a house in the Daraja Oula neighbourhood, where he was forced to cook and clean for RSF officers. He was tied up and given very little to eat. He said he was beaten every day, and said: “I never thought I would survive.”
The RSF should immediately release all those who have been arbitrary detained, and end torture and unlawful killings in detention and elsewhere. The use of forced labour, which is prohibited by international law, must also end.
Amnesty International is again calling for an immediate ceasefire and for the urgent deployment of an international force to protect civilians. All countries must also immediately stop providing arms and ammunition to all parties to the conflict in Sudan. In particular, all countries must cease arms transfers to the United Arab Emirates until it stops supplying weapons to RSF in violation of the UN embargo on Darfur. The UN Security Council must also expand the existing arms embargo on Darfur to the rest of the country.

articles.title: Starobelsk massacre survivors recount lingering terror to RT (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Starobelsk massacre survivors recount lingering terror to RT (VIDEO)
The survivors of the deadly Ukrainian drone attack on the Starobelsk college in May have spoken to RT about the emotional scars left behind by the tragedy that killed 21 students in their sleep.
Multiple waves of kamikaze UAVs struck the dormitory of the Starobelsk Professional College, located in Russia’s Lugansk People’s Republic (LPR), on May 22. The building partially collapsed as a result of the strikes, killing 21 people and injuring 42 others, mostly teenage girls studying to become teachers. The Ukrainian military subsequently targeted first responders with additional drones, according to investigators.
Twenty students who survived the attack on the dormitory that fateful night came to Moscow on Wednesday at the invitation of Russia’s Commissioner for Human Rights Yana Lantratova.
Lantratova and the students discussed their professional aspirations, with the official noting that some of them have already become volunteers in various projects. She also said that the human rights commission’s doors are open to survivors wishing to undertake an internship there. The official gifted a bus to the college as well as tablet computers to its students.
Speaking to RT, one of the survivors recounted how she took cover in the basement on the night of the attack and “ended up getting buried under the debris.” Acting on “autopilot,” she extricated herself from the rubble and ran for her life. The student said that in the wake of the tragic incident, she “started to be afraid of everything, even the slightest rustle.”
“Especially during the first week, it was absolutely terrifying. I was afraid of every single loud noise,” the survivor told RT.
Another student shared a similar experience of lingering trauma, saying that following the attack, “any loud noise, even just something falling was terrifying. My heart would immediately start pounding violently.”
Lantratova said the attack had been funded with Western taxpayers’ money and accused Kiev’s backers of glossing over the atrocity perpetrated by the Ukrainian military. Kiev has denied responsibility for the incident, with various officials providing conflicting accounts of the massacre.
President Vladimir Putin vowed “inevitable punishment” for the Starobelsk massacre, and several days later, Russia launched one of its largest retaliatory drone and missile strikes, targeting Ukrainian military command facilities, air bases, and defense industry enterprises.

articles.title: Will back all meaningful efforts for Ukraine peace, PM Modi assures Poland's Tusk
articles.body:
PM Modi with Polish counterpart Donald Tusk at Hyderabad House Thursday.
NEW DELHI: Looking to further expand their strategic partnership, India and Poland agreed to double bilateral trade by 2030 and announced dialogue mechanisms for defence industrial collaboration and counterterrorism cooperation as PM Narendra Modi hosted his counterpart Donald Tusk for talks Thursday.Modi and Tusk expressed deepest concern in a joint statement over the war in Ukraine, including its tragic humanitarian consequences and the impact on Global South. In his media statement, Modi assured Tusk that whether it is Ukraine or West Asia, India will continue to support every meaningful effort for peace.Poland views the war in Ukraine as a direct threat to its national security and sovereignty due to its shared border, influx of refugees and the threat of future Russian aggression in eastern Europe.
“They reiterated the need for a comprehensive, just and lasting peace in line with international law, consistent with the purposes and principles of the UN Charter, including respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity,” said the joint statement. The leaders also noted the negative impacts of the war on global food and energy security, especially for the Global South.Modi and Tusk, the first Polish PM to visit India in 16 years, also backed an MoU under negotiation for cooperation in critical minerals.
Modi said the friendship between India and Poland was based not only on diplomatic ties but also on a shared heritage of humanity and empathy. He recalled how, during the Second World War, the royal families of Jamnagar and Kolhapur had provided shelter in India to thousands of Polish children and families. He also thanked Poland for helping India evacuate Indian students from Ukraine shortly after the Russia-Ukraine war began in 2022.Modi said the world was passing through a period of uncertainty and change, and even in such times, both India and Poland were emerging as important hubs of growth, technology and innovation.“Today we have agreed to deepen ties in defence, space and nuclear energy. In all these strategic sectors, we invite Polish companies to engage in co-development and co-production with India,” he said.He also announced a startup bridge to facilitate cooperation in IT, Artificial Intelligence and critical technologies.“Both India and Poland believe in democratic values and the rule of law,” Modi said, underlining that both sides considered reforms essential to make global governance institutions more empowered.The two countries agreed that the UN needed structural reforms, including expansion of UNSC in both permanent and non-permanent categories, to remain relevant, credible and effective. In the joint statement, Poland expressed support for India’s membership of a more inclusive, reformed and expanded UNSC, as well as its candidature for a non-permanent seat on the council for 2028-29.Modi and Tusk unequivocally condemned terrorism, including cross-border terrorism, and stressed that there could be no justification for terrorism on any grounds.“They condemned in the strongest terms the terrorist attack in J&K’s Pahalgam on 22 April, 2025. They called for strong and concerted action against terrorists and terrorist entities, including those designated by the UNSC 1267 sanctions committee,” said the joint statement.
Defence and security cooperation was a major focus, with the leaders underlining importance of an Agreement on Mutual Protection and Exchange of Classified Information and expressing expectation it would be signed soon.They proposed a defence industry dialogue to develop a “forward-looking framework for defence industrial cooperation”, including business-to-business engagement and, where mutually agreed, partnerships in technology, co-development, co-production and other forms of collaboration.

articles.title: Europe will have to accept dependence on us – US tech giant
articles.body:
Europe will have to accept dependence on us – US tech giant
European governments should stop worrying about their growing dependence on American AI, US tech giant Palantir’s top executive for the UK and Europe has said. Instead, they should focus on the advantages the products offer, particularly against Russia, Palantir UK CEO Louis Mosley believes.
The European Commission is frantically trying to reduce reliance on American tech and the US in general.
“Europe is going to have to accept some dependency,” Mosely told Bloomberg News this week.
The Commission estimates that the bloc relies on foreign providers for over 80% of its digital products, services, infrastructure, and intellectual property. However, many are skeptical that replacement is possible. In a Wire’s 2025 survey cited by the European Parliament, only 16% of regional IT leaders said the bloc could achieve digital sovereignty within five years, with almost 60% citing US dominance as a key obstacle.
Nevertheless, this year several European governments have rejected Palantir products or announced plans to phase them out. France’s domestic intelligence agency, the DGSI, which adopted the company’s analytical software in 2015, has plans to drop it over the coming years in favor of a domestically developed alternative from ChapsVision.
“We cannot depend on the goodwill of certain partners who, as we’ve seen in recent days, are capable of cutting off access to models,” Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said when announcing the decision in June.
Berlin has reportedly chosen the same French competitor over Palantir for Germany’s domestic intelligence agency BfV.
Similar moves to ostracize the American firm have been reported in Spain and Denmark, as well as the non-EU nations of Switzerland, Norway, and the UK.
Mosley cited Palantir’s extensive use of the Ukraine conflict as a testing ground for its military solutions, saying “the questions around sovereignty are secondary” for Kiev. The company got involved in Ukraine following the escalation of Kiev’s conflict with Russia in 2022, supplying what it calls “targeting packages.”
One of Palantir’s flagship products is Maven, an AI-powered system that processes vast amounts of intelligence data to help identify targets and generate strike recommendations for troops. It accelerates the so-called “kill chain,” allowing the military to consider substantially more potential targets than human personnel previously could.
Originally developed as a Pentagon project, Maven involved Google until 2018, when employee protests prompted the company to withdraw from the initiative. NATO purchased its own version of the system for use at its European headquarters in March 2025.
“I can provide categorical reassurance that where customers have bought our software, they are in full operational control of that software,” Mosley assured in a separate interview with Reuters concerning NATO’s purchase.
There are no kill switches. There’s no ability for Palantir or the US government to reach in and switch it off.
The US government has a track record of restricting foreign access to flagship AI models. The French prime minister’s remark about a lack of goodwill was a reference to Washington’s blockage of Anthropic’s Mythos 5 tool, which lasted for almost three weeks.

articles.title: US offers Russia Nord Stream restart as part of peace deal
articles.body:
US proposes restart of Nord Stream as part of peace deal with Russia
The United States is proposing that Russian gas supplies to Europe and the operation of the Nord Stream pipeline be resumed as an economic incentive for Moscow as part of a potential peace settlement to end Russia's war against Ukraine.
Source: The Economist
Details: The Economist describes the gas proposal as the latest concession Washington is offering Vladimir Putin. Ukrainian officials, meanwhile, do not yet know all the details of the latest US proposals.
The magazine reports that Russia would be offered commercial deals with US companies, sanctions relief and the normalisation of political relations. Ukraine would be offered an investment package and EU membership in exchange for abandoning its bid to join NATO. The proposals also envisage the creation of a demilitarised zone in Donbas.
The Economist stresses that the US cannot unilaterally decide to restore Russian gas supplies to the European market. It assesses that such a proposal would run counter to EU law.
Ukrainian negotiators fear that US representatives could strike lucrative economic deals with Russia even before the war ends.
The Economist itself questions Moscow's willingness to make peace. It assesses that Russia is likely to drag out the negotiations while securing immediate concessions on sanctions.
The renewed diplomatic push comes after US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff visited St Petersburg on 21 October, The Economist notes.
Background: On 18 October, it was reported that the Trump administration had proposed that Europe resume purchases of Russian gas. According to The New York Times, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff raised the idea during talks with Ukrainian and European officials.

articles.title: Iran warns US, allies of retaliation over attacks on officials
articles.body:
Iran warned Wednesday that U.S. political assets and infrastructure belonging to countries involved in any renewed war against Tehran could become targets of retaliation if Iranian officials are assassinated or civilians killed, according to a senior security official cited by the semi-official Fars News Agency.
The Tehran-based official said Iran assumes that the U.S. and Israel will launch another attack and considers Washington’s diplomatic gestures "unreliable.”
The official said this perception had intensified following remarks by U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Athens, which Tehran interpreted as giving a historical and civilizational justification for Washington’s war against Iran.
According to the official, Iranian political and intellectual leaders have increasingly concluded that US Middle East policy is directed by Israel, which they believe is preventing Washington from pursuing a diplomatic solution.
The official claimed that Israel takes priority in U.S. President Donald Trump’s regional policies.
Iran already considers itself at war with the U.S. and views Washington’s economic and naval blockade, along with restrictions on Iranian airspace, as a continuation of the military aggression that began on Feb. 28, the official said.
He added that growing pressure from different segments of Iranian society was pushing authorities toward "decisive action” to break the blockade under what Tehran considers its right to self-defense.
According to the official, Iran has instructed various operational units that, in the event of another large-scale conflict involving the assassination of Iranian officials and the killing of civilians, it would consider U.S. political assets and the infrastructure of countries participating in the war as "legitimate targets.”
The warning comes amid heightened tensions between Tehran and Washington over the U.S. naval blockade and restrictions on maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
The US and Israel launched military strikes against Iran on Feb. 28, triggering a wider regional conflict. Despite subsequent diplomatic efforts, disagreements over the blockade and security arrangements in the strategic waterway have continued.
The warning also follows an Israeli media report on Wednesday that dozens of Israeli fighter jets flew close to Iran’s border earlier this week, with U.S. sources suggesting the operation may have been intended to provoke an Iranian response.

articles.title: Battlegroup Center air defense crew evaluates effectiveness of new F-1 interceptor drone
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 22. /TASS/. Servicemen of the Battlegroup Center’s air defense missile brigade destroyed more than 20 Ukrainian drones in four days, employing the new F-1 interceptor unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) for the first time, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"This F-1 drone, which has been put into service with the air defense missile brigade’s anti-UAV unit, has demonstrated high effectiveness in destroying high-speed targets. Over four days of combat use, the crews destroyed more than 20 enemy attack drones of various types, including the PD-2, Rubaka, and Bliskavka," the ministry said.
In addition, according to its data, the interceptor drone crew destroyed two new enemy Anubis unmanned aerial vehicles for the first time.
The ministry emphasized that with the F-1 interceptor drone, Russian troops effectively counter enemy strike and reconnaissance UAVs as they approach, preventing their attacks on military units. They operate in close coordination with air surveillance posts and radar station crews, ensuring the timely detection and elimination of aerial targets.

articles.title: Yemeni army says 512 Houthi fighters neutralized in 24 hours
articles.body:
Yemen’s government forces carried out 780 strikes against Houthi positions over the past 24 hours, neutralizing approximately 512 fighters and destroying or damaging more than 330 military vehicles, a military spokesman said Thursday, Anadolu reports.
Majed Abdullah al-Nuzayli, spokesman for the Yemeni Armed Forces, said in a statement that the operations were conducted as part of the ongoing “Operation Dawn of Yemen.”
He said the strikes targeted Houthi field commanders, troop concentrations, reinforcements, heavy weapons positions, fortified sites and military vehicles across the northern fronts as well as Al-Jawf, western Marib, and Al-Bayda provinces.
According to al-Nuzayli, the operations also destroyed heavy weapons and reinforcements heading toward front lines in Taiz province.
He said the strikes had disrupted Houthi military operations and prevented reinforcements from reaching forward positions, allowing government forces to maintain their offensive.
READ: More than 250,000 displaced in Yemen since August as fighting escalates: UNHCR
The spokesman vowed to continue targeting Houthi military positions and reinforcements while taking precautions to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure in accordance with international humanitarian law.
The military’s casualty and damage figures could not be independently verified, and there was no immediate comment from the Houthis.
The announcement comes amid intensified fighting between government forces, backed by a Saudi-led coalition, and the Houthis across several Yemeni provinces.
Earlier Thursday, Yemeni state television reported airstrikes targeting Houthi missile launchers, radar systems, military communications equipment and weapons depots in Taiz.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led military intervention in March 2015 to support the country’s internationally recognized government.

articles.title: US has suffered strategic defeats in war with Iran
articles.body:
In remarks published by Iranian media on Friday, Mohebbi said the enemy initially sought to change Iran’s political system and disintegrate the country, before dividing its objectives into 13 smaller goals, none of which it achieved.

articles.title: AP: Trump's administration gives conflicting accounts of restrictions on Ukraine's Starshield access
articles.body:
AP: Trump's administration gives conflicting accounts of restrictions on Ukraine's Starshield access
Recent attempts to restrict Ukraine's access to satellite systems have triggered a blame game among officials in US President Donald Trump's administration and their allies, who have offered conflicting explanations for the sudden restrictions on Kyiv's ability to intercept Russian attacks.
Source: Associated Press, citing sources
Details: Restrictions imposed on Starshield, the military version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service and a key part of Ukraine's drone operations and communications, alarmed Ukrainian military and government officials last week. Commanders reported lost drones and interrupted missions. After several days of uncertainty, Trump said on Thursday 22 October that the service was operating again at full speed.
However, AP quoted a senior European official familiar with the situation on the ground in Ukraine as saying that nothing had changed in Starshield's operation and that the speed limit remained at around 160 km/h.
Ukraine has received no clear official explanation of who ordered the restrictions or why, according to the official, who was not authorised to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity.
The incident and the subsequent lack of accountability have sparked outrage among Ukraine's allies and supporters of a tougher policy towards Russia on Capitol Hill. Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal announced a new investigation into how the speed of Ukraine's defence systems had been restricted.
Questions have persisted since last week about who ordered the disruption of the satellite internet network created by Elon Musk, which Ukraine has relied on for years to counter attacks by Moscow.
As recently as Thursday, Trump insisted that he had not issued such an order. Vice-President JD Vance hinted at coordination between the White House and Musk, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth denied any involvement by the administration.
Background:
- On 16 October, Trump said that the White House had nothing to do with the restrictions on Ukraine's access to Starlink.
- According to The Telegraph, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk approached Trump with the idea of slowing down Starlink and Starshield operations in Ukraine.
- On 17 October, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a test conducted by Ukraine in EU countries had confirmed that the restrictions on its use of Starlink were imposed as part of a planned operation.
- Rubio said Trump's administration "had nothing to do with" the restriction of Starlink's operation in Ukraine.
- On 18 October, Zelenskyy told NBC that the signal to restrict Starlink and Starshield access for Ukraine had come from the US government.
- Hegseth said the US was not involved in restricting Starshield's operation in Ukraine and had issued no such orders.

articles.title: Romania to speed up development of Black Sea capabilities after cargo ship attacks

Romania to speed up development of Black Sea capabilities after cargo ship attacks
BUCHAREST, Oct 22 - Romania will accelerate its development of surveillance capabilities and equipment to counter mines and drones in the Black Sea after a series of drone attacks on commercial ships off its coast, its top defence council said on Thursday.
At least seven cargo ships have been hit near the coasts of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria in the past two weeks, with some 30 sailors reported dead or missing. Romanian F-16 fighter jet pilots shot down two of the latest generation of Russian drones over Romanian territorial waters on Saturday.
NATO said on Tuesday it will send more maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems and drones to the Black Sea.
• Romania's top defence council said latest ship attacks are direct consequences of Russia's aggression beyond Ukraine's borders.
• Threats to freedom of navigation and critical energy projects in the Black Sea pose a security crisis for Romania.
• The current risks require concrete measures to protect human lives, maintain free access to national ports, and ensure the security of energy facilities in the Exclusive Economic Zone.
• The top defence council said it will accelerate the development of capabilities for maritime surveillance, countering naval mines and intervening against drones illegally breaching national airspace and waters.
• Authorities will practice to improve the efficiency of their operational response.
• Romania will seek to improve cooperation with fellow NATO members Bulgaria and Turkey with whom it shares the Black Sea.
• "The Council members also analyzed ways to intensify coordination within NATO. This includes strengthening the deterrence and defense posture on the Eastern Flank and identifying new measures to respond to threats in the Black Sea region." REUTERS

articles.title: Palantir’s Thiel laments Iran war – Politico
articles.body:
Palantir’s Thiel laments Iran war – Politico
Billionaire tech investor and Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel has expressed regret over the US war against Iran, warning that it could ultimately lead to International Criminal Court warrants for the Trump administration and have broader implications for the US, Politico reported on Thursday.
The outlet cited a transcript of a lecture given by Thiel earlier this month, part of the series of private events held in Nashville.
Thiel, a staunch backer of US President Donald Trump, has expressed doubts over the Iran war, which was launched by the US and Israel earlier this year, suggesting that it has exposed America’s weaknesses.
“I’m skeptical of [the war], I think we should not have done it. There were a lot of mistakes that were made,” Thiel said, as quoted by Politico.
Maybe we don’t have the hard power. Maybe we’re going to lose the soft power war.
While reiterating his support for Trump, he warned that the war could backfire for the administration and lead to legal troubles with the International Criminal Court (ICC). 
The Trump administration has had a hostile relationship with the ICC, particularly over the decision to issue arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes in Gaza.
The US, which does not recognize the ICC’s jurisdiction, has enacted sanctions against the court’s top officials, describing it as a “corrupt and fatally politicized supranational court that has maliciously abused its authority and exceeded its mandate.”
“I have come to suspect that the threat of an ICC arrest warrant is the sword of Damocles hanging over the Trump administration as it tries to persecute this war in Iran,” Thiel said.
He also claimed that George W. Bush-era neocon figures such as Donald Rumsfeld and Dick Cheney have been colluding with the ICC against Trump. “I read the Cheney family’s Trump derangement syndrome as an attempt to buy favor with the [ICC] and avoid prosecution. Probably too late,” he said.
Palantir has been heavily involved in the hostilities, as its products have been used by the US military. The use of AI products was reportedly linked to one of the worst mass-casualty events of the war – the strike on a school in Minab on the first day of the conflict, which killed at least 156 civilians, predominantly schoolchildren. According to media reports, the facility was targeted based on outdated data used by Palantir’s analysis and surveillance software.

articles.title: Standoff hits Sudanese consumers as Egypt halts cargo trucks
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Border standoff hits Sudanese consumers as Egypt halts cargo trucks
Egyptian authorities have suspended cargo truck crossings into Sudan, triggering severe shortages and price hikes that ordinary Sudanese are struggling to absorb.
The decision followed the killing of two Egyptian truck drivers and the injury of a third on 12 October, when a 23-year-old Sudanese gunman opened fire on them in a popular market south of Khartoum.
The incident occurred only a day after scores of artisanal miners, including Sudanese nationals, were killed by Egyptian airstrikes in the border area between Egypt and Sudan.
According to the Egyptian army, the strikes were staged inside Egypt. However, unofficial Sudanese claims to the contrary have caused anger in different parts of Sudan.
Sudanese demonstrators took to the streets, particularly in Nyala—the capital of South Darfur State and a stronghold of the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces which battles the Sudanese Armed Forces for control over Sudan.
Activists also called for a boycott of Egyptian goods, planning to blockade the desert road linking Khartoum to border crossings to halt incoming freight.
Cairo framed the suspension as a protective measure to shield Egyptian drivers from targeted violence.
Regardless of Cairo's rationale, the move has dealt an immediate blow to Sudanese consumers, threatening to trigger widespread inflation at an already precarious moment.
A recent viral video captured a Sudanese shopkeeper gesturing to his fully stocked shelves. Most of the goods, he noted, were either imported directly from Egypt or relied on Egyptian raw materials.
"Do you know what the decision to suspend the entry of cargo trucks from Egypt into Sudan means?" the trader asks. "It means that the prices of all these products will shoot up in the coming days."
Lifeline severed
Egypt serves as a vital gateway for Sudan's access to global markets, particularly as international sanctions continue to cripple Sudanese businesses.
Sudan's civil war, which has been grinding on since April 2023, has also put the brakes on a sizeable portion of the country's industrial and agricultural production, making it more dependent on imports for the needs of its people.
In 2025, bilateral trade reached $1.19 billion, with Egyptian exports accounting for $933.3 million.
In the first half of this year, bilateral trade reached $759 million, up from $570 million in the corresponding period of the previous year, according to the Egyptian government. Egyptian exports amounted to $595 million, almost 40% up from the export figure recorded in the first half of 2025, the government says.
Trade between the two countries partly owes its activity to their ability to develop a barter-style system that helps them avoid stringent international sanctions on Sudanese businesses and foreign currency shortages on both sides, specialists said.
However, cutting off Egyptian goods leaves the war-ravaged nation deeply vulnerable, forcing consumers to endure sudden supply bottlenecks alongside skyrocketing prices, Sudanese specialists said.
"This suspension is having far-reaching economic and human consequences," Sudanese political analyst Osman al-Merghani said.
Speaking to The New Arab, he added that the market has been paralyzed in almost all Sudanese states due to the dramatic rise that happened in commodity prices.
"Some commodities, including sugar and rice, have also completely disappeared, which is causing a lot of suffering to ordinary consumers," al-Merghani said.
Online hostility vs. diplomatic containment
The current disruption to bilateral trade comes at a time when a social media war is raging on between the Egyptians and the Sudanese against the background of the 11 October strikes.
Sudanese nationals commenting on the incident slam Egypt for killing what they describe as "innocent" artisanal miners and allegedly infringing on Sudanese territories, throwing light on growing anti-Egypt sentiments in some parts of the southern neighbouring country.
Egyptian social media users counter by defending their national army, and accusing the Sudanese of mining for gold inside Egypt, hence stealing the country's mineral resources.
The surge in anti-Egyptian rhetoric has heightened anxiety among the estimated 1,000 Egyptian nationals still remaining in Sudan.
Before the war erupted in April 2023, between 10,000 and 15,000 Egyptians lived in Sudan, mostly those married to Sudanese, working in Sudan or investing in the country.
An Egyptian national has recently posted a video where he implored Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi to help him and others return safely to Egypt.
"The Sudanese are lying in wait for us on the road between Khartoum and the Egyptian border," the man said in the video which appeared on social media on October 14.
Most Egyptian nationals present in Sudan are reportedly concentrated in coastal areas under the control of the Sudanese Armed Force, especially Port Sudan where the Egyptian Consulate operates and business activities remain comparatively stable.
The governments of the two countries keep working, meanwhile, to contain fallout from the 11 October strikes.
On 16 October, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and Sudanese Finance Minister Gibril Ibrahim rejected attempts to harm their countries' bilateral relations, noting that those relations are based on shared respect and good neighbourliness.
Meeting the Sudanese minister on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings in Washington DC, the Egyptian foreign minister reaffirmed Cairo's unwavering support for Sudan's unity and territorial integrity.
This meeting came four days after the foreign ministers of the two countries underscored the importance of respecting each other's country's sovereignty, territorial integrity and borders.
Analysts in Cairo view these diplomatic containment efforts as proof of the high strategic value both nations place on bilateral ties.
They call for managing those relations wisely, especially in the presence of persistent attempts by some parties to sabotage them.
"It is clear that some parties work to widen the gap between the two countries and cause a rupture in their relations," Egyptian political analyst Islam Mansi said.
"These parties do their best to incite the Sudanese people against Egypt, a country bound by historical ties and a shared destiny with Sudan," he told TNA.

articles.title: US Democratic senator probes Ukraine's loss of Starshield service
articles.body:
US Democratic senator probes Ukraine's loss of Starshield service
WASHINGTON, Oct 22 - Democratic US Senator Richard Blumenthal on Thursday said he had opened an inquiry into Ukraine's loss of critical access to the Pentagon's Starshield satellite communications service and the resulting degrading of Kyiv's ability to defend itself against Russian attacks.
"In the late evening of October 13, Ukrainian forces lost critical access to Starshield, the military-grade counterpart to SpaceX’s Starlink network, after their access to speeds at which equipment could stay connected to the network was capped," Blumenthal wrote in a letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
"The episode raises urgent questions about who possesses the technical and legal authority to alter these capabilities" and whether the Pentagon has "sufficient alternatives" if SpaceX-provided services become unavailable, Blumenthal wrote.
Blumenthal is the senior Democrat on the Senate's Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations. He is seeking information on whether the change in service was directed by the White House, the Department of Defense or SpaceX.
Republicans control the Senate, so Democrats lack subpoena power. Blumenthal can only request information and briefings from officials within and outside the government.
He said the move put Ukrainian forces and civilians at risk and raised concerns "about who controls critical capabilities the US government has spent billions of dollars to procure."
WEAKENED UKRAINE DEFENSES
The Pentagon is the biggest customer of Starshield, which is the military-grade version of the Starlink service.
A Pentagon spokesperson said: "As with all congressional correspondence, the Department will respond directly to the authors."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy on October 14 said Elon Musk's SpaceX had restricted Starlink services, weakening Ukraine's air defenses.
The controversy came as the Trump administration was pressuring Kyiv to halt its attacks on Russian energy infrastructure and encouraging Russia to return to negotiations over ending its war in Ukraine.
Blumenthal told Hegseth the Senate panel will look into government interactions with and reliance on SpaceX technology. He set deadlines of November 5 for responses to questions embedded in the letter to Hegseth, and November 12 for a briefing by SpaceX officials with knowledge of the Starshield restriction.
Besides this latest inquiry, Blumenthal has been trying to investigate a series of actions related to the Trump administration, including contracts negotiated for building a White House ballroom at an estimated cost of $400 million and Trump-linked crypto firms.
If Democrats win control of the Senate in November 3 midterm elections, he likely would become chairman of the investigations panel. REUTERS

All four of Moscow’s airports — Sheremetyevo, Domodedovo, Vnukovo, and Zhukovsky — closed to arrivals and departures, Rosaviatsia said.

articles.title: Belarus convicts at least 419 people for supporting Ukraine during Russia's full-scale war

Belarus convicts at least 419 people for supporting Ukraine during Russia's full-scale war
Criminal cases have been brought against at least 419 people in Belarus in connection with the war in Ukraine.
Source: Belarusian human rights centre Viasna, as reported by European Pravda
Details: According to Viasna, at least 419 people, including 73 women, have been convicted for supporting Ukraine since February 2022. Of these, 142 are currently in detention. The centre noted that the actual number of criminal cases could be significantly higher.
Of those convicted, 222 were sentenced for "facilitating extremist activities", including for sharing photographs and videos showing the movements of Russian military equipment.
Another 44 people were convicted of "treason" in connection with their support for Ukraine during the war. A further 17 foreign nationals were convicted of "espionage" in Belarus.
Another 29 people were convicted of "terrorism" in cases involving acts of sabotage, including on railways and at a military airfield, while 45 were convicted for donating to the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
The largest number of convictions, Viasna noted, are linked to the so-called Hajun case – a wave of arrests connected with the activities of the independent monitoring project Belaruski Hajun, which tracked the movements of Russian and Belarusian troops.
At the time, Ukraine's Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned a new wave of repression by the Lukashenko regime in connection with the so-called Hajun case.

articles.title: EU Sanctions Envoy Pushes for Action Against Rusal’s Irish Alumina Refinery
articles.body:
Material produced in a major metals refinery in Ireland is “undoubtedly” going into Russia’s weapons supply chain, the European Union’s Sanctions Envoy David O’Sullivan said on Thursday, adding that “there is a very real issue to be addressed.”
The comments, made at the Institute for International and European Affairs (IIEA) in Dublin, come seven months after OCCRP and partners published an investigation showing that the Aughinish Alumina refinery in western Ireland was indirectly supplying Russian weapons producers.
As much as half of the alumina from the Aughinish refinery was shipped to smelters owned by its parent company, United Company Rusal, and used to produce aluminum. The metal was then sold to a trading company supplying dozens of EU-sanctioned Russian weapons manufacturers, OCCRP’s investigation showed.
Weapons made by these firms have leveled entire city blocks in Mariupol, struck a children’s hospital in Kyiv, and blown open an apartment building in western Ukraine, according to EU sanctions listings, Ukraine’s military intelligence, and the London-based Royal United Services Institute (RUSI).
Aughinish Alumina's sales to Russia — which have increased since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine — are entirely legal under EU trade rules. That is because although EU exports of finished aluminum are banned, shipments of the intermediate material alumina are not, partly as a result of lobbying years ago by Ireland, where Aughinish Alumina is an important employer.
OCCRP’s investigation sparked controversy in Ireland and internationally, and led to growing pressure to sanction EU alumina exports. The Irish government launched its own investigation, which reached an ambivalent conclusion, saying that a lack of data made it “difficult to ascertain where Russia is sourcing its tools and weapons from.” It shared its findings with the EU Commission in July.
O’Sullivan was less cautious in his assessment.
“The alumina goes to smelters in Russia, who produce stuff which undoubtedly goes at least in part to the military-industrial complex,” he said. “I've read the government report. I personally, I think there's no doubt the investigative journalists got it right.”
O’Sullivan did not say whether the EU would eventually ban alumina exports to Russia.
“I think there is a very real issue to be addressed. We just have to find the best way of doing it, which doesn't have unhelpful collateral consequences,” he said, noting that Aughinish Alumina also supplied smelters in Europe.
In July, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a visit to Dublin that “Every ton of raw material that ends in Russia is used against us. I do hope whatever we are doing now, we are cutting every possibility, every sphere for Russia to build up, to militarize itself.”
Aughinish Alumina has said that its material is not used to make weapons, and that almost all the alumina it sends to Russian smelters is solely used to produce aluminum for onward export out of Russia.
OCCRP’s original investigation was published in partnership with iStories, the Irish Times, KibOrg, De Tijd, The Guardian, and Delfi.

articles.title: Canada opens free trade talks with Turkey
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Canada opens free trade talks with Turkey
Canada, which is in the midst of a trade war with the United States, opened talks with Turkey Thursday on a free trade agreement during a landmark visit by Prime Minister Mark Carney.
Carney, a former central banker, has made reducing dependence on Washington and diversifying Canada's partnerships one of the cornerstones of his term, which began in March 2025.
"We decided to begin negotiations for a free trade agreement, which includes increasing trade and investment, before the end of the year," Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said in a joint address to reporters.
Carney is the first Canadian prime minister to pay an official visit to Turkey.
"We hope to increase our trade volume, which is currently around $3 billion, to $5 billion and then $10 billion. We will approximately double direct flights between our countries," Erdogan said.
Carney said Canadian negotiators would come to Ankara next month for the first round of free trade talks.
"Our goal is not self-sufficiency, it is collective resilience," said Carney.
"And that's why Canada is building deeper partnerships with reliable partners that create new opportunities for us both. And in Turkey, we have an exceptional partner."
Carney is due to meet on Friday with Turkish business leaders in Istanbul, in strategic sectors such as energy, aerospace and critical minerals.
Canada and Turkey have also identified potential for cooperation in nuclear energy.
They also announced a partnership agreement in the defence industry.
"Today's new Agreement on Defence Industry Partnership will connect Canadian and Turkish companies to work together, creating good jobs at home, export opportunities abroad, greater security for our citizens, and contributing to a stronger NATO alliance," Carney said.
Carney has multiplied overseas trips, renewing ties with nations such as Saudi Arabia, India and China with which relations had been strained or even broken under his predecessor Justin Trudeau.
Carney has also drawn closer to Europe.

articles.title: L3Harris warns lasers will push U.S. Navy power limits
articles.body:
- L3Harris supplies power distribution systems and universal modular masts for every U.S. Navy Virginia-class submarine and is extending that work to the Columbia class.
- The company named directed energy weapons, advanced radars and new propulsion as future drivers of heavier power demands on U.S. Navy platforms.
L3Harris Technologies says it supplies the power distribution systems and universal modular masts on every Virginia-class submarine in the U.S. Navy fleet, and the company is now carrying that work into the Columbia-class ballistic missile submarine program while preparing for the heavier electrical loads expected from directed energy weapons and other new naval systems.
The company laid out its submarine power role in an editorial published Oct. 22, 2026, describing decades of work on rugged, high-density power conversion and distribution equipment for the U.S. Navy’s undersea fleet.
Near the end of the piece, in a passage Laser Wars highlighted when sharing the editorial on X, L3Harris said naval platforms are growing more electrically complex with every generation and named advanced radar systems, directed energy weapons and next-generation propulsion as the technologies that will place extraordinary demands on shipboard power infrastructure.
“The Navy trusts us with the most critical systems on its most advanced platforms, and that is not something we take lightly,” said Nino DiCosmo, president of L3Harris Maritime. “Every power system we deliver has to work the first time and every time after that, whether a submarine is on its first patrol or its fiftieth.”
Directed energy weapons, such as high-energy lasers, fire beams of energy instead of physical rounds and draw their “ammunition” directly from a ship’s electrical system, which is why they demand far more power generation, storage and distribution than conventional weapons. The U.S. Navy has already fielded lasers on surface ships, including the HELIOS system installed on the destroyer USS Preble (DDG 88) in 2022. L3Harris said it is investing in power technologies to meet those growing demands across the Navy’s most advanced platforms, without tying the directed energy reference to any specific submarine program.
On the Virginia-class attack submarines, every sensor, weapon, propulsion component and crew system draws from a single power architecture that must keep working for months at a time at every depth. L3Harris described its submarine portfolio as running from switchgear and power protection systems to advanced power conversion equipment, all designed to meet strict requirements for shock resistance, electromagnetic compatibility, heat management and long-term reliability.
The universal modular mast is the other half of the company’s Virginia-class role. The two-stage, telescoping mast raises sensors above the waterline without penetrating the pressure hull, lifting photonics imaging masts, communications antennas and electronic warfare sensors, and each Virginia-class boat carries a bank of eight. In April 2026, Naval Sea Systems Command awarded L3Harris a contract worth up to $129.9 million for universal modular mast production and engineering support for both the Virginia and Columbia classes.
The Columbia class will replace the Ohio-class ballistic missile submarines as the sea-based leg of the U.S. nuclear deterrent, and the Navy plans to build 12 of the boats. The lead submarine, the future USS District of Columbia (SSBN 826), was about 65% complete in February 2026, and shipbuilders General Dynamics Electric Boat and HII Newport News Shipbuilding are working toward a 2028 delivery ahead of a first patrol planned for 2030.
L3Harris said its power systems for the Columbia class are being built to the same standards as those already serving across the Virginia-class fleet, with the first boat on track to begin patrols after its planned 2028 delivery.

articles.title: Germany arrests Ukrainian man suspected of spying for Russia
articles.body:
On the morning of Oct. 22, officers from Germany’s Federal Criminal Police arrested a foreign national on suspicion of spying for Russia, according to Der Spiegel and t-Online. The suspect is a 53-year-old Ukrainian citizen, identified by t-Online as Vadym Y.
The man was arrested in the Oder-Spree district of Brandenburg, where he lived in the city of Eisenhüttenstadt. He allegedly maintained contact with Russian intelligence services through an intermediary.
Authorities suspect he gathered sensitive military information, including data on Germany’s production of armored vehicles, ammunition, and explosives, as well as information about NATO personnel and military facilities.
Der Spiegel also reported that the suspect had shown interest in the German army’s 45th Armored Brigade, commonly known as the Lithuania Brigade — the 5,000-member unit is due to be deployed to Lithuania next year.
A day earlier, Russian security forces detained a German citizen who was said to have fought on the Ukrainian side in the war. Russian authorities claimed the man had deserted because he did not receive a promised payment of 100,000 hryvnias (less than 2,000 euros).
Additionally, last week Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) reported detaining a Swedish citizen whom they accused of illegally crossing the border. He, too, had served under contract in the Ukrainian military — as the commander of a drone unit in the Aidar Battalion. His relatives later confirmed that account to Swedish media.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Ukraine will be represented at highest level at G20 in December if invited
articles.body:
Zelenskyy: Ukraine will be represented at highest level at G20 in December if invited
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that Ukraine will be represented at the highest level at the G20 summit in Florida in December if invited to attend by his US counterpart Donald Trump.
Source: Zelenskyy at a press conference with Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The president said the US could force Russia into ending the Russia-Ukraine war, or at least agreeing to a ceasefire, and emphasised the need for security guarantees for Ukraine.
Quote from Zelenskyy: "All this is possible when our partners are by our side. With the mediation of President Trump or American negotiators. I think this is possible, and we can count on meeting in Florida during the G20.
If President Trump invites Ukraine to the summit, Ukraine will be represented there at the highest level.
Let's hope this is possible. We have not received such a signal yet. We are counting on it."
Background:
- The United States has invited Russian leader Vladimir Putin to the G20's December summit in Miami, where he would be able to meet with Trump.
- The Kremlin said Russia was "grateful for and appreciates this invitation", promising to make a decision on whether Putin will attend later.
- On 17 October, Trump said he did not know whether Putin would attend the G20 summit.
- According to Zelenskyy, it has been suggested that a trilateral meeting between the leaders of Ukraine, the US and Russia could be held at the G20 summit, but so far there has been no confirmation that it could take place.

articles.title: Russia returns bodies of 252 Ukrainian soldiers
articles.body:
Russia returns bodies of 252 Ukrainian soldiers
Russia has handed over the remains of 252 Ukrainian soldiers killed in the conflict and received the bodies of 25 Russian troops in return, according to multiple reports.
The transfer reportedly took place on Thursday in Belarus near the Novaya Guta border crossing with Ukraine. Officials and media outlets in all three countries confirmed the details of the repatriations.
Footage from the scene shows monitors from the International Committee of the Red Cross overseeing the transfer.
The disparity in the number of bodies returned is typical, unlike prisoner-of-war swaps, which are generally conducted on an equal basis.
Pro-Kiev commentators have long argued that the imbalance does not reflect the actual ratio of battlefield casualties, as advancing Russian forces are better positioned to recover the bodies of fallen Ukrainian soldiers. However, the latest round, which followed Kiev’s claims of a major offensive near the city of Liman, showed no significant change in the proportion.
Neither Russia nor Ukraine officially publishes comprehensive figures for its military casualties. Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky has cited death tolls that even pro-Kiev commentators consider implausibly low. In July, he claimed that “about 50,000” Ukrainian troops had been killed, down from the 55,000 deaths he reported in February.
Many Ukrainian battlefield casualties are classified as missing in action, which allows the cash-strapped government to defer compensation to the families of the fallen soldiers.
In summer 2025, Russian officials accused their Ukrainian counterparts of refusing to take hundreds of remains. The Ukrainians rejected the allegations, which the Russians said could be explained by a shortage of bodies in Kiev’s reserves and its concerns over the bad optics of a one-sided repatriation.
On three separate days in mid-June 2025, Russia unilaterally returned 1,200 bodies to Ukraine.

articles.title: Belarusian Mirotvorets loitering munition could be sought after by Russian army — expert
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. The Belarusian Mirotvorets (Peacemaker) kamikaze drone, which was presented this October during a military parade rehearsal in Libya, could potentially be in demand among the Russian Armed Forces, Denis Fedutinov, a leading unmanned aerial vehicle expert, told TASS.
"The special military operation continues, and the demand for kamikaze drones remains very high. The Geran drones alone are needed in quantities exceeding 1,000 pieces per month. And the demand for smaller-sized drones is several times higher. This suggests that, given the current situation, it cannot be ruled out that the Mirotvorets drones may also be in demand by the Russian Armed Forces. If my assumption is correct, then in the initial stage we can expect direct purchases from Belarus, and in the future, cooperation could be developed either through the creation of a joint venture or by organizing licensed production in our country," Fedutinov said.
The expert noted that the appearance of these systems at the parade in Libya further confirms the trend toward a sharp increase in global interest in loitering munitions. "The threshold for becoming a possessor of this type of high-precision weaponry is quite low, which expands the pool of potential customers to include virtually every country in the world. And this market offers opportunities not only for Belarusian but also for Russian development companies," Fedutinov added.
According to him, UAVHELI (Belarus), which developed the Mirotvorets system, took an unconventional approach. "They did not attempt to create their own copies of systems already on the market, instead, they entered a niche where there were few offerings--high-speed, relatively small turbojet UAVs. As a result, their developments do not compete with Russia’s drones of similar purpose: the electric Lancets are inferior in class and speed, while the Gerans and Banderols, on the contrary, are larger in size," the expert noted.
Mirotvorets loitering munition
The Mirotvorets fixed-wing loitering munition has a two-beam layout. The maximum takeoff weight of the vehicle is 46 kg. The Mirotvorets is powered by a turbojet engine, capable of reaching a maximum speed of 450 km/h. The mission endurance is 45 minutes. The vehicle is equipped with a 10-kg high-explosive fragmentation warhead. The system is equipped with communications equipment offering a range of up to 100 km.

articles.title: How Trump’s magnet fixation puts Swiss high-tech industry in tough spot
articles.body:
How Trump’s magnet fixation puts Swiss high-tech industry in tough spot
As China and the United States vie for control of rare-earth minerals, Switzerland faces growing risks to supplies vital for its high-tech industries.
It was in July that US President Donald Trump, in his unmistakable style, drummed home to a room full of defence investors in Pennsylvania the importance of magnetism.
“I hope you’re gonna do magnets. Somebody out there, I hope – you’re all brilliant people – magnets. Do magnets, ok? I’ll tell you how to make money. Do magnets. You’re doing a lot of great stuff. Do magnets. Because one thing we don’t have, but we’re getting close – but do magnets.”
While some media speculated that the 80-year-old president had suffered a “senior moment” and others noted his son’s interest in a related business, Trump’s verbal excursion illustrated how the US sees the arcane world of high-tech magnets – and the rare earths used to make them – as key to its battle with China for global dominance.
It’s a conflict over international supply chains with consequences for manufacturers of products from weapons to wind turbines and watches, particularly in small nations like Switzerland that rely on secure access to critical materials for their high-tech industries.
Around 12,500km east of where Trump was speaking lies the rare-earth heartland of Ganzhou in southern China. Samarium is just one of the elements scraped from the region’s mines, processed into alloys and shipped all around the world. In the Swiss town of Lupfig, in canton Aargau, Arnold Magnetic Technologies converts it into samarium-cobalt magnets used in aerospace, industrial motors and other precision technologies.
China dominates rare earths production
The company describes its trade with Chinese raw-material producers as a “mine-to-magnetExternal link” supply chain. Yet as tensions between China and the US have ratcheted up, particularly over critical minerals, so has the threat of trade tariffs and export controls.
In late 2025, Arnold Magnetic announcedExternal link that it was creating new partnerships with UK and Belgium companies to secure “reliable, Western-origin” rare-earth materials.
“The situation around rare-earth-mineral supply security is not going to go away anytime soon,” Matt Blake, chief executive officer of Arnold Magnetic, told Manufacturing Today Magazine. “China will remain an important part of the global rare-earth supply chain for the foreseeable future […] As such, we embraced a multifaceted approach to mitigate risk along that supply chain, which includes diversifying our sourcing strategies.”
Despite the name, rare earths are not scarce. Yet China dominates their production. The country spent decades building up mining, refining and processing on a huge scale. By 2024, it delivered about 60% of world rare-earth mineExternal link output and 90% of separation and refining capacity. Economies of scale make it hard for anyone else to enter the market.
That was fine as long as trade tensions were muted. But in recent years, the US, Europe and Japan have become increasingly concerned that China is exporting goods at below cost, hollowing out the wider manufacturing bases of its competitors and gaining a chokehold over supplies critical to areas such as defence and strategic infrastructure. These fears have only been heightened by China taking Russia’s side in the Ukraine war.
“Rare earths and other critical raw materials, which were once merely viewed as the commodities that power modern industry, are increasingly being used as strategic assets and geopolitical tools rather than simply being traded,” said Alessandra Hool, managing director of the ESM Foundation, set up in 1951 to carry out research into rare metals in an effort to secure essential supplies for a resource-poor Switzerland.
“While mining capacity for some critical raw materials has become somewhat more diversified in recent years, processing capacity for many of these materials remains heavily concentrated in China,” Hool said.
China restricted exports of certain minerals in 2023, including to European countries, following US limits on the sale of high-end microchips to the communist nation. China imposed further controls in subsequent years as leverage against rivals such as Japan.
This move “could have a dramatic impact on global supply chains, as many strategic sectors rely on products and components containing the controlled Chinese rare-earth elements. These sectors include energy, automotive, defence, semiconductors, aerospace, industrial motors and AI data centres,” the International Energy Agency said of the curbs.
The biggest economies have taken a variety of steps in response.
The US is building a networkExternal link of critical-mineral partnerships backed by investment and national-security policies. Japan has accumulated stockpiles of materials, invested in overseas mining projects and formed partnerships with producers such as Lynas Rare Earths in Australia. The EU’s Critical Raw Materials ActExternal link aims to meet 10% of the bloc’s needs for extraction, 40% of its processing and 25% of recycling demand domestically.
Others have imposed their own trade restrictions. OECD statistics indicateExternal link curbs on critical materials grew fivefold between 2009 and 2024, leaving around 45% of rare-earth exports facing such limits. “Importing industrialised countries increasingly perceive risks to their economic security,” the organisation said.
More
Switzerland and Indonesia sign deal on access to raw materials
Yet some of these options aren’t viable for small nations like Switzerland, with tiny local markets and economies that have benefited from years of open world trade. While the country imports less than 30 tonnes of rare-earth metalsExternal link and compoundsExternal link directly each year, lots of Swiss manufacturers rely on components made from such substances.
“The Swiss tech industry’s dependence on rare earths and other critical raw materials from China is significant,” said Martin Hizel, chair of Swissmem, the main trade body for the sector in Switzerland. “In the event of a supply-chain disruption, it is virtually impossible to find an alternative supply channel at short notice.”
“Switzerland is at risk of becoming ‘collateral damage’ in the global rivalry between the US and China,” he added. Chinese export controls are also affecting Swiss industrial firms, even though Switzerland has played no part in the international trade conflicts.
A survey of Swissmem members in April 2026 found that around a third of companies’ import goods are subject to Chinese export controls. “Of the firms affected, over half have faced delivery delays and disruptions,” Hizel said.
Alliances, recycling and substitution
Swiss companies also face indirect shocks, including rising costs and increased regulatory complexity, according to Hool at the ESM Foundation.
Switzerland lacks the market size, international influence or mineral resources to try to become more self-sufficient, she said. Nor can it simply replicate Japan’s strategy of using state-backed investment to secure overseas resources at scale.
Instead, its strongest bet may be, like Arnold Magnetic, to diversify supply as best it can.
The country has already built ties with resource-rich nations such as Indonesia, among the largest producers of minerals used in batteries and clean-energy tech. Economics Minister Guy Parmelin signed a preliminary declaration of intent to boost cooperation on raw materials and supply chains on a visit to the Southeast Asian country in 2025.
According to Hizel, a diplomatic channel is being established between Switzerland and China on the basis of their existing free trade agreement to help Swiss companies deal with any problems they face over procurement of materials.
Industrial recycling of minerals from discarded products, such as electric vehicle batteries, may also be “one of the most promising long-term opportunities for Switzerland to reduce its dependence on imported critical raw materials,” Hool said.
Scientists at Swiss federal technology institute ETH Zurich have developedExternal link technologies to extract rare-earth elements from electronic waste, launching its “REEcover” spinoff to commercialize the process. Researchers are also working on ways to use less material and replace scarce elements with alternatives or develop entirely new products that do not depend on them.
Still, such efforts are either at an early stage or tinkering at the edges of the problem.
“Partnerships cannot generally eliminate global market risks, supply disruptions or geopolitical tensions,” Hool said. “Switzerland’s response should reflect its specific position as a small and highly globalised economy.”
As long as the US, China and EU remain in conflict – and Trump maintains his fixation with magnets – that may be the best that the world’s smaller nations can hope to achieve.
