articles.title: NORTHCOM Wraps Radar Test to Boost Arctic Early Warning
articles.body:
U.S. Northern Command and multiple research organizations just wrapped up a joint, three-year experiment to test new radar technology that could enable the Northern Warning System to detect incoming threats at longer ranges across Alaska and northern Canada.
The Sept. 7-14 test event marked the conclusion of live-fly testing in the experiment series, which explored how existing radar infrastructure and emerging technology could complement current surveillance capabilities, according to an Oct. 19 release from Alaskan Command, a subordinate command under NORTHCOM. The Arctic air domain awareness experiment series focused on closing surveillance gaps across a region where vast distances, harsh weather and limited infrastructure present challenges for air surveillance.
The Air Force Research Laboratory and Defense Research and Development Canada also participated in the exercise alongside scientific organizations in the region. The Air Force and NORAD have relied on the AN/FPS-117 and AN/Transportable Phased Array System-77 radar systems to detect and track incoming threats out to 250 miles throughout the region.
The experiment paired an existing high-frequency transmitter, paired with a newly developed, low-cost receiver array, according to the release.
Initial results show the system was “successfully able to achieve full skywave (beyond line of sight) detections” of an E-3 Sentry from the 962nd Airborne Air Control Squadron, HC-130J Combat King IIs from the 211th Rescue Squadron, and KC-135 Stratotankers from the 168th Air Refueling Wing—aircraft that served as cooperative targets, providing known positions against which researchers could compare the experimental data, the release states.
Researchers used the University of Alaska Fairbanks’ High Frequency Active Auroral Research Program, or HAARP, facility and a receiver array in Cold Bay developed by MITRE to collect data on participating aircraft over the Gulf of Alaska and Bering Sea.
The effort supported a broader focus of Alaskan Command to improve how units detect and track aircraft across Alaska and its approaches and help commanders assess potential threats for homeland defense, the release states.
“Understanding what this technology can do in the Arctic starts with collecting data under real operating conditions,” Dr. Carolyn Stwertka, chief scientist for Alaskan Command, said in the release. “Working with operational units allows us to compare the experimental observations with known aircraft positions and assess where this approach could help address gaps in air surveillance.”
The experiment occurred as NORAD is building and deploying high-frequency systems to detect hypersonic missiles with over-the-horizon radar, modernizing the Northern Warning System and building a polar over-the-horizon radar network.
The Homeland Defense OTHR, which kicked off in 2022, is being funded by both the United States and Canada at an estimated $6-7 billion and $3.1 billion, respectively. Initial Operating Capability is slated for 2028-29, with Full Operational Capability targeted for 2031.
Meanwhile, the Air Force is looking to replace its Air Route Surveillance Radar-4, a three-decade-old radar warning system that protects the coastlines and borders of the United States and a few remote locations.
The ARSR-4 system, which was built in the 1990s, was designed to help operators distinguish aircraft or potential missile threats from other radar “clutter,” which is more prevalent at lower altitudes. The system has been very effective, but Air Force officials maintain that newer additions to the cluttered landscape, namely wind farms, can distort the radar’s ability to “see” clearly, according to a recent Air Force Life Cycle Management Center sources sought notice.

articles.title: FSB orders Russian critical infrastructure websites taken offline over PHP vulnerabilities
articles.body:
FSB orders Russian critical infrastructure websites taken offline over PHP vulnerabilities
Russia’s Federal Security Service’s cybersecurity center has ordered organizations that run the country’s critical information infrastructure to temporarily shut down their websites if they cannot quickly update their software to protect against the PHP vulnerabilities.
The National Coordination Center for Computer Incidents (NKTsKI) sent the directive on October 22 through the state cyberattack defense system GosSOPKA. The Russian business news outlet RBC obtained a copy, and three recipient organizations confirmed the document’s authenticity.
NKTsKI instructed organizations to install the patched version of PHP, scan servers with antivirus software, and review logs for signs of intrusion. If the system cannot be updated quickly, the FSB instructs them to “consider temporarily restricting external access to vulnerable web servers, up to and including taking them offline.”

articles.title: European, Mideast foreign ministers hold talks in Istanbul
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
European, Middle East foreign ministers hold security talks in Turkey's Istanbul
Foreign ministers from eight European and Middle Eastern countries are set to meet in Istanbul on Friday in an unprecedented format for talks on the Strait of Hormuz and wars across the Middle East.
Ministers from Britain, France and Germany—the so-called E3—as well as Italy will meet counterparts from the newly created R4 group comprising Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt to discuss the Palestinians, developments in Yemen and Hormuz, and ways to end the Russia-Ukraine war, a Turkish foreign ministry source said.
British foreign minister Ed Miliband's office said the talks would essentially revolve around "the Strait of Hormuz and the situation in Saudi Arabia".
It said Miliband "will advocate for a diplomatic solution to the (Hormuz) crisis that restores full navigational rights and freedoms".
He will also stress "how Iranian tactics are being replicated across the region, with attacks on Saudi Arabia further destabilising the region and increasing pressure on vital waterways and global chokepoints, such as Bab al-Mandeb and the Suez Canal", it added.
France confirmed the talks on "the Iranian crisis in its various ramifications", hailing it as a first "in this format... against a backdrop of extreme instability and uncertainty in the region."
The meeting will aim to "strengthen coordination between Europeans and Middle Eastern countries in the face of crises that we did not choose and that affect us all," the French foreign ministry said.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan is hosting the meeting, as Turkey steps up efforts to strengthen its regional role, including through the Mecca Defence Alliance, a defence pact launched with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia in August.
Turkey has said the pact is not aimed at any specific country and remains open to others, including Egypt.
Cairo has yet to decide whether to join the alliance. On Wednesday, President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said Egypt would "defend Saudi territory" and would not take part in any attack on Yemen.
Intensifying attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis have forced Saudi Arabia to close its main airport and postpone a major investment conference, while a maritime blockade has threatened oil exports from the world's largest crude exporter.
Riyadh has since secured backing from its allies.
During a surprise visit on Wednesday, President Emmanuel Macron said French forces would help protect the Red Sea oil terminal of Yanbu.
Britain announced a day earlier that it would deploy fighter jets to help Saudi Arabia defend against the growing threat of Houthi attacks.
'Chance of success'
Fidan praised regional cooperation Friday, saying, "Lasting solutions cannot be imposed from outside."
During the talks, Fidan is expected to stress that regional security requires countries in the region to "assume responsibility" and that Turkey prioritises cooperation mechanisms based on "regional ownership", according to Turkish officials.
He is also expected to say that "existing disputes should not be allowed to feed one another, conflicts should not be allowed to spread to new areas, and regional tensions should not be allowed to turn into broader instability".
Fidan is expected to call for increased international pressure on Israel over settlement expansion and what Ankara describes as "settler terrorism".
He will also reiterate Turkey's support for Saudi Arabia's security in the face of Houthi attacks and underline the need to safeguard freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandeb.
The Black Sea is also expected to feature prominently, with Fidan highlighting Turkey's efforts to prevent the Russia-Ukraine war from spilling into the region.

articles.title: Putin slams European warmongering as ‘political schizophrenia’ (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Putin slams European warmongering as ‘political schizophrenia’ (VIDEO)
Repeated claims by European officials that Russia poses a threat of war to their countries amount to “political schizophrenia,” President Vladimir Putin has said.
He made the remarks on Thursday while speaking to Russian journalist Pavel Zarubin after participating in the Union of Theatre Workers congress at the Bolshoi Theater in Moscow.
Putin strongly denied the repeated allegations that Moscow has been gearing up for war with Europe in any fashion, dismissing them as a part of the ongoing “anti-Russian campaign” on the continent. 
“They now go so far as to constantly speak of a ‘Russian threat’ and even discuss preparations for a war with Russia – which, in my view, amounts to a kind of political schizophrenia. But I hope that it will pass,” Putin stated.
The Ukraine conflict has clearly demonstrated that Russia cannot be defeated on the battlefield, the president argued, adding that the idea of inflicting a “strategic defeat” on the country was “simply not realistic.” Putin expressed hope that those still entertaining such a scenario would “come to recognize the realities of modern life.” 
“They will hopefully realize that it is better to live in harmony with Russia – a path that truly serves the interests of their own peoples. If you look at the political processes currently underway in Europe, it becomes evident that the European peoples have no desire to go to war with Russia,” the president stated.
In fact, Russia does not want to fight Ukraine either, Putin said, pointing at the shared past and the longstanding ties between Russians and Ukrainians. Still, Kiev itself chose war in 2014, when it opted to fight the people of then-Ukrainian Donbass, who had rejected the Maidan coup, the president said, adding that Ukraine has also rejected Moscow’s repeated attempts to mediate that conflict.
“If the current Ukrainian leadership wishes to fight, then let them fight. But why do they expect everyone else to foot the bill and supply them with weapons? I suppose they have their arguments – likely rooted in past promises of help. But it seems that the ‘help’ was intended to last until the very last Ukrainian,” Putin said.
The Russian president also touched upon the territorial issues between Moscow and Kiev, pointing out that the loss of formerly Ukrainian regions should not be treated as such, since they were never Ukrainian in the first place.
“It is not their territory, it is a part of historic Russia,” he stressed, adding that local residents voted to secede from Ukraine and reunify with Russia.
Russia remains ready to resolve the Ukraine conflict through diplomacy, Putin said, reiterating Moscow’s willingness to resume trilateral talks with Washington and Kiev.
“The purpose of these negotiations will be to discuss how to ensure the security of both Ukraine and Russia following the conclusion of peace agreements, specifically, definitive, long-term agreements, rather than a mere temporary cessation of hostilities,” the president said, adding that the discussions should involve a wider all-European security architecture.
Moscow announced it was ready to resume the trilateral talks following Putin’s meeting with US special envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg on Wednesday. Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov subsequently said the next round could take place in Abu Dhabi around mid-November.

articles.title: Britain must outproduce its adversaries, says Streeting
articles.body:
Britain must be able to manufacture critical defence components at home in sufficient quantities, increase production and replenish stockpiles when threats increase, and sustain its armed forces through a prolonged conflict, according to the Defence Secretary.
Wes Streeting was speaking at the official opening of the UK Gun Hall at Telford, the Rheinmetall facility that returns large-calibre weapon production to Britain.
He said: “But those armaments do not get produced by waving a magic wand. Nor in the event that this country finds itself in a war fighting state, can that capability and capacity in industry be conjured up.”
He said: “To make sure we can deter and, if necessary, defeat, our adversaries, Britain must have the capacity to manufacture critical defence components at home and in sufficient quantities. We must have the capacity to increase production and replenish stockpiles when threats increase. We must have robust supply chains to back them up, and we must have the wider industrial resilience to sustain our armed forces through prolonged conflict.”
On the balance between technology and mass, Streeting said: “Despite the advent of drones and data of AI and autonomy, it is not enough to simply out-innovate those who would wish us harm, though we must. We must also outproduce them too, because advantage increasingly belongs to those who can manufacture at scale and field capability fastest.”
He referred to remarks made at the event by the Chief of the General Staff, saying: “As the Chief of the General Staff just said, we are making daily discoveries about the changing nature of the conflict in Ukraine. Yet, as was also pointed out, for all of the technological advances we’re seeing on the battlefield, what you might call more traditional weaponry still has its place in modern warfare.”
On the facility itself, Streeting said: “And so what we’re opening the doors to here is more than a manufacturing plant. We’re opening the doors to something much greater and much more ambitious. And that is readiness and resilience. For the first time in decades, artillery gun barrels will be produced in Britain. They will be made using British steel from Forgemasters. As we’ve heard, their production will create one hundred jobs here and hundreds more across the supply chain right across the country.”
He added: “Gun Hall will also support the next generation of equipment for the British Army, helping to deliver the firepower that will make us warfighting ready by 2030.”
The Telford facility will manufacture 120mm and 155mm weapon systems, including those supporting Challenger 3 and future artillery platforms, with a peak capacity of up to 245 barrels a year across both calibres and more than fifty breeches annually. Rheinmetall turned an empty building into an operational manufacturing capability in eight months, with breech production beginning in May and barrel production in June.
Streeting also set out the case for combining domestic production with allied integration, saying: “And this factory is a reminder that stronger domestic industries and deeper allied integration are not contradictory. Done right, each strengthens the other.”
He said: “The defining test is not where every single component of a piece of kit or equipment was made. It is whether our combined industrial base can give our armed forces what they need, when they need it, because an alliance that can mobilise its armies must also be able to mobilise its industries.”
The Defence Committee reported this week that general munition stocks are among the capabilities European NATO members lack in sufficient numbers, and that the unglamorous enablers of warfighting capacity including logistics networks and ammunition stockpiles have withered through decades of underinvestment across the alliance.
Ministers confirmed in Parliament this month that there is no current requirement to procure new 105mm barrels for the L118 Light Gun, and consequently no plans to restore domestic production of that calibre. This publication has reported on the wider effort to rebuild Britain’s ability to manufacture large calibre guns.

articles.title: Japanese troops test-fire air defense missiles at New Mexico range
articles.body:
- Japan’s Ground Self-Defense Force has been conducting live-fire air defense training since July 2026 at Shizunai, Rokkasho and other ranges in Japan.
- At McGregor Range in New Mexico, its Type 03 medium-range missile units are firing alongside Japan Air Self-Defense Force Patriot units.
Japan’s Ground Self-Defense Force has been carrying out live-fire air defense training since July 2026 at ranges in northern Japan and in the United States, where its medium-range missile units are firing alongside Japan Air Self-Defense Force Patriot batteries at McGregor Range in New Mexico.
The Ground Self-Defense Force, Japan’s army, said on X that units at home are firing at the Shizunai range in Hokkaido, the Rokkasho range in Aomori Prefecture and other sites. The training covers the force’s layered short-range air defense weapons: the Type 81 short-range surface-to-air missile, the Type 93 close-range surface-to-air missile and the Type 87 self-propelled anti-aircraft gun.
Those systems cover the lowest and closest layers of Japan’s ground-based air defense.
The Type 93 mounts short-range missiles on a light utility vehicle, while the tracked Type 87 carries twin 35 mm cannons to engage aircraft, helicopters and other low-flying targets at close range.
In New Mexico, the Ground Self-Defense Force is firing the Type 03 medium-range surface-to-air missile, known in Japan as Chu-SAM, in coordination with Air Self-Defense Force Patriot units. Built by Mitsubishi Electric, the Type 03 replaced the U.S.-designed HAWK missiles Japan had used since 1965 and has a range of about 50 km (31 miles), with the system designed to hit aircraft, air-to-surface missiles and cruise missiles directly.
The Type 03 has a long history at the New Mexico range. Japanese forces fired it in a live training exercise for the first time at McGregor Range in late 2006, after six earlier test launches at nearby White Sands Missile Range.
McGregor Range, part of the Fort Bliss training complex, offers the open airspace and distances needed for live missile firings that are difficult to arrange in Japan. The Air Self-Defense Force has held annual Patriot live-fire training there since 1963, and recent iterations have included combined live firing with Ground Self-Defense Force anti-aircraft units, bilateral firing with U.S. Army Patriot units and, in 2025, counter-drone training.
Pairing the two services lets Japan’s army and air force practice defending against air threats as a single network, with the medium-range Type 03 and the longer-range Patriot covering different layers of the airspace.
The Ground Self-Defense Force said it will continue firing training at home and abroad to further strengthen its air defense capabilities.

articles.title: Austria foreign ministry expels four Russian diplomats from Vienna over suspected espionage
articles.body:
Austria's foreign ministry said on Friday it was expelling four Vienna-based Russian diplomats over "activities incompatible with their diplomatic status," a term usually used for spying.
"Based on findings by the Austrian security authorities, the Austrian foreign ministry has taken measures against four Russian diplomats in Vienna," it said in a statement, adding that they had been declared personae non gratae and ordered to leave the country.
Three of them worked at Russia's embassy to Austria and one at the Russian delegation to the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) on military security and arms control, the ministry said.
Russia will respond to the expulsions, Russian news agencies cited a foreign ministry official as saying soon after Friday's announcement, without elaborating.
The move brings to 18 the number of Russian diplomats Austria has expelled since 2020. While Austria is a neutral country, politically its governments have sided with Ukraine since Russia launched its all-out invasion in 2022.
While Austria does not usually comment on the specifics of such expulsions, during the last round in May, when it expelled three Russian diplomats, it said it was because of an "antenna forest" on the roofs of Russian diplomatic buildings that could be used for spying.
Vienna is major diplomatic center for OSCE, UN organizations
Vienna is a major diplomatic center, hosting the OSCE and United Nations organizations such as the International Atomic Energy Agency.
Larger countries like Russia and the United States often have separate ambassadors to Austria, the OSCE, and UN organizations, each running an embassy or mission.
Vienna, which was divided into Allied sectors after World War Two, has long had a reputation as a den of spies. The large diplomatic presence offers the opportunity to station intelligence agents there under cover of diplomatic immunity.

articles.title: EU will ‘inevitably’ restore economic ties with Russia – Putin aide (VIDEOS)
articles.body:
EU will ‘inevitably’ restore economic ties with Russia – Putin aide (VIDEOS)
European countries will inevitably resume economic cooperation with Russia, following Washington’s lead, Russian presidential aide Kirill Dmitriev has predicted. Politicians who continue to blame Moscow for their domestic problems rather than address them risk losing power, he warned.
Dmitriev, who also heads Russia’s sovereign wealth fund, made the remarks on Thursday at the 19th Verona Eurasian Economic Forum in Istanbul.
The Russian official hailed Trump’s readiness to restore dialogue with Russia and reverse a “very dangerous situation where top nuclear powers don’t communicate.”
He said the recent Russia-US diesel deal could lay the groundwork for broader cooperation between Moscow and Washington, potentially paving the way for further agreements on energy and fertilizers. Under the deal, Russia has agreed to release more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to US and global markets, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and additional supplies thereafter.
Commenting on Europe’s problems, including high energy costs and mass migration, Dmitriev accused European politicians of “using Russia as a boogeyman” to distract from more fundamental issues, warning that they have come to believe their own narratives and are unwilling to correct their mistakes.
However, Dmitriev argued that attitudes within the EU were beginning to shift, with more voices calling for renewed dialogue with Moscow. “Cooperation with Russia economically will be inevitable,” he said, adding that “as soon as we do more deals with the US, European companies” will want a piece of the action, too.
Dmitriev suggested that European politicians who stubbornly refuse to change course, such as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, would be replaced by “new forces” that are more realistic and pragmatic. He also predicted that the Nord Stream 1 and Nord Stream 2 gas pipelines, three of whose four strings were damaged by underwater explosions in September 2022, would “inevitably” resume operation “at some point in the future” for economic reasons.
“Once people start paying double, triple their bills of energy in Europe, the resumption of energy supplies from Russia is absolutely inevitable and politicians who refuse that will lose in any way possible,” Dmitriev argued.
“Once people are rational, once people stop reading fake stories in the media, once they stop sort of living in this matrix of fake narratives…, they’ll understand that only through dialogue, through cooperation, through working together, we can go forward successfully.”
Dmitriev also argued that many of today’s “great leaders,” including Russian President Vladimir Putin, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, prioritize national sovereignty over what he described as the “failed policy of globalism.”

articles.title: Saudi-led coalition intercepts Houthi ballistic missile targeting southwestern Saudi Arabia
articles.body:
Sahin Demir
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
The Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognized government said Thursday that it intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by Yemen’s Houthi group toward Najran in southwestern Saudi Arabia, near the border with Yemen.
Coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki said in a post on US social media company X that the missile was intercepted and destroyed after being launched toward Najran.
No casualties or damage were immediately reported.
In a separate statement, the coalition rejected Houthi claims about Saudi threats to target tribal and civilian gatherings in Yemen, describing the allegations as baseless and fabricated.
The coalition said the claims were part of what it called continued attempts to mislead public opinion, divert attention from the Houthis’ actions and practices, and involve Yemeni tribes in the group’s conflicts.
It stressed that Yemeni tribes remain an integral part of Yemen’s social and historical fabric and “serve as a bridge of brotherhood” between the Saudi and Yemeni peoples.
The coalition also reaffirmed Saudi Arabia’s commitment to Yemen’s security and stability and its opposition to attempts to exploit Yemeni tribes or drag them into conflicts.
The incident comes amid renewed military escalation between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition since July, with both sides exchanging attacks.
Earlier Thursday, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree claimed that the group had launched four missile and drone attacks against targets in Saudi Arabia over the previous 48 hours, including facilities in Riyadh, Dammam, Yanbu and Abha.
Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognized government against the Houthis since March 2015.

articles.title: Future talks on Ukraine and "political schizophrenia" in Europe: statements by Putin
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. Russia is not preparing for war with Europe, while the statements about the "threat of the war" with Russia are "political schizophrenia," President Vladimir Putin told Vesti journalist Pavel Zarubin.
In its contacts with Washington, Moscow reached an agreement to be ready to resume Russia-US-Ukraine talks that will focus on ensuring the security of Russia and Ukraine once peace is achieved.
Moreover, Putin spoke about the situation in the Ukrainian army: the number of deserters there is half a million, if not more. The motivation of Ukrainian citizens is declining.
TASS has gathered the main statements by the Russian leader.
"Political schizophrenia" in Europe
Russia is not preparing for war with Europe, the president said.
"If we look at the political processes underway in Europe, we will see that the peoples of Europe don’t want to fight with Russia. I would like us to be heard: we don’t want [to fight with Europe] either," he said.
EU statements about the "threat of the war" with Russia are "political schizophrenia": "This [Donbass and Novorossiya’s decision to reunify with Russia], as is well known, became the reason or the pretext for some of our ill-wishers abroad - primarily, as we see today, in European countries - to launch an anti-Russian campaign in all directions. Now they are also constantly talking about a threat from Russia and the start of preparations for the war with Russia, which, in my view, is a kind of political schizophrenia," Putin said.
"This too shall pass," he added.
Ukrainian conflict and trilateral talks
Russia called for a peaceful solution to the Ukraine conflict from the very beginning, "from the very first days, in 2014," offering its help to facilitate a negotiated solution, but Kiev resorted to force instead.
The Russian leader also mentioned the Minsk agreements. "We have always sought to ensure that they could reach an agreement with the part of Ukraine that does not accept coup d'etat. However, they refused to do so," he said.
For its part, Russia does not want war, it’s Kiev that wants to go to war with Moscow, "let it have it," Putin stressed.
That said, the war against Russia in order to weaken it cannot be Ukraine’s national idea. "Certain countries of Europe, for example, or from other global regions want to wage war against Russia in order to weaken it. But is this really a national idea for Ukraine itself?" the president asked rhetorically.
Defeating Russia on the battlefield is impossible, and inflicting a strategic defeat on it is improbable, Putin emphasized, adding that it is "better to live in friendship" with Russia: "I think people who have sought to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia - and, unfortunately, such people still exist today - will come to terms with reality and understand that it is better to live in friendship with Russia. This is in the interests of their nations."
Regarding trilateral talks on Ukraine, Russia has reached an agreement with the US to be ready to resume them. They will focus on ensuring security of both Russia and Ukraine once peace is achieved, Putin stated.
According to the president, US Special Presidential Envoy Steve Witkoff said at the October 21 meeting that, when discussing issues related to ensuring "the future security of both Ukraine and Russia, it will be surely necessary to address the European security architecture as well." "Basically, I agree with that," Putin added.
Prior to the start of the Russia-US-Ukraine talks scheduled for November, Moscow will be monitoring the situation "in the coming days."
Russia remains ready to make agreements and seek solutions to the situation surrounding Ukraine, Putin said, adding that Russia has always called for settling the conflict peacefully. However, if Kiev wants a different solution to the conflict, that is its will. Moscow will continue the special military operation and achieve all its goals through it, the president noted.
Loss of motivation among Ukrainians and 500,000 deserters in Ukrainian army
Ukrainian citizens are being picked up off the streets like stray dogs and forcibly conscripted, which results in lower motivation among Ukrainians. "This is leading to severe consequences as troops' motivation declines. Yes, there are still formations made up of motivated nationalists. There are some. But it’s not always them fighting on the frontline. Those who have been forcibly rounded up are being thrown onto the frontline," Putin said.
The president pointed to the fact that the Kiev regime and its Western sponsors are treating Ukrainian citizens as expendable. "They [in the West] have always said they are ready to fight until the last Ukrainian is standing. And what about the Ukrainian authorities and their attitude to their own people? Do they share the approach of those abroad who want to fight with us and treat Ukrainians as expendable? They are their fellow citizens, after all," Putin noted.
Meanwhile about 500,000 servicemen have already deserted from the Ukrainian armed forces, but the real figure may be even higher, the Russian leader added. "Well, the figures are almost official: [there are] half a million deserters. Officially, over 300,000 criminal cases have been initiated, but in reality - and they are already talking about this almost publicly as well - it is 500,000, half a million," he said.
On territories lost by Ukraine
The lands lost by Kiev are not Ukrainian territory, those are historically Russian lands. Putin believes it is inappropriate for Kiev to speak of any territorial losses after Donbass and Novorossiya residents voted to reunite with Russia.
"The people who live there voted for, first, state independence, and, second - I would like to point out - for reunification with Russia," the Russian leader stated. "This is why I think it’s inappropriate to speak of any territorial losses. Still, it’s a debatable issue, and debates can go on indefinitely," he added.
Russians and Ukrainians genetically one people
Russians and Ukrainians are not merely close, they are genetically one people, Putin stressed. That said, the head of state expressed respect for the fact that a political division of the broader Russian nation occurred historically.
"Someone has a different opinion, fine," he admitted. "Alright, we agree, this is how the history of Russia shaped out, and such are the realities of today. But everything is negotiable."

Iran will not reopen the Strait of Hormuz or return to negotiations until seven new conditions presented through intermediaries are met, said Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council.
“We will not return to the diplomacy of the past, yet we are not abandoning diplomacy altogether,” Rezaei said in a statement carried by ISNA news agency, adding that Tehran was “no longer interested in agreements whose only guarantee was political good faith.”

articles.title: Oil hits five-month high amid fears US will renew strikes on Iran
articles.body:
Oil has hit its highest level in more than five months as fears of fresh escalation in the Middle East conflict grip the energy markets.
Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, rose by 1% on Friday morning to $114.72 a barrel – its highest level since May.
The increase came after Tehran said it would strike oil facilities, undersea cables, datacentres and AI facilities in the Gulf region if a new US-Israeli attack was launched against Iran.
“Widespread reports that the US is considering renewed military strikes on Iran after the midterm elections rather than pursuing a diplomatic route was enough for the price to pop, after what many had considered would be a brief conflict is now in its eighth month,” said Richard Hunter at the broker Interactive Investor.
Oil had traded at about $72 a barrel back in February, before the Iran war began, but soared to $126 a barrel by the end of April.
Tensions in the region have been rising this week; Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps claimed to have struck four commercial ships in the strait of Hormuz on Wednesday. The US state department ordered some diplomats and the families of US government employees to leave Saudi Arabia, which has faced continued attacks from Houthi rebels in Yemen.
Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategists at the broker Wealth Club, said fears were rising that American and Israeli forces would be ordered to launch strikes on Iran’s energy infrastructure after the US elections on 3 November.
“At the same time, the attacks on Saudi Arabia’s facilities by Houthi rebels have intensified this week, and for ships attempting to cross the strait of Hormuz, it’s still a dangerous journey, with projectiles still being fired,” she said.
Streeter said Ukraine’s bombardment of Russian diesel refineries was also adding to supply concerns.

articles.title: Putin reaffirms Russia’s readiness to resume trilateral peace talks on Ukraine war
articles.body:
Burç Eruygur
23 October 2026•Update: 23 October 2026
Russian President Vladimir Putin reaffirmed Moscow’s readiness to resume trilateral peace talks on the war in Ukraine, saying the negotiations would focus on ways to ensure postwar security for both sides.
In an interview Thursday with Vesti news outlet, Putin discussed Russia’s negotiations with representatives of US President Donald Trump’s administration, recalling an agreement to resume trilateral talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine.
“The objective of these talks will be to discuss how to ensure the security of both Ukraine and Russia following the conclusion of peace agreements – specifically definitive, long-term agreements rather than merely a temporary cessation of hostilities,” he added.
Putin said they are ready to resume contacts to achieve this goal, noting that during their meeting in St. Petersburg on Wednesday, US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff stressed they must address the broader architecture of European security if they are to discuss future security arrangements for both Russia and Ukraine.
“I agree with that too. Well, let’s see how the situation develops over the coming days,” he added.
His remarks came a day after he hosted the US envoy at St. Petersburg’s Constantine Palace, after which Russian presidential aide Yury Ushakov told reporters that Putin conveyed Moscow’s readiness "in principle" to resume trilateral peace negotiations on Ukraine in November.
“Our president informed Steve Witkoff that we are, in principle, prepared to resume the aforementioned trilateral negotiations around the 10th of November,” Ushakov said following the talks, adding that Moscow’s readiness for trilateral negotiations particularly concerned the issue of building a post-war “security system” for Russia and Ukraine.
Separately, Witkoff announced on US social media platform X that he and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner held “constructive” discussions in St. Petersburg and the Norwegian capital Oslo, the latter of which took place Tuesday, and that these discussions will continue with trilateral talks “at the technical level.”
Russia and Ukraine last held US-mediated peace negotiations earlier this year, with three rounds of talks on Jan. 23-24, Feb. 4-5, and Feb. 17-18. The first two were held in Abu Dhabi, while the third took place in Geneva.
Commenting on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's remarks on Wednesday to Fox News on being open to freezing the front line in Ukraine in an effort to end the war, Putin argued that it seemed "inappropriate" to describe the issue as amounting to “any territorial losses.”
"To begin with, my view on this matter is that this is not their territory. It is the territory of historical Russia," Putin said, further arguing that the residents of these territories "chose" to be part of Russia through referendums in September 2022.
The referendums were widely condemned as illegal by the international community.

On the U.S.-Iran dispute, he is expected to stress that diplomacy and dialogue offer the only lasting solution, warning that military action risks widening the conflict.
He will also emphasize the need to ensure freedom of navigation through the Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb straits.

articles.title: Trump claims Iran is 'making up fake hits' on tankers to drive up oil costs ahead of elections
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump accused Iran of fabricating reports of attacks on oil tankers and naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz to drive up oil prices ahead of the November midterm elections in a Truth Social post on Thursday.
“Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of Oil prior to the US Midterm Election,” Trump wrote.
“They are even making up fake hits, mines, and everything else, because more Oil is coming through the Hormuz Strait now than it did even prior to the beginning of the Conflict."
Trump also accused Iran's regime of killing protesters and reaffirmed his commitment that Iran would not be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon.
The post came as Trump continued to defend the US campaign against Iran and its impact on American energy prices ahead of the November 3 congressional elections.
Speaking to reporters at the White House before departing for a campaign rally in Iowa on Thursday, Trump said the war had come at a political cost but maintained that preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon was necessary.
“There’s a price to pay, which I knew immediately when I did it,” Trump said. “But we can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.”
Asked about public reaction to the war, Trump said Americans had mixed feelings about the campaign.
“In one way they love it because I’m doing what should have been done by other presidents. In another way, maybe they don’t,” he said.
Trump also suggested the US could carry out further military action against Iran, saying Washington had already inflicted significant damage but “may do it a little bit further.”
Tensions surrounding the Strait of Hormuz
The Strait of Hormuz has remained a key point of contention during the conflict, as attacks on commercial shipping and restrictions on maritime traffic have threatened the flow of oil through the waterway.
Iran's IRGC Navy reported that four oil tankers were hit and caught fire overnight, according to the Iranian state media IRNA. The incidents added to concerns about a renewed escalation in the region and the potential effects on global energy supplies.
Trump, meanwhile, argued that oil was moving through the strait at a higher rate than before the war, despite what he described as fabricated reports of attacks.

articles.title: The US is letting a convicted Bolsonaro spy chief stay in Florida. Brazil wants answers.
articles.body:
LATIN AMERICA
The US is letting a convicted Bolsonaro spy chief stay in Florida. Brazil wants answers.
Former intelligence director Alexandre Ramagem fled after his conviction for trying to overturn Brazil’s 2022 election. Authorities there are investigating whether he had help.
It was an unusual request. On Nov. 21, 2025, the owner of an apartment in a luxury complex north of Miami drafted a message asking the building’s management to remove his houseguest immediately, the same man his family had vouched for in writing two months earlier.
The guest was Alexandre Ramagem, a Brazilian congressman and spy chief under former President Jair Bolsonaro. In September, Ramagem had fled Brazil days before being sentenced to 16 years in prison for his role in Bolsonaro’s plot to overturn the 2022 election. The message was drafted the same day the country’s Supreme Court ordered Ramagem’s arrest and two days after a Brazilian news site published photos of him and his wife strolling through the Miami complex in workout clothes, causing outrage back home.
The message was written in the name of Rodrigo Martins de Mello, who was convicted of running an illegal mining operation on protected indigenous land in the Amazon. De Mello claimed he had only just learned from the press that his guest was barred from leaving Brazil. “In order to avoid any issues for the condominium or for myself, I hereby request that the condominium IMMEDIATELY notify him of my directive for him to leave my property,” De Mello wrote.
But Brazilian investigators say De Mello and his family knew all along that Ramagem was on the run. Messages, notes and photos from confidential records reviewed by ICIJ and Agência Pública show that they housed Ramagem for months, vouched for him to building management and sought paperwork needed to obtain a Florida driver’s license for him, including a lease drafted to make it look as if he was renting a room.
The records, obtained by Agência Pública and shared with ICIJ, are part of a sealed investigation by Brazil’s Federal Police into Ramagem’s escape, conducted within the Supreme Court’s sprawling investigation into the plot to overturn the 2022 election.
The Federal Police had an officer in Miami working alongside the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. With the officer’s help, the confidential records say, ICE found Ramagem, who Brazil wants to extradite, and arrested him in Orlando in April for overstaying his visa.
Then the case took an unexpected turn. After two days, ICE released Ramagem while he pursues asylum. Days after that, the State Department told the Brazilian officer who had helped locate Ramagem to leave the country, accusing him of trying to extend “political witch hunts” to U.S. soil.
There’s a lot of favoritism and discrimination and double standards in the immigration system now. — Tessa Petit, Florida Immigrant Coalition
Six months later, Ramagem remains free in Florida. Officials in Brazil declined to say whether the U.S. has responded to its extradition request.
Ramagem’s treatment stands in sharp contrast with that of thousands of asylum seekers who have been deported since Trump returned to office.
“There’s a lot of favoritism and discrimination and double standards in the immigration system now,” said Tessa Petit, executive director of the advocacy group Florida Immigrant Coalition.
Most immigrants don’t get the break Ramagem got, said Petit, who fled Haiti in 2001 and was initially denied asylum before winning her case in immigration court. “The reality for the majority of people is: Be vigilant, be careful, and hopefully be lucky enough to not get picked up.”
Neither Ramagem nor the De Mellos responded to requests for comment for this story.
In Brazil and in the U.S., supporters of Jair Bolsonaro, a close ally of President Donald Trump, praised the White House for Ramagem’s release.
On Oct. 25, Brazilians will vote in a presidential runoff in which the narrow front-runner, Flavio Bolsonaro, a son of the former leader, has promised pardons for everyone convicted in the coup plot.
‘An illegal alien from Brazil’
Ramagem’s only known run-in with U.S. authorities came after months of living in plain sight in Florida and publicly accusing the Brazilian government of persecution.
Ramagem entered the country legally on Sept. 11, 2025, with permission to stay six months, the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, told ICIJ. But he “chose to illegally overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws,” the agency said, calling him, “an illegal alien from Brazil.”
Brazil filed a formal extradition request with the State Department on Dec. 30, 2025, according to Brazil’s Justice Ministry.
On April 13, police detained Ramagem in Orlando during a traffic stop and handed him over to ICE. Two days later, ICE let him go, pending the outcome of his removal proceedings, the agency said. He paid no bail, according to Paulo Figueiredo, a U.S.-based Brazilian commentator and Bolsonaro ally who said his immigration consulting firm has assisted Ramagem. Detained immigrants usually must go before a judge to seek release, but ICIJ found no record of Ramagem petitioning the court for his freedom. ICE told Brazilian police at the time that the release was an administrative decision and that Ramagem could remain free while his asylum claim was reviewed, according to Brazilian media reports citing police sources.
Ramagem’s allies credited Washington for his release. “Thank you, President Trump and everyone in the administration,” Figueiredo wrote on X. Eduardo Bolsonaro, another son of the former president, thanked Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Sóstenes Cavalcante, a leader of Bolsonaro’s party in Brazil’s Congress, said Rubio had helped speed up the release, which he said would otherwise have taken at least two weeks.
RAMAGEM IS FREE AND BACK HOME!
My deepest thanks go to Donald Trump @realDonaldTrump and @SecRubio for their sensitivity and attention in addressing the case of this true national hero, who, even under persecution, has never wavered.
Alexandre Ramagem deserves asylum in the land of freedom, alongside his courageous wife – tireless in fighting for his liberty – and their beautiful daughters.
— Eduardo Bolsonaro🇧🇷 (@BolsonaroSP) April 15, 2026
Ramagem himself suggested he had U.S. government support. In November, after the publication of photos showing him in Miami, Brazil’s Supreme Court had ordered his arrest. The next day, in a livestreamed interview, Ramagem said he was safe in the United States “with the consent and knowledge of the American government.”
On April 20, five days after Ramagem’s release from immigration custody, the State Department asked Marcelo Ivo de Carvalho, the Brazilian Federal Police liaison officer posted in Miami to work with ICE, to leave the country. “No foreigner gets to game our immigration system to both circumvent formal extradition requests and extend political witch hunts into U.S. territory,” the department’s Bureau of Western Hemisphere Affairs wrote on X.
The government in Brasília retaliated and suspended the duties of a U.S. immigration agent posted there, who then left the country on April 22. In a statement, the Foreign Ministry said the U.S. had failed to consult Brazil first, as the two countries’ agreement on police liaisons requires, and ignored “good diplomatic practice of dialogue between friendly nations, such as Brazil and the United States, over more than 200 years of relations.”
Neither the State Department nor the White House responded to multiple requests for comment. In its statement, DHS did not explain why Ramagem was released, saying only that he was freed “pending the outcome of his removal proceedings” and “will receive due process.” It added that a pending application “does NOT confer any type of legal status in the United States” and that “illegal aliens are not welcome in our country.”
The handling of Ramagem’s case stands out among those of hundreds of thousands of asylum seekers in the United States.
Since Trump returned to office, immigration judges have ordered more than 440,000 asylum seekers removed, more than in the previous eight years combined, according to a recent Washington Post analysis. Release from ICE detention has also become the exception. By late 2025, ICE was deporting more than 14 people directly from detention for every one it released to await a hearing, according to the American Immigration Council, an advocacy group that analyzed ICE data. In December, the administration paused decisions on all asylum applications pending with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.
Ramagem’s release was not just an immigration matter. A career federal police officer, he headed Bolsonaro’s security when Bolsonaro was president-elect. He was then appointed head of Brazil’s intelligence agency, becoming part of the inner circle of a president whose prosecution the Trump administration has criticized. In July 2025, Trump imposed 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods, calling Bolsonaro’s trial a “witch hunt,” and his administration sanctioned Alexandre de Moraes, the Supreme Court justice who oversees the coup case against Bolsonaro and Ramagem. A White House executive order that month accused Brazilian officials of politically persecuting the former president.
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a leftist who defeated Bolsonaro in the 2022 election, has accused Washington of meddling in Brazil’s affairs. Last month, Lula used his speech at the United Nations General Assembly to warn against foreign interference in the upcoming election there.
Investigation in Brazil
According to the confidential records, Federal Police investigators in Brazil believe De Mello’s November plea for his condo to expel Ramagem was drafted as a “precaution,” after the press linked the family’s apartment to Ramagem’s escape.
But the note didn’t spare the De Mello family. In December, on orders from Brazil’s Supreme Court, the Federal Police arrested Rodrigo’s son Celso, on suspicion of helping Ramagem flee. In a statement, the family said Celso is innocent. Moraes also ordered Rodrigo’s arrest, and Rodrigo remains a fugitive. (This week, another Supreme Court justice rejected Rodrigo’s request to overturn the order, the Brazilian news site Amado Mundo reported.)
Ramagem has denied that Celso helped him. In an Instagram post after the ICE arrest, he said he didn’t know “a certain” Priscila or Celso. “They arrested a young man, a kid, who only met me when I was already in the U.S.,” he said. “In fact, this young man is American.”
Celso now wears an ankle monitor while the investigation, which is under seal, continues.
The confidential records show the De Mello family’s alleged involvement began early. Since June 2025, Ramagem, then a member of Brazil’s Congress, had been barred by court order from leaving Brazil and was required to surrender all his passports while on trial. He was charged with using the country’s intelligence agency to help Bolsonaro discredit its voting system. (Ramagem’s defense told the Supreme Court that the evidence against him was “extremely timid.”)
On Sept. 9, while on medical leave from Congress, he crossed from the northern town of Bonfim into Lethem, Guyana. A photo found on the phone of Priscila Freitas de Mello, then Rodrigo’s wife, shows him there the next day, smiling, at what appears to be an immigration post in Guyana. Brazilian Federal Police investigators say Rodrigo took the picture, according to the records.
On Sept. 11, as Brazil’s Supreme Court convicted him, Ramagem flew to the United States on a diplomatic passport that he had kept.
On Sept. 15, Celso messaged Priscila asking for a utility bill in his father’s name so Ramagem could apply for a Florida driver’s license, the confidential records show.
“Hi Pri, good evening,” Celso wrote to his stepmother. “Can you send me a bill for your apartment in my dad’s name? Water, electricity, phone, internet… We’re going to try to get Alexandre’s driver’s license tomorrow at the DMV.” He had drafted a lease, Celso wrote, to make it look as if Ramagem “had rented the room.”
“Let me see,” Priscila replied.
Two days later, Priscila wrote to the condominium’s management asking for a new gate access card. “Since we are traveling, we won’t be able to pick it up,” she said. “Therefore, we authorize a friend of ours, Alexandre Rodrigues Ramagem, to collect the new card on our behalf.” Celso also contested parking fines Ramagem had run up at the complex, the records show.
On Nov. 17, Ramagem’s spouse and daughters joined him in the apartment, according to the wife’s social media posts.
Investigators in Brazil allege in the confidential records that the De Mello family played a key role in keeping Ramagem hidden, both by housing him and by helping him deceive U.S. authorities with false documents. It is unclear whether a driver’s license was ultimately issued.
Rodrigo, the De Mello patriarch, has denied helping Ramagem escape. In November, he called the escape story a “fallacious narrative” meant to persecute the right, and said that when Ramagem was with him, he faced no conviction or legal impediment to leaving Brazil. The two men appeared together publicly in March 2025, when Rodrigo posted a photo of Ramagem’s visit to Boa Vista, De Mello’s longtime base in the state of Roraima, near the Guyana border, calling him “a great ally” of Bolsonaro.
Gold and politics
The De Mellos’ ties to Florida go back decades.
Rodrigo de Mello registered to vote in Florida in 1997, according to voter records from the Miami-Dade Department of Elections obtained by ICIJ, an action that requires attesting to U.S. citizenship. Celso is a U.S. citizen and a registered Florida voter.
Public records link Rodrigo, Celso and Celso’s mother to several companies registered in Florida, including a yacht-charter business and a freight company tied to the Sole Mia apartment where the family hosted Ramagem. Rodrigo and Celso’s mother also owned a home in Boca Raton.
Known in Brazil as Rodrigo Cataratas, De Mello ran what Brazilian federal prosecutors describe as a criminal organization mining illegally in the Yanomami Indigenous territory, a vast stretch of rainforest along the Venezuelan border. In January 2023, Brazil’s government declared a public health emergency in the territory, citing malnutrition and disease among the Yanomami and mercury contamination linked to illegal mining.
In February, a federal court in Roraima sentenced Rodrigo to 16 years and 7 months in prison for leading the enterprise, which prosecutors say extracted gold and cassiterite, a tin ore used in electronics, from the territory with the support of a fleet of helicopters. Celso was sentenced to eight years for managing the operation’s finances and logistics. Both remain free pending appeal.
Rodrigo has made no secret of his politics. His Instagram profile picture shows him alongside Jair Bolsonaro, with the words “anistia já,” or “amnesty now.” In 2020, the Bolsonaro government sent Congress a bill to allow mining on Indigenous lands. His administration also reportedly had a poor track record of acting on complaints about deforestation tied to illegal mining.
Rodrigo has also sought public office himself. He ran unsuccessfully for Congress in 2022 with Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party, and, before his conviction, he announced a run for the Senate with the right-wing Democratic Renewal Party. In October 2023, weeks after a federal court made him a defendant for the fifth time in cases tied to the Yanomami territory, he announced he was relocating to Guyana, where he opened a gold-mining company, according to Brazilian media.
Pardon promises
From Florida, the Bolsonaro camp has kept fighting for power in Brazil. Eduardo Bolsonaro, who moved to the United States in 2025, lobbied the Trump administration to pressure Brazilian authorities over his father’s prosecution. Washington later sanctioned Moraes, the Supreme Court judge in charge of the criminal trial against Bolsonaro, and imposed tariffs on Brazilian goods, both measures Eduardo had publicly sought.
Brazilian prosecutors argued that Eduardo’s campaign amounted to coercion, saying he had used his political position to pressure the justices and officials handling his father’s case. This month, the Supreme Court ordered his arrest to serve a sentence of four years and two months, which is unlikely to happen as long as he remains in the United States.
Earlier this month, Ramagem’s wife, Rebeca, ran for Congress in Rio de Janeiro, the state her husband represented as a lawmaker, saying she was running in his place. She campaigned without leaving Florida. Her campaign workers carried life-size cardboard cutouts of her and her husband through the streets of Rio, according to newspaper Metrópoles. The cutouts popped up at the launch of Flávio Bolsonaro’s presidential campaign on Copacabana beach, where Flavio’s wife, Fernanda Bolsonaro, posed with them. At the event, Flávio displayed a T-shirt that read “Bring the Ramagem family back, do justice!”
Rebeca Ramagem received 1.5 million reais, about $275,000, in public party funds for her campaign, Agência Pública found. She lost the election on Oct. 4.
On Oct. 25, Brazilians will choose between Flávio Bolsonaro and Lula. Flávio, who won the first round and holds a narrow lead in the polls, has promised a “broad, general and unrestricted” amnesty for his father and others convicted in the coup plot.
While Brazil’s extradition request awaits a response from the U.S., Ramagem lives in a lakefront house in Orlando, about half an hour from Disney World, and co-hosts a YouTube show with a pro-Bolsonaro blogger who is also wanted in Brazil.
“Of course, I wasn’t going to stay in Brazil,” Ramagem said in a livestream, adding that he didn’t want his daughters to see him arrested. “I don’t know how long it will take,” he said, “but we’re going to turn Brazil around.”
Natalia Viana and Ethel Rudnitzki from Agência Pública, and Gerardo Reyes from N+ Univision Investiga contributed to this report.

articles.title: Czech firm develops patrol drone armed with interceptors
articles.body:
- Czech company KBP International unveiled GRYF, a long-endurance drone that carries interceptor drones or small missiles to counter hostile UAVs.
- GRYF can fly up to 12 hours with a 500 km range and a 50 kg payload across four hardpoints.
Czech company KBP International has unveiled GRYF, a long-endurance drone designed to carry interceptor drones and small missiles aloft so it can hunt down hostile unmanned aircraft, presenting the aircraft on Oct. 21, 2026, at the Future Forces Forum in Prague in the presence of Czech President Petr Pavel.
GRYF works as a flying weapons carrier: the aircraft itself is not the weapon but a platform that patrols for long periods and brings counter-drone effectors into position, where they can be launched at incoming threats. KBP said the platform is built for long-endurance operations as a carrier for interceptors and mission-specific payloads, as part of a layered approach to air defense.
The company told visitors at the unveiling that GRYF can stay airborne for up to 12 hours and has an operational range of 500 km (310 miles). The drone is powered by a four-cylinder piston engine, cruises at 150 km/h (93 mph) and has four hardpoints with a maximum payload of 50 kg (110 pounds), Militarnyi reported from the show floor, enough to carry a lightweight interceptor missile of around 5 kg (11 pounds) on each hardpoint.
KBP displayed GRYF in two configurations at the Prague exhibition, one armed with small interceptor missiles and the other with interceptor drones, showing that the same airframe can switch between effectors depending on the mission.
The company presented the aircraft as an answer to the demand for effective and affordable ways to protect airspace against drones. Using a cheap, long-endurance carrier to loiter near a protected area and release small interceptors is intended to engage drones at a lower cost per shot than firing conventional ground-based air defense missiles, while extending coverage beyond the reach of fixed sites.
GRYF draws on KBP Group’s more than 30 years of experience building composite aircraft structures. The group combines in-house design and production of unmanned aircraft, piston aero engines and advanced manufacturing, and it says it can handle the full process from initial design and prototyping to series production of key drone components. KBP is expanding its facilities to support both its own products and work with other European aerospace and defense manufacturers.
The company used the same Prague exhibition to show two one-way attack drones, the piston-powered TARON and the jet-powered SABRE. KBP International was also a main partner of this year’s Future Forces Forum, the 16th edition of the event, which brought together around 530 exhibitors and official delegations from 65 countries at the PVA Expo Prague exhibition grounds.
KBP’s announcement focused on the platform’s design and role, with production timelines and first customers for GRYF still to be announced as the company moves the new carrier beyond its public debut.

articles.title: Blaze that killed 4 on Canadian military base sparked on grenade launcher range
articles.body:
Blaze that killed 4 soldiers on Canadian military base sparked on grenade launcher range, officials say
A blaze that killed four soldiers and injured several dozen more on a military base in the Canadian province of Alberta last week broke out on a grenade launcher range during training exercises, officials said Thursday.
The fire sparked Oct. 17 on the automatic grenade launcher range of Canadian Forces Base Wainwright "during routine military training activities," Brig. Gen. Vanessa Hanrahan, the Canadian Forces Provost Marshal, said in a statement Thursday.
The fire initially remained within the range's "Permanent Danger Area 2," which limited the ability of firefighters to battle it directly, Hanrahan said, and crews were forced to monitor it throughout the day instead.
However, it then spread due to "a subsequent change in wind direction and velocity" that "significantly increased the fire's intensity and rate of speed which led to these tragic events," Hanrahan added.
There was no indication that natural gas infrastructure was involved in the fire, she disclosed.
The fire killed four soldiers and injured 39 others. The Canadian Armed Forces said Thursday that 27 soldiers remained hospitalized, while 12 had been treated and released.
Earlier this week, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said that the fire was "driven by ferocious winds" and "jumped nearly a kilometer in less than a minute to where soldiers were gathered."
Carney said that 50 investigators had been brought in to probe the fire. The Canadian Forces National Investigation Service was leading the investigation, with support from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
"We will get the answers to what caused this terrible tragedy, as expeditiously and transparently as necessary," Carney told reporters Monday.
The fire overtook soldiers from the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry, and Army reservists conducting live-fire training.
Maj. Gen. Wade Rutland said Sunday that military officials knew about the fire for hours but believed it was contained and allowed training to continue before winds suddenly shifted.
About 84 soldiers from Charlie Company were training at two locations, one for throwing grenades and another for practicing attacks on simulated enemy positions. The fire swept into the second area.
Carney said the soldiers were preparing for a mission next spring to reinforce Canadian troops serving with NATO in Latvia.
Rutland said investigators would examine whether winds drove the flames toward the soldiers or whether the fire spread unseen through vegetation. They will also examine whether military safety procedures need to change, he said.
The military identified those killed as Sgt. Morgan Wong of Edmonton; Pvt. Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Saskatchewan; Pvt. Aidan Goulding of North Vancouver, British Columbia; and Pvt. Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, British Columbia.

articles.title: Why the US can’t cut India off from Russian crude
articles.body:
Why the US can’t cut India off from Russian crude
India will not cut off Russian crude supplies even if the current US push for it to take in more Venezuelan oil to cool global fuel prices masks the larger goal of weakening New Delhi’s energy ties with Moscow.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in Mumbai on Tuesday that India diversifying its energy supplies is a “smart thing to do.”
Some analysts see a hidden geopolitical and economic goal behind those words and Rubio’s push for Indian conglomerate Reliance to buy and refine more Venezuelan oil.
“A key US goal is to weaken the Indo-Russian relationship by steering India farther away from Russian crude,” geopolitical analyst Brahma Chellaney posted on X on Thursday.
“Washington’s underlying diplomatic objective is to get India to substitute Russian oil with US crude and US-controlled Venezuelan oil.”
Washington imposed an additional 25% tariff on Indian goods in August 2025 to pressure New Delhi over its Russian oil purchases, arguing that Moscow’s energy revenues were helping finance its military in the Ukraine conflict. The penalty was withdrawn in February this year.
Last week, US President Donald Trump also waived separate sanctions and steep tariffs targeting major buyers of Russian energy under a recently passed law, citing ongoing US efforts to negotiate an end to the Ukraine conflict.
During his Indian tour, Rubio sought to get India to buy more U.S. energy as well as more oil from Venezuela, whose export revenues are directly deposited into an account controlled by the U.S. Treasury, with Washington determining when, how much and for what purposes the funds are released. Rubio wants the world’s largest oil-refining complex in Jamnagar to process more Venezuelan crude. Washington appears not to be content with India’s rapid emergence since May as a top global buyer of U.S.-sourced and U.S.-controlled energy supplies. The U.S. has already become India’s largest supplier of both liquefied natural gas (LNG) and liquefied petroleum gas (LPG). At Washington’s urging, India has also become the largest destination for Venezuelan oil exports. A key U.S. goal is to weaken the Indo-Russian relationship by steering India farther away from Russian crude. While Rubio framed India’s efforts to diversify its energy portfolio as a “smart thing to do,” Washington’s underlying diplomatic objective is to get India to substitute Russian oil with U.S. crude and U.S.-controlled Venezuelan oil.
— Dr. Brahma Chellaney (@Chellaney) October 21, 2026
“What America is trying to do is gain greater control over the international oil market,” Jindal School of International Affairs adjunct professor and former Jawaharlal Nehru University professor, Anuradha Mitra Chenoy, told RT.
“India will continue purchasing Russian oil,” she added.
Russia remains India’s largest oil supplier amid global energy disruptions. Russian crude made up more than half of India’s oil purchases in July, although the share fell to 33.5% in September as Middle Eastern supplies recovered and competition from China intensified, Reuters reported.
The scale of available supplies in the global market makes replacing Russian oil difficult, especially for a country such as India, Chenoy explained. The world’s most populous nation imports more than 85% of its energy.
“Venezuela alone cannot provide all the alternatives,” Chenoy said. “There are only a limited number of major sources available internationally, and Russia remains one of the most important suppliers.”
Venezuela produced approximately 1.16 million barrels per day of crude in September, compared with Russia’s 8.43 million, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA). India’s Russian imports alone exceeded Venezuela’s entire output that month.
India, looking to widen its crude basket amid the global uncertainty, has already expanded Venezuelan purchases substantially. New Delhi’s Venezuelan imports surged from $255 million in all of FY2026 ended March, to $3.6 billion in the April-August period this year, data shared by the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI) think tank showed.
India is a fast-growing major economy and one of the few bright spots amid the macroeconomic headwinds blowing across the world. The IMF forecasts it to grow at 7% this year and next.
Sustaining that growth depends heavily on the availability and affordability of energy, Chenoy pointed out. “India cannot simply abandon Russian oil because Washington wants it to.”
Why Venezuelan oil cannot easily replace Russian crude
Venezuela’s Merey grade is being offered at around $25 per barrel below benchmark Brent, but that cost advantage disappears when the $35-a-barrel freight to India’s west coast is added in, energy analyst Natalia Katona told the Indian Express.
The discounts on Russian crude have also narrowed and freight costs risen, making its delivered price comparable to some Middle Eastern grades, particularly Iraqi oil, reports said.
Still, it would be tough for Venezuelan oil to compete with Russian crude, let alone replace it for Indian buyers, because of the limited production, higher cost, and specialized equipment needed to refine the heavy grade
Reliance’s Jamnagar complex, which can process around 1.4 million barrels daily, is among the refineries equipped to handle the Venezuelan grade.
From the American perspective, Merey has one advantage that likely prompted Rubio to rush to India amid higher fuel prices back home: it can produce a higher volume of diesel.
However, that is not a great reason for India to replace Russian crude with Merey.
The sanctions that were levied on Venezuela by Washington – before US forces kidnapped Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January – had forced India to stop buying oil from the South American country and froze billions of dollars in Indian investments in oil fields there.
“India must consider whether another shift in US policy could again put its investments and earnings at risk,” said GTRI founder Ajay Srivastava.
The time-tested and deep friendship between India and Russia must also be considered.
Chenoy pointed out that there is a broad consensus across Indian society and politics about the friendship with Russia. “India’s relationship with Russia has been among its most stable international relationships for decades,” she said.
Any designs the US has on India-Russia ties are bound to fail because of that one reason alone.
